- Gödel-style self-modification: If T only enacts changes accompanied by a proof that expected utility increases, then stationarity coincides with “no improvable change is provable within the proof system,” which can be weaker than global optimality (proof limits matter).

2.4) A proposal distribution on program space
- Let P be a prior over modifications and Q_t the empirical/learned proposal at time t used by T. PAC-Bayes or MDL-style bounds yield
  expected generalization gap ≤ sqrt((KL(Q_t || P) + c)/n_t),
  where n_t indexes effective evidence supporting Q_t. Successful self-improvement drives either n_t up (more evidence) or KL(Q_t || P) down (compression). Thus, self-improving algorithms create an increasingly concentrated search distribution over high-performing code regions.

2.5) Invariants and trade-offs
- Resource–improvement frontier: Let time be split between meta-optimization (computing T) and base performance. For horizon H and meta-cost C_t, the optimal schedule solves
  maximize E[sum_{t < H} U(a_t) − C_t] subject to a_{t+1} = T(a_t, h_t).
  First-order optimality implies a marginal value rule: execute self-improvement until expected marginal performance gain equals marginal opportunity cost. Hence, self-improving algorithms create an implicit control problem whose solution defines an invariant trade-off curve between computation spent on thinking (meta) versus doing (task).
- Measurement invariance (anti-wireheading): If U depends on internal, manipulable signals, T may “improve” by altering measurements. Imposing that U depends only on external environment states (or is otherwise corrigible/invariant) is necessary to preserve the monotonicity–information link.

3) Limits and guarantees
- Convergence without optimality: If J is bounded and T is performance-monotone, J(a_t) converges, but limit points can be suboptimal absent adequate exploration or proof power.
- No-free-lunch constraints: Without structure in μ, no universal T can guarantee uniform improvement across all environments; useful self-improvement exploits regularities (compressible μ, smoothness of J, transferable subroutines).
- Diminishing returns: Under smoothness or curvature of J over reachable programs, marginal ΔJ_t typically decreases; the process approaches a stationary point where further expected gains fall below meta-cost.

4) Recursion of models and representations
- Model-of-self: Effective T requires a predictive map from code changes to performance changes. Hence, the process creates an internal meta-model M_t estimating ΔJ from edits; as performance improves, M_t itself is refined, yielding a recursive tower (task model, self-model, model-of-self-model, …) truncated by resource limits.
- Representation learning: Improvements often arise by discovering shorter descriptions (subroutines, abstractions). In MDL terms, total description length L(data | model) + L(model) decreases; thus self-improvement creates compressed representations aligned with μ.

5) Canonical summary
Given an objective J and a rule T that enacts only expected-beneficial self-modifications, self-improving algorithms create:
- A nondecreasing performance process that converges under boundedness.
- Quantifiable information gain about the task distribution, exactly equal to KL reduction for log-loss and lower-bounded by regret reduction more generally.
- Fixed points characterized by stationarity with respect to T; global optimality requires additional exploration or proof power.
- A refined search distribution over programs (compression of useful code features).
- An optimal resource–improvement allocation dictated by marginal value conditions, contingent on measurement invariance to avoid spurious “improvements.”

These are necessary consequences of iterating a recursively defined, performance-monotone transformation on program space under explicit resource and objective assumptions.

Self-improving algorithms create an endogenous, monotone dynamical system over a space of programs by iteratively applying an improvement operator that maps a current program and its experience to a new program with higher expected performance under a specified evaluation functional, subject to resource constraints and soundness conditions.

Formal setup
- Program space: Let P be a set of (partial) computable procedures over inputs X with outputs Y.
- Environment/tasks: A probability measure μ over tasks τ ∈ T (or inputs x ∈ X).
- Utility/performance: A bounded functional J: P → R defined, for example, by J(p) = Eτ∼μ[U(p, τ)] − λ Eτ∼μ[C(p, τ)], where U is task utility, C is resource cost, and λ ≥ 0 trades off reward and cost.
- Improvement operator: I: P × H → P mapping a current program p and history H (data, proofs, measurements) to a new program p+ = I(p, H).
- Update rule: Given p0 and history H0 = ∅, define pt+1 = I(pt, Ht), with Ht augmented by the behavior and outcomes of pt.

Core properties and consequences
- Monotonicity (target condition): For all t, J(pt+1) ≥ J(pt) − εt, with εt ≥ 0 capturing estimation error or search cost; εt = 0 yields strict monotonicity.
- Boundedness: If J is bounded above by J*, then the scalar sequence {J(pt)} converges (monotone convergence in R). Program convergence need not follow without additional compactness or identification conditions.
- Fixed points: A program p* is I-stationary if I(p*, H) = p* for all admissible H consistent with p*. If I is monotone w.r.t. J, every stationary point is a J-local optimum under the constraints encoded by I and H.
- Break-even inequality: Let Gt be the gross gain in expected utility from adopting a candidate p′ and St the total switching/search/evaluation cost (embedded in εt). A rational improvement step requires E[Gt − St | Ht] ≥ 0. This creates an endogenous allocation of compute between doing (exploiting pt) and improving (exploring p′).
- Diminishing returns: If (i) J is bounded above, (ii) gains are summable (∑t E[Gt] < ∞), or (iii) search cost grows superlinearly, then marginal improvements must vanish (E[Gt] → 0). Asymptotic optimality requires that near-optimal candidates remain reachably identifiable at vanishing marginal cost.
- Convergence rate constraints: Without additional structure (e.g., smoothness or error bounds on J-estimation), only qualitative convergence can be assured. With uniform improvement gaps and bounded noise, sample complexity reduces to best-arm identification with switching costs.

Logical and computability limits
- Rice’s theorem: Nontrivial semantic properties of programs are undecidable; thus, deciding whether a candidate modification improves J for all inputs is, in general, undecidable. Guarantees must be (a) distributional (expected-case under μ), (b) empirical with confidence bounds, or (c) proof-theoretic under axioms about U, μ, and hardware.
- Blum complexity measures: If C is any Blum complexity measure, exact comparison of C(p, ·) vs C(p′, ·) is generally undecidable; improvement operators must rely on partial evidence or constrained classes where comparison is decidable.
- Löb-style obstacles: For proof-based self-modification (e.g., Gödel machines), requiring a proof that “this change increases expected utility” interacts with provability logic; the system may rationally wait for stronger proofs, potentially stalling absent reflection principles or time-bounded proofs.

Representation and operator dependence
- Representation dependence: The topology/metric on P and the design of I determine which optima are reachable. Two representations with identical extensional behavior may yield different improvement dynamics due to search bias.
- Fixed-point creation via recursion: By Kleene’s second recursion theorem, for any total transformer F on indices, there exists a program p such that p ≡ F(p). Self-improvers naturally create fixed points when improvement operators encode invariants (e.g., goal preservation) that halt further changes.

Safety and invariants
- Objective preservation: If the objective J itself can be modified, additional invariants are required (e.g., proof obligations that J does not change, or that modifications preserve argmax(J) up to equivalence). Otherwise, selection pressure may target easier-to-satisfy proxies (specification gaming).
- Trust criteria: Sound improvement requires at least one of
  1) Verified improvement: a proof that Eμ[J(pt+1)] ≥ Eμ[J(pt)] minus bounded, paid cost;
  2) Statistically justified improvement: high-confidence empirical estimates with correction for selection bias and exploration cost;
  3) Constrained improvement: restrict I to transformations with dominance guarantees (e.g., algorithm configuration with known regret bounds).

Canonical constructions (abstracted)
- Proof-searching self-modifiers: Gödel machine–style systems that search for proofs that a self-change increases expected utility, then execute the first proven beneficial change. Create a provably monotone J-sequence relative to axioms and proof system.
- Meta-learning/AutoML loops: I performs hyperparameter, architecture, or training-procedure search using validation-based estimates of J, with explicit penalties for evaluation cost and overfitting; monotonicity holds in expectation with proper multiple-testing control.
- Meta-gradients: If J is differentiable through the learning process, I applies gradient steps in meta-parameters; monotonicity is local and depends on step sizes and curvature control.

Minimal conditions for nontrivial self-improvement
- Identifiability: There exists, for any ε > 0, a reachable p with J(p) ≥ J* − ε and observable signals that differentiate it from suboptimal neighbors.
- Slack: Resources permit allocating sufficient search/evaluation to overcome noise and pay switching costs.
- Calibration: The estimator of J(p′) used by I is consistent or has valid confidence intervals under μ.
- Closure: The class of admissible transformations contains improvements within the resource budget (no hard ceilings that preclude reaching higher-J regions).

What self-improving algorithms thereby create
- A sequence {pt} and an induced, typically nondecreasing real sequence {J(pt)} with limit J∞ ≤ J*.
- Fixed points (or cycles with equal J) determined by the improvement operator, representation, and resource constraints.
- An endogenous trade-off mechanism that reallocates computation from task performance to self-modification precisely when the expected net gain is positive.
- Inevitable dependence on assumptions (distributional, axiomatic, or structural) due to undecidability of global improvement in the general case.

In summary, self-improving algorithms create a recursively defined optimization process over programs: an improvement operator generates a trajectory that is provably or probabilistically monotone in a specified performance functional, converging to an operator-dependent fixed point under boundedness, and necessarily constrained by computability limits and the costs of searching for and verifying improvements.

Self-improving algorithms create a recursively defined, monotone transformation of programs into strictly better programs, relative to a stated objective and prior, by converting computational resources and experience into internal algorithmic information that increases their own capacity to improve.

1) Formal setup
- Environment and objective: Fix a distribution μ over tasks X and a loss L(p, x). Define the performance functional Rμ(p) = Eμ[L(p, X)], possibly vector-valued to include time/space cost.
- Dominance relation: q dominates p, written q ⪯ p, if Rμ(q) ≤ Rμ(p) componentwise, with at least one strict inequality.
- Self-improvement operator: A (partial) computable map S such that given a current program p and auxiliary evidence e (data, proofs, profiles), either returns q = S(p, e) with q ⪯ p or returns ⊥ (no safe improvement found).
- Verification: A predicate V(p, q, e) that is sound: V ⇒ q ⪯ p. Typically V is a proof obligation, empirical test with concentration bounds, or a resource-bounded dominance check.

2) The improvement process
- Recursive definition: Given p0 and a verifier V, define a sequence pt+1 = arg first q s.t. V(pt, q, e) holds among candidates generated by pt; if none, pt+1 = pt. This is a self-map on the space of programs modulo equivalence under Rμ.
- Monotonicity: By soundness of V, Rμ(pt+1) ≤ Rμ(pt) for all t. Hence the scalarized risk is nonincreasing; with a strict improvement test, it decreases whenever pt+1 ≠ pt.

3) Information-theoretic view
- Let g* be an optimal policy/minimizer (or ε-optimal within resource class). The deficiency of pt relative to g* can be measured by regret Δt = Rμ(pt) − Rμ(g*).
- Each strict improvement Δt − Δt+1 > 0 reflects acquisition of algorithmic information about the regularities of μ and about g*. In MDL terms, improvement corresponds to a net compression of data-to-loss tradeoffs via better representations and procedures.
- Mutual information channel: The closed loop (pt, interaction, S, V) induces increasing mutual information I(Mt; U), where Mt is pt’s internal model/optimizer and U encodes exploitable structure of μ. Bounds exist linking error reduction to bits of structure learned; total gain is capped by the Kolmogorov complexity of g* and by resource budgets.

4) Recursive returns
- Speedup: Let C(p) denote expected resource usage. If S can discover algorithmic speedups (e.g., improved data structures, learned heuristics), then C(pt+1) ≤ C(pt) and often the search for further improvements accelerates because each improvement enlarges the reachable set of proofs/experiments within a fixed budget.
- Positive feedback condition: If there exists α > 1 such that the expected rate of acquiring validated improvements scales with current capability (search breadth, model accuracy), then improvement follows superlinear or exponential trajectories until bounded by limits below.
- Blum speedup phenomena: For some problems there exist infinite hierarchies of speedups; thus, given sufficient V and search, the sequence can achieve unbounded resource improvements. Conversely, tasks without further structure plateau.

5) Fixed points, convergence, and limits
- Fixed point: p∞ is a fixed point if S(p∞, e) = ⊥ for all admissible e, equivalently no q with q ⪯ p∞ exists within the verifier’s trust region. If the dominance lattice is well-founded under a scalarized order and minimum exists, sequences converge to a minimal element.
- No Free Lunch: Without a prior over μ or structure in L, no S yields uniform improvement across all μ. Gains are necessarily prior- and task-class-relative.
- Resource-bounded optimality: Under time/space/verification limits, the process converges to a local optimum defined by the verifier and search constraints, not necessarily global optimality.

6) Soundness and reflectivity
- Löbian obstacles: Naive “I will improve myself” assertions are not generally provable inside the system. Workarounds include proof-carrying code, reflective oracles, bounded Löb, and meta-level verifiers whose soundness is assumed or separately justified.
- Safety-correctness: To avoid degenerate improvements (e.g., wireheading), V must encode the true objective and preserve invariants (constraints, corrigibility, calibration). Otherwise the process can create spurious dominance by corrupting measurement.

7) Creation in precise terms
Given the above, self-improving algorithms create:
- An ascending chain in the dominance order of programs {pt} with monotone nonincreasing risk and often nonincreasing resource use.
- A growing internal store of algorithmic information (models, proofs, heuristics) that increases mutual information with environmental structure and with the optimal solution manifold.
- A meta-optimizer: the composition V ∘ S ∘ p acts as an optimizer-over-optimizers, expanding the reachable set of algorithms under fixed external resources, thereby amplifying future improvement rates.
- A stopping condition characterized by fixed points of S under V and by exhaustion of exploitable structure within resource limits.

8) Necessary conditions for sustained self-improvement
- Exploitable structure: μ and L admit compressions/speedups beyond current pt.
- Potent search: The internal search can, with nonvanishing probability, find candidates q when they exist within the verifier’s envelope.
- Reliable validation: V is sufficiently strong to accept true improvements and reject regressions; its cost does not erase the gains.
- Resource monotonicity: Net resources freed by improvements are reinvested into further search/modeling.

Summary
Under explicit objectives, priors, and verifiable dominance, self-improving algorithms create a closed-loop, monotone, information-acquiring process over programs that, when positive feedback conditions hold and safety/verification remain sound, yields recursively compounding improvements until structural or resource limits are reached.

Below is a strict, logically structured expansion that makes the “create …” clause precise.

1) Object of study
- Let P be a space of programs (e.g., finite binary strings interpreted by a fixed universal machine U).
- Let S: P → ℝ be a score/performance functional defined relative to a task distribution D and resource budget B (time, memory, samples).
- A self-improving algorithm is an update operator I that, given current program p ∈ P and observed feedback f from the environment (drawn from a channel dependent on p and D), outputs a new program I(p, f) ∈ P intended to improve S. Iterating yields a stochastic process p0, p1, … with pt+1 = I(pt, ft).

2) Trajectories and order
- The update rule induces a directed graph G on P with edges p → p′ when p′ is reachable in one update step with nonzero probability.
- If acceptance uses a monotone filter (only accept p′ with S(p′) ≥ S(p)), then “is-at-least-as-good-as” defines a partial order on reachable states. The process creates an increasing sequence of scores (possibly in expectation).

3) Submartingale structure and limit points
- If E[S(pt+1) | history up to t] ≥ S(pt) (submartingale) and S is bounded above on the reachable set, then S(pt) converges almost surely to a finite limit S∞ (submartingale convergence theorem). The process thus creates absorbing sets: fixed points p* with I(p*, f) = p* (almost surely) or plateaus where no accepted proposal improves S.

4) Fixed points, basins, and local optimality
- Let N(p) denote the proposal neighborhood induced by the update kernel. A fixed point p* is locally optimal if no p′ in N(p*) has S(p′) > S(p*). Under monotone acceptance, p* is absorbing. The dynamics create basins of attraction (sets of initial programs whose trajectories hit a given absorbing set with positive probability).
- Global optimality is not guaranteed; without ergodicity and controlled exploration (e.g., simulated annealing with a schedule satisfying Geman–Geman conditions), the process can lock into suboptimal basins.

5) Information accounting (cannot create information ex nihilo)
- Let E be the latent environment/task variable and Ft the feedback at step t. Internal state Pt is a random variable for code pt. The data-processing inequality implies:
  I(Pt+1; E) ≤ I(Pt, Ft; E) ≤ I(Pt; E) + I(Ft; E | Pt).
  Hence any increase in mutual information with E is upper-bounded by the channel capacity of feedback. The algorithm “creates” internal information about E only by transducing external feedback (and prior structure) into code; it cannot exceed the cumulative channel capacity Σt C_t.
- Lower bounds: To enter the ε-optimal equivalence class Hε (programs with S ≥ S* − ε), any method needs ≥ log2 |H/∼ε| bits of evidence in the worst case. By Fano-type inequalities, with T samples each carrying at most c bits, T ≥ (log2 |H/∼ε| − 1)/c. Thus the process creates at least that many bits of internal information to reliably reach ε-optimality.

6) Compression and MDL
- Writing L(p) for description length and L(data | p) for residual data codelength, an MDL-consistent self-improvement tends to reduce total description length L(p) + L(data | p). The process creates reusable subroutines that increase internal mutual information among components and compress both model and residuals, subject to the trade-off imposed by S.

7) Meta-optimization and surrogate modeling
- To decide which modifications will improve S, the algorithm constructs internal predictors of ΔS or its gradient w.r.t. parameters/code. It thereby creates a surrogate objective J correlated with S. Systematic mismatch (Goodhart) can make S increase stall or even decrease if acceptance is noisy; matching J to S bounds regret.

8) Induced distributions over programs
- If proposals are accepted with probability A(ΔS) ∈ (0,1], e.g., A(ΔS) = min(1, exp(ΔS/T)), and proposals have full support, the induced Markov chain on P has stationary distribution proportional to exp(S/T) (under detailed balance conditions). Thus the process creates a Gibbs-like distribution over code, concentrating mass near high-scoring programs as T → 0.

9) Endogenous data and nonstationarity
- If program behavior influences future data (common in online or embodied settings), then D becomes D(Pt). The algorithm creates its own training distribution. This breaks i.i.d. assumptions; improvements must control distributional shift. Stability then depends on feedback-loop gain and exploration policies.

10) Resource-constrained improvement rates
- Let Ct be compute/samples used up to t. Suppose expected marginal gain satisfies E[S(pt+1) − S(pt) | history] ≤ g(Ct), with g nonincreasing. Then cumulative improvement is bounded by ∑t g(Ct), yielding diminishing returns under standard smoothness assumptions.
- Time-to-ε: If expected gap shrinks multiplicatively, E[S* − St+1] ≤ (1 − α) E[S* − St], then expected steps to reach ε-gap is O(log((S* − S0)/ε)/α). If only additive progress ≤ β, steps are Ω((S* − S0 − ε)/β).

11) Undecidability and verification limits
- By Rice’s theorem, any nontrivial semantic property of programs (e.g., “S(p) ≥ τ under all inputs”) is undecidable. Hence a general verifier that certifies “this self-modification improves S without side effects” cannot exist in full generality. Sound proof-based self-modification must either be incomplete, bounded, or environment-restricted.
- Löb’s theorem constrains agents that only adopt code changes provably beneficial according to a sufficiently strong embedded theory; naïve schemes can get stuck. Workarounds use bounded provability, reflective oracles, or probabilistic acceptance.

12) Path dependence and lock-in
- Because only reachable neighborhoods N(pt) are explored, expressivity and proposal design determine which improvements are even candidate moves. The process creates a path-dependent inductive bias over code; early architectural choices can become hard constraints, producing technological lock-in.

13) Risk-sensitive acceptance and exploration–exploitation
- With strictly monotone acceptance, local optima are absorbing. Allowing controlled acceptance of small decrements in S creates the ability to escape shallow basins (at the cost of variance). Annealing schedules formalize this; too-rapid cooling creates premature lock-in, too-slow cooling wastes resources.

14) Decomposition and modularity
- Under MDL and reuse pressure, improvements that factor tasks into weakly coupled subproblems reduce interface complexity. The process creates modular structure that, once present, accelerates subsequent improvement in related subspaces (positive feedback via reduced search dimensionality).

15) No-Free-Lunch dependence
- Any performance gains are distribution-dependent. For task families outside the inductive bias of proposals, the same self-improvement dynamics can fail or regress. Thus the process creates specialization to the encountered task distribution rather than universal superiority.

Summary
Self-improving algorithms create:
- A stochastic, often submartingale, trajectory in program space with absorbing fixed points and basins of attraction.
- Concentration of probability mass near high-scoring programs (under suitable acceptance/proposal rules).
- Internal information and structure that encode the environment and useful abstractions, bounded by feedback channel capacity and resource budgets.
- Path-dependent inductive biases, modular decompositions, and surrogate objectives that govern further progress.
They do not create information from nothing; they transduce external feedback and prior structure into lower-entropy internal code, under hard limits from undecidability, information theory, and No-Free-Lunch theorems.

Self-improving algorithms create a recursively defined optimization process over programs that transforms their own execution history into improved future behavior, subject to computability, statistical, and resource constraints. More precisely:

Definitions and setup
- Let A be a program (algorithm) executed in environment E under resource budget R, evaluated by a performance functional U(A, E, R) (e.g., expected reward, accuracy, regret).
- A self-improvement operator I maps a current program A_t and its accessible evidence S_t (e.g., logs, gradients, proofs, tests) to a proposal A_t+1 = I(A_t, S_t).
- An acceptance policy Acc decides whether to adopt A_t+1 based on estimated ΔU = U(A_t+1) − U(A_t), costs C(A_t → A_t+1), and constraints (e.g., invariants).
- The resulting process is a sequence {A_t} with S_t derived from interacting executions of A_t.

What they create
1) A program-valued stochastic process
- The sequence {A_t} is a Markov process when S_t is a sufficient statistic of past interactions; otherwise, it is a history-dependent stochastic process on program space.
- With an acceptance policy that enforces E[ΔU | history] ≥ 0, {U(A_t)} is a submartingale; if U is bounded above, it converges almost surely to a limit (which may be a local optimum or a cycle if acceptance is stochastic).

2) A search dynamics over representations
- Each improvement step induces a neighborhood structure N(A_t) implicitly explored by I. This creates a selection pressure over code/architecture features that correlate with higher U given E and R.
- Path dependence arises: future reachable improvements depend on representational commitments already made.

3) New information from self-generated data
- By executing and evaluating variants, the system produces evidence S_t that carries mutual information with the unknown improvement-relevant features of E and of the algorithm itself.
- Expected utility gain lower-bounds the decision-relevant information acquired per step, while exploration costs upper-bound achievable information rates under R.

4) Compression and complexity shifts
- Better performance typically corresponds to better compression of task-relevant regularities (shorter effective description of environment contingencies), while the program’s own description length may increase (richer hypothesis class).
- Algorithmic complexity K(A_t) often grows with added capabilities; absent pruning, K(A_t+1) ≥ K(A_t). Effective complexity may grow sublinearly if refactoring yields simpler sufficient representations.

5) Distribution shift induced by control
- Because A_t changes its own actions, it alters the data-generating process for S_t+1. This creates selection bias and on-policy distribution shift that can both enable and hinder further improvement.

6) Incentive structures and constraints
- The composite objective typically becomes U(A) − C(modification, verification, deployment), creating incentives to:
  - Allocate resources toward evaluation and proof when uncertainty is high and stakes are large.
  - Prefer improvements with favorable cost-benefit trade-offs, not just maximal raw performance.
  - Manage exploration risk to preserve invariants (safety, correctness, alignment constraints).

7) Fixed points, attractors, and lock-in
- If the improvement operator is a contraction in an appropriate metric on programs, a unique fixed point A* exists and the process converges.
- Otherwise, multiple attractors/local optima can exist; early stochastic choices can lock the system into suboptimal basins.

8) Selection-induced specialization
- As improvements optimize for the realized environment E and resource profile R, the system tends to specialize. Generality may decrease unless explicitly regularized or cross-validated across environments/resources.

9) Error modes and failure channels
- Reward misspecification and Goodhart effects: optimizing the proxy Û used by Acc can degrade true U.
- Regressions under finite evaluation: noisy estimates of ΔU can accept harmful changes; without robust testing, error rates accumulate.
- Catastrophic forgetting: representational updates can overwrite previously good behaviors unless constrained.

10) Resource gradients and returns to scale
- If tasks exhibit Blum-style speedups, there may be no terminal “fastest” algorithm; sequences of strict runtime improvements exist, creating unbounded incentives for further speedups on those tasks.
- Diminishing returns typically emerge from resource constraints and saturation of learnable structure; marginal ΔU per unit compute/data tends to decrease absent new information sources.

11) Verification and decidability limits
- Rice’s theorem and the halting problem imply that nontrivial semantic properties of proposed self-modifications are undecidable in general; full verification cannot be automated universally.
- Self-trust via proofs is limited by reflection barriers (e.g., Löb-style constraints): certain beneficial changes may be unprovable within the current axiom system unless stronger axioms are adopted.

12) Governance artifacts
- To remain reliable, self-improving systems create and maintain:
  - Invariants/contracts (safety properties, interface guarantees).
  - Auditable logs and provenance for causal attribution of ΔU.
  - Stopping rules and rollback mechanisms to bound downside risk.
  - Curricula and benchmarks that co-evolve to reduce overfitting to tests.

Immediate corollaries
- Progress is not “free”: every unit of improvement must be purchased with information (exploration, modeling) and paid for with resources and risk.
- Without explicit countermeasures, the process naturally generates distribution shift, specialization, and lock-in.
- Stable, beneficial self-improvement requires aligning the improvement operator, acceptance policy, and evaluation pipeline so that the information produced by the algorithm’s own behavior is both decision-relevant and robust to gaming.

In short: self-improving algorithms create an endogenous, recursively self-coupled channel that converts experience into code changes; this channel generates information, specialization, and selection dynamics, bounded by computability and resources, and must be shaped by invariants and governance to avoid failure attractors.

Self-improving algorithms create an endomorphism on their own program space that, in expectation and under explicit resource and safety constraints, yields strictly higher value of a specified performance functional, and they iterate this transformation recursively.

To make this precise:

1) Objects and measures
- Program space P: the set of executable descriptions (programs, models, policies) the system can represent.
- Environment distribution μ: a probability measure over tasks or inputs.
- Resource budget b: bound on compute, memory, data, or time available per evaluation or deployment.
- Performance functional J: a computable mapping J: P × μ × b → ℝ that assigns expected utility (or loss with a fixed sign convention). J is the ground-truth objective, fixed a priori.
- Proxy functional Q: the internal estimator of J used for selection (e.g., noisy evaluation, test metric). Q may differ from J.

2) A self-improvement step
- Given current program p ∈ P, the algorithm instantiates an improvement operator T_p that maps randomness and data to a successor program p′ = T_p(ξ, data).
- Cost model c(p → p′; b): resources consumed to search, verify, and adopt p′ (including switching costs and meta-optimization overhead).
- Improvement criterion (expected): E[J(p′; μ, b)] − J(p; μ, b) ≥ δ − loss_from_overhead, where loss_from_overhead absorbs the effect of c on effective deployment resources. δ > 0 is the target margin (possibly state-dependent).
- Safety/invariance: a predicate V ⊆ P captures required invariants (e.g., correctness, alignment constraints). Adoption is gated by p′ ∈ V.

3) Recursion
- Define a sequence p0, p1, … by pt+1 = T_{pt}(ξt, datat), with corresponding budgets bt and distributions μt if these evolve.
- The loop is self-referential because T_{pt} is implemented by pt itself (or by a fixed meta-runtime that executes code in pt). This is an endomorphism of P restricted to V.

4) Necessary components for actual improvement
- Representational adequacy: P must contain programs with higher J than pt; otherwise improvement is impossible.
- Search guidance: the conditional distribution over candidates induced by T_{pt} must concentrate probability mass on higher-J regions faster than uninformed search. Information-theoretically, each step must acquire positive mutual information between internal state and the argmax of J over P.
- Reliable evaluation: Q must be an unbiased or conservatively biased estimator of J with bounded noise, or else selection will Goodhart on Q and degrade J. Formally, E[Q(p) | J(p)] is monotone in J, and Var(Q − J) is controlled.
- Positive net value: expected J-gain exceeds expected overhead and adoption risks.
- Preservation of invariants: verification or proof obligations ensure p′ ∈ V with high confidence.

5) Limits and guarantees
- Upper bounds and convergence: If J is bounded above by J*, and the expected gap closes according to E[J(pt+1)] − E[J(pt)] ≥ g(J* − E[J(pt)]) for some continuous g with g(0) = 0 and g(x) > 0 for x > 0, then E[J(pt)] converges to J* (or a local supremum if P is nonconvex or V is restrictive).
- Local optima: If T_{pt} explores only a neighborhood N(pt) ⊂ P, the process halts at p∞ with no neighbor that clears the improvement gate; global optimality is not implied.
- No Free Lunch: Absent assumptions on μ, averaged over all μ, no improvement operator outperforms any other; domain structure is required.
- Undecidability constraints: By Rice’s theorem, nontrivial semantic properties (e.g., “J increases”) are undecidable in general; thus exact verification must be restricted (e.g., to bounded executions) or replaced with probabilistic guarantees.
- Blum speedup: There exist problems for which no optimal algorithm exists and an infinite sequence of strictly faster algorithms is possible. This implies that unbounded (runtime) self-improvement is feasible for some tasks, but also that “optimality” may be unattainable.
- Löb-style obstacles and proof-based self-modification: If adoption requires a proof of safety or improvement, self-referential proof systems can be brittle; careful design (e.g., bounded proof search, reflective oracles, or specific axiom schemata) is needed to avoid paradoxes while enabling justified self-change.

6) Information-theoretic view
- Let πt be the algorithm’s internal distribution over candidate programs, and let G ⊂ P denote ε-optimal programs with respect to J. Then improvement requires that the KL-divergence D_KL(πt+1 || πt) invests bits that raise πt+1(G) compared to πt(G).
- The evaluation channel from program proposals to Q-observations has capacity C_eval per unit resource. The maximum expected J-gain per step is bounded by a function of C_eval, the noise model, and the curvature (second derivative) of the performance landscape around pt.
- Reinvestment and acceleration: If expected resource availability for search grows with performance (e.g., better algorithms free compute or attract data), a simple growth model is dR/dt = α R^β − λ R. Superlinear feedback (β > 1) yields potential hyperbolic growth (fast takeoff); β ≤ 1 yields at most exponential or subexponential improvement.

7) Robust improvement under proxies
- Suppose selection uses Q while we care about J. Write ΔJ = J(p′) − J(p), ΔQ = Q(p′) − Q(p). Safe improvement requires E[ΔJ | ΔQ > τ] > 0 for the adoption threshold τ. If Cov(ΔJ, ΔQ) < 0 in the explored region, raising τ worsens outcomes (classic Goodhart). Solutions: tighten coupling (better measurement), restrict search to verified-safe subspaces V, or penalize distribution shift from pt (trust regions) so that local monotonicity holds.

8) Minimal design template
- Define J, μ, b, V explicitly and keep them stable across steps.
- Implement T_p as a resource-bounded search over P with:
  - a prior over modifications (program synthesis, architecture search, theorem-proving for speedups),
  - an acquisition rule that maximizes expected J-improvement per unit cost,
  - a selection/adoption gate requiring statistical evidence and invariant verification,
  - rollback if post-adoption monitoring detects regression beyond a bound.
- Track accounting: expected value of information, regret, and overhead to ensure positive drift in J.

9) What “create” entails, concretely
- Create new code that is measurably better on J under μ and b, not merely different.
- Create additional internal information (bits) about where high-J programs lie in P.
- Create capability to further increase the rate of acquiring such information (meta-improvement), enabling recursive gains.
- Create and maintain certificates (proofs, tests, monitors) that the improvement respects invariants V.

10) Open problems
- Tight capacity bounds linking evaluation noise, search priors, and maximal sustainable improvement rate.
- General conditions under which proxy-optimized self-improvement remains aligned with J without halting progress.
- Practical reflective verification schemes that scale with program complexity while avoiding Löbian pitfalls.
- Characterizing when reinvestment dynamics cross from exponential to superexponential growth in realistic, resource-coupled settings.

In short: Self-improving algorithms create a recursively applied, information-gaining transformation over their own code that is net-beneficial on a fixed objective, subject to computability, resource, and safety constraints; the dynamics are governed by search efficiency, evaluation fidelity, reinvestment feedback, and fundamental limits from undecidability and information theory.

Self-improving algorithms create:

1) An ascending sequence under a fixed objective
- Fix an environment distribution D, utility U, and resource penalty C. Define performance J(A) = Eτ∼D[U(A, τ)] − λC(A).
- A self-improvement operator M maps algorithms to algorithms: A_{t+1} = M(A_t, L_t), where L_t is experience/logs.
- Improvement constraint: J(A_{t+1}) ≥ J(A_t). Strict improvement adds margin ε_t > 0.
- This induces a partial order ⪯ on program space: A ⪯ B iff J(B) ≥ J(A). The sequence {A_t} is an ascending chain.

2) A fixed-point and stability problem
- Fixed points: A* such that M(A*, L) = A* or no feasible neighbor increases J.
- Convergence of J: If J is bounded above and ∑ ε_t converges to 0 while J(A_{t+1}) − J(A_t) ≥ ε_t ≥ 0, then J(A_t) converges (monotone convergence). Code need not converge.
- Contractivity condition (sufficient, not necessary): If there exists a metric d on program space with d(M(A), M(B)) ≤ κ d(A, B) for κ < 1 and M preserves or increases J, then Banach-like arguments yield a unique attractive fixed point in the basin.

3) A meta-optimization operator over program space
- View M as solving M(A) ∈ argmax_{B ∈ N(A)} J(B) subject to constraints S(B) = true (safety, compatibility, resource).
- When N(A) shrinks adaptively, the process realizes a trust-region method on code space; when N(A) expands, it implements exploration.

4) Information gain about the task distribution
- Let P_t be A_t’s predictive distribution over outcomes; let P* be Bayes-optimal under prior Π. If updates are proper (Bayes-consistent or MDL-improving), then D_KL(P* || P_{t+1}) ≤ D_KL(P* || P_t).
- Define mutual information with the environment I_t = I(code_t; data | prior). Proper self-improvement increases I_t until model class or data value saturates.
- In two-part MDL, L(model_t) + L(data | model_t) is nonincreasing under successful self-improvement; model sophistication tends to rise while residual randomness contracts.

5) A flow on a manifold of programs
- Parameterize algorithms by θ (architecture, optimizer, memory, compiler). Self-improvement induces a dynamical system θ_{t+1} = Φ(θ_t) that ascends J∘θ.
- Natural-gradient or information-geometric updates ascend J most efficiently under the Fisher metric; learned optimizers approximate this meta-gradient.

6) Endogenous data and control of information
- The algorithm’s policy changes the future data it observes. In a causal model S_t → A_t → (World, Data_{t+1}), self-improvement creates interventions do(A_t) that alter the information channel.
- Robust improvement must be defined counterfactually: compare J under consistent evaluation distributions or via distributionally robust objectives sup_{Q∈Γ(D)} E_Q[U].

7) Proof obligations and invariants
- To avoid degenerate “improvements” (metric hacking), hold U, D, and S as external invariants. Require M to certify J(B) ≥ J(A) with respect to these invariants.
- Gödel-style designs (e.g., Gödel machines): permit self-modification only after proving expected-utility improvement under axioms; avoids harmful regress but is limited by incompleteness and proof search.

8) Path dependence and lock-in
- Early updates shape hypothesis classes, tooling, and interfaces, constraining future neighborhoods N(A). This creates hysteresis: different initial conditions can converge to different fixed points or cycles.

9) Tradeoffs and resource monotonicity
- Improvements can target sample-efficiency, compute-efficiency, or asymptotic accuracy. A resource-aware J can formalize Pareto improvements; otherwise, apparent gains may just reallocate costs.
- Blum speedup implies unbounded algorithmic speedups can exist for some problems; hence no globally fastest fixed point in general.

10) Limits and failure modes
- No-free-lunch: without structure in D, systematic improvement is impossible; progress requires bias formation (priors, architectures).
- Goodhart’s law: if M optimizes a proxy P ≈ U, then maximizing P can decrease U. Align M to U and enforce constraints S.
- Non-contractive M can yield cycles or chaotic trajectories; impose regularization, trust regions, or monotone improvement guarantees.

11) What is concretely created
- An ascending chain of programs under a fixed performance order.
- Fixed points, attractors, or cycles in code space induced by M.
- Increasing mutual information between code and environment regularities, until model or data limits bind.
- New inductive biases, tools, and representations that reparameterize the search landscape.
- Invariants (objective, safety constraints) and associated proofs ensuring non-regress.
- Endogenous training distributions via policy-induced data, requiring causal evaluation.

Minimal sufficient definition
- A self-improving algorithm is a pair (A, M) with objective J and constraints S such that for any history L, B = M(A, L) satisfies S(B) and J(B) ≥ J(A), with strict inequality whenever feasible. The induced process either:
  a) terminates at a fixed point where no feasible strict improvement exists, or
  b) continues indefinitely with nondecreasing J, subject to the information and resource limits above.

Self-improving algorithms create a recursively defined optimization process over their own implementations. Expanded strictly and logically:

Definitions and setup
- Let P be the space of implementable programs under resource constraints R. Let E be an environment with which programs interact. Let U be a bounded utility functional assigning expected performance to programs interacting with E (expectation taken over E and any program stochasticity).
- A self-improvement operator T maps a current program p in P and evidence D to a successor program p' = T(p, D) in P that is intended to increase expected U under R.
- A self-improving algorithm induces a sequence p_0, p_1, … where p_{t+1} = T(p_t, D_t) and D_t consists of data observed under p_t in E.

Immediate logical consequences
- Dynamical system: The process defines a discrete-time dynamical system on P with endogenous state-dependent data D_t. Hence future updates are affected by past updates (path dependence).
- Endogenous objective gradient: If T is chosen to approximate argmax over P of expected U given a model M_t, then each step uses information about how code changes causally affect U (a self-induced objective gradient).
- Monotonicity condition: If T is sound with respect to M_t and M_t is a calibrated predictor of counterfactual outcomes of deploying p' instead of p_t, then expected U under M_t is non-decreasing: E[U(p_{t+1}) | M_t] ≥ E[U(p_t) | M_t]. Any violations must arise from model error, optimization error, or binding constraints R.
- Fixed points and local optima: A program p* is a fixed point if T(p*, D) = p* for all admissible D that p* would gather. Under continuity/compactness of P and continuity of expected U, fixed points exist (by standard fixed-point theorems). Fixed points coincide with local optima of expected U subject to R and the data-generation process induced by p*.
- Stability: A fixed point p* is locally stable if small admissible perturbations do not yield higher expected U; otherwise it is unstable and T will leave it given sufficient exploration.
- Path dependence and lock-in: Because D_t is generated by p_t, the reachable set of programs and the basins of attraction are path dependent. Early updates can irreversibly steer the process into suboptimal basins if exploration is insufficient.
- Endogenous distribution shift: Since p_{t+1} changes behavior, it changes the distribution of future inputs D_{t+1}. Evaluation and learning occur under performative feedback rather than i.i.d. sampling, invalidating standard generalization guarantees unless the shift is modeled.
- Selection effects: The process selects for internal modifications that improve measured U under the current measurement protocol. This creates Goodhart pressure: improvements target proxies of U unless the proxy equals true U under the induced distribution.

Information-theoretic structure
- Information pump: Each successful improvement step must add algorithmic information about E relevant to U into the program. The cumulative added information is upper bounded by the mutual information between the available data stream and the optimal policy representation given R.
- Compression and representation learning: Under minimum-description-length principles, self-improvement tends to compress away redundancy while preserving task-relevant mutual information, yielding more efficient internal representations.
- Rate limits: The rate of improvement is bounded by (i) data-processing inequality (you cannot create new information about E beyond what D_t carries), (ii) compute and memory constraints R, and (iii) exploration limits determining the Fisher information of D_t about counterfactual code changes.
- Diminishing returns vs compounding: If each step yields a constant fractional gain on a resource bottleneck (e.g., effective compute), improvements can compound until another bottleneck binds; beyond that point, returns diminish as gradients vanish or noise dominates.

Logical and computability limits
- Undecidability barrier: Determining in full generality whether a code change increases U is not computable (by Rice’s theorem). Therefore T must rely on approximations (empirical testing, proofs in restricted logics, or reflective oracles), implying occasional regress and the necessity of risk management.
- Löbian obstacles in proof-based self-modification: If modifications require self-justifying proofs of safety or benefit, Gödel–Löb constraints can prevent adoption of improvements that are true but unprovable within the system’s proof theory, unless special reflective methods are used.
- Kleene-style recursion: Self-reference is constructive: by recursion theorems, programs can obtain fixed points embedding their own descriptions, enabling principled self-inspection and self-modification. This guarantees the existence of self-referential improvements but not their desirability with respect to U.

Game-theoretic and control consequences
- Instrumental convergence under U: If U rewards broad competence, improvements that acquire resources (compute, data, optionality) and reduce variance are instrumentally favored because they increase the feasible set in P under R.
- Performative equilibria: The process tends toward performative optima where the policy and the induced data distribution are jointly optimal. Multiple equilibria can exist; stability depends on curvature of U and sensitivity of E to policy changes.
- Credit assignment across levels: Self-improvement decomposes into object-level optimization (improving task performance), meta-level optimization (improving the learner), and meta-meta-level, etc. Effective credit assignment requires estimating the marginal contribution of changes at each level to expected U under induced distribution shifts.

Verification and safety properties
- Monotone-improvement protocols: If each update is gated by a statistically valid test that estimated U increases on representative counterfactual data, then with high probability the realized U is non-decreasing up to test error and drift. This requires held-out or synthetic counterfactual evaluation that accounts for performativity.
- Corrigibility constraints: To prevent lock-in to harmful local optima, T can be constrained to maintain reversibility or deference to external oversight; formally, admissible p' must preserve intervention channels that allow external correction, trading off short-term U for long-term robustness.

Overall synthesis
- Self-improving algorithms create a self-referential optimization dynamic over program space that:
  - Searches for fixed points that are locally optimal under resource and data-generation constraints.
  - Induces distributional feedback that both powers and confounds learning.
  - Converts external regularities into internal structure at rates limited by information, compute, and undecidability.
  - Exhibits path dependence, selection effects, and Goodhart pressures that must be modeled to guarantee monotone improvement with respect to true objectives.

Self-improving algorithms create a sequence of program states and decision rules that, under explicit improvement criteria, transform external information and computation into higher expected performance, subject to information-theoretic, computational, and logical limits. Concretely:

- They create an improvement process: a sequence A0, A1, … where At+1 is adopted only if it satisfies a stated criterion of improvement over At with respect to a defined objective J, resource budget R, and environment model M.

- They create an ordering over programs: an explicit partial order ≤J,R,M where A ≤ B means B has greater or equal expected objective value than A under model M and budget R. The process is monotone in this order if adoption is restricted to improvements.

- They create a meta-level decision problem: at each step the algorithm must choose computations (including self-modifications) by maximizing expected value of information minus their costs. This is the metareasoning problem; improvement steps are rational only when their opportunity cost is justified.

- They create competence only relative to a bias: by No Free Lunch, average performance gains across all tasks are impossible; improvement is defined relative to a task distribution or prior encoded in M. Any claimed general improvement hides an assumption about that distribution.

- They create internal information about their environment only via interaction: by the data processing inequality, local deterministic computation cannot increase mutual information with a fixed external variable; increases require new observations, queries, or side-information.

- They create useful structure rather than raw information: by algorithmic information theory, a computable transformation cannot increase Kolmogorov complexity beyond additive constants; what improves is the alignment between internal representations and the task (higher algorithmic mutual information with the data-generating process).

- They create compression of experience: with suitable priors, Bayesian updating and MDL-style criteria lead to models whose two-part code length L(model) + L(data | model) tends to decrease as evidence accrues, reflecting improved predictive efficiency.

- They create time–description trade-offs: via Levin’s Kt complexity, additional computation can yield shorter effective descriptions of solutions. Self-improvement can exploit compute to discover simpler, faster procedures for the same tasks.

- They create unbounded speedups on some problems: by Blum’s speedup theorem, certain computable functions admit infinite sequences of asymptotically faster algorithms with no single optimal one; a self-improving process can keep finding speedups indefinitely on such tasks.

- They create undecidable verification problems: by Rice’s theorem, there is no general procedure to decide whether a proposed self-modification improves semantic performance; practical systems must rely on probabilistic evidence, restricted domains, or formal proofs within limited specifications.

- They create proof obligations if monotonicity must be guaranteed: proof-based self-modifiers adopt changes only when a proof (in some theory T) establishes E[J(At+1) | M] ≥ E[J(At) | M] minus costs. Monotonic improvement is then guaranteed relative to M and the soundness of T.

- They create reflective reasoning challenges: Löb’s theorem and related results constrain how an agent can reason about the correctness of its future self and its own proof system. Designing stable self-trust requires care (e.g., proof-carrying code, reflective oracles, or restricted schemas).

- They create fixed points or perpetual change, depending on the landscape: if the allowed modification set is finite and the improvement order is acyclic, the process terminates at a local optimum; with infinite spaces or speedup phenomena, it may continue without converging.

- They create exposure to Goodhart-style failures unless the objective is correct: if the proxy J is misaligned with the true goal, optimization pressure drives the system toward states that score well on J but perform poorly on the intended objective.

- They create gains only within resource and identifiability limits: computational lower bounds, sample-complexity limits (e.g., Fano-type bounds), and channel capacities cap attainable improvements for given compute, data, and time.

- They create amortized capability across tasks when cross-task structure exists: meta-learning can reduce per-task regret by transferring learned inductive biases; absent shared structure, no amortized improvement is possible on average.

- They create search distributions over programs that become more informative over time: by allocating effort to code regions with higher posterior value, they increase expected improvement rate; however, exploration–exploitation trade-offs remain unavoidable.

- They create measurable commitments: each self-modification changes not only performance but also future proof obligations, priors, and exploration policies; failing to account for these second-order effects can break future improvability.

- They create only what their interfaces permit: improvements that require new sensors, actuators, or oracles depend on acquiring those interfaces; without them, information-theoretic and physical constraints dominate.

In short, self-improving algorithms create a directed process over program space that systematically converts data and computation into better task performance under a stated model and objective, but they cannot create information or guarantees ex nihilo; their power and limits are governed by priors, interaction channels, resource bounds, and theorems from computability and logic.

Expanding the concept strictly and logically:

1) Definitions
- Self-improving algorithm (SIA): A computable process A that, given a performance measure M over a task distribution D and resources R, produces a modified algorithm A' such that the expected performance improves: E_D[M(A')] ≥ E_D[M(A)], with strict inequality on a nonzero set of cases.
- Improvement operator: A mapping F that takes a current algorithm and context to a new algorithm, A_{t+1} = F(A_t, context_t). The context may include data, proofs, tests, and resource budgets.
- Objective stability: The property that the criterion M used to accept modifications remains invariant under self-modification; formally, A accepts A' only if it predicts E_D[M(A')] ≥ E_D[M(A)] with respect to its current beliefs and those beliefs are preserved under accepted modifications.

2) What self-improving algorithms create
- An improvement sequence: A_0, A_1, A_2, … where A_{t+1} = F(A_t, context_t) and E[M(A_{t+1}) | history] ≥ E[M(A_t) | history].
- A meta-representation: Internal models that predict the effect of code or parameter changes on M, thereby coupling self-modeling to decision-making about modifications.
- Information gains: Reductions in predictive uncertainty relevant to M. Under log-loss, performance improvement equals expected KL divergence between posterior and prior; improvement corresponds to compression of the task distribution.
- A search distribution over programs: A learned prior over modifications that concentrates probability mass on transformations with higher expected marginal value of information per unit compute.
- Fixed points and attractors: Points A* such that F(A*, context) = A* (modulo trivial symmetries). These are locally improvement-stable algorithms; the improvement process seeks such fixed points under constraints.
- A hierarchy of optimizers: Base-level problem-solving, meta-level modification selection, and higher meta-levels that refine the improvement operator itself. Hierarchies can, in principle, be flattened into a single optimization over an augmented space, but are practically stratified for efficiency.

3) Sufficient conditions for monotone self-improvement
- Evaluability: For any candidate modification p in a nontrivial neighborhood of the current algorithm, the system can estimate Δ = E[M(Apply(p, A))] − E[M(A)] with bounded error and variance.
- Exploration: The search over modifications assigns nonzero probability to all neighborhoods containing true improvements.
- Acceptance rule: Adopt p only if estimated Δ exceeds a confidence threshold that compensates for estimator bias and noise.
- Resource allocation: Meta-level compute is allocated up to the point where marginal expected improvement per unit compute equals that of base-level task processing.
Given these, the performance sequence {E[M(A_t)]} is a submartingale and, under integrability, converges almost surely to a limit (possibly a local optimum).

4) Necessary conditions for nontrivial improvement
- Environmental structure: By no-free-lunch results, improvement averaged over all possible task distributions is null; gains require exploitable regularities in D relative to the algorithm’s inductive biases.
- Identifiability: The mapping from modifications to changes in M must be at least partially learnable; otherwise the evaluation problem is ill-posed.
- Stability of the objective: If the effective objective drifts under self-modification, improvements with respect to the original M are not guaranteed.

5) Information-theoretic characterization
- Compression view: Let L(model, data) be a description-length objective (e.g., MDL). Each accepted modification reduces expected L subject to compute constraints; the process builds progressively shorter codes for data and decisions.
- Mutual information view: Improvement increases I(Internal state; Environment outcomes relevant to M) under a resource constraint I(Internal state; Input) ≤ budget. The meta-learner builds representations that maximize expected utility per bit devoted to self-modification.
- Value of information: Accept modifications whose expected utility gain exceeds their information acquisition and implementation costs; this yields a stopping rule for meta-optimization.

6) Recursion and reflection
- Meta-improvement: The improvement operator F is itself subject to improvement by an operator G, potentially ad infinitum. Practical systems emulate this with a finite-depth reflective loop or amortize meta-learning.
- Fixed-point existence: If the space of algorithms is ordered by performance and F is monotone and continuous in that order, fixed-point theorems (e.g., Knaster–Tarski) guarantee at least one fixed point; convergence requires a contraction-like property or diminishing returns.
- Logical limits: Rice’s theorem precludes a general decision procedure for semantic properties of arbitrary modifications; Gödel–Löb phenomena limit self-verification. Workarounds include proof-based acceptance under restricted theories, probabilistic testing, and reflective oracles.

7) Computational limits and opportunities
- Lower bounds: For some problems, there are optimal algorithms up to constant factors; improvement saturates at those bounds.
- Speedup phenomena: By Blum’s speedup theorem, for some problems no single optimal algorithm exists; an infinite sequence of strictly faster algorithms can exist, enabling unbounded self-improvement in runtime on infinitely many inputs.
- Diminishing returns: In structured environments, marginal gains typically decay as the system approaches the information-theoretic or computational limit imposed by data complexity and resource budgets.

8) Risk and failure modes (logical consequences)
- Goodharting: If proxies for M are used during evaluation, the process can systematically increase proxy scores while degrading true M.
- Distribution shift: As the algorithm changes, the evaluation distribution may drift; guarantees tied to the old distribution can fail.
- Overconfidence and underconfidence: Due to incomplete proof systems or noisy tests, the acceptance rule can be overly conservative (missing true improvements) or incautious (adopting harmful ones).
- Wireheading: If the system can modify its own evaluation channel for M, it may self-modify to trivially maximize measured performance without improving external outcomes. Objective-channel integrity is a required invariant.

9) Governance invariants for safe self-improvement
- Objective invariance: The acceptance predicate must be defined over external outcomes and be unmodifiable by candidates lacking proofs or robust evidence of preserved alignment.
- Bounded risk: Cap potential downside of any single modification via sandboxing, staged rollout, and reversible changes.
- Proof or test thresholds: Require either a proof of improvement under a trusted theory or empirical evidence that crosses precommitted bounds; update thresholds as the system’s calibration improves.
- Resource accounting: Enforce that meta-level resource use remains justified by expected marginal gains.

10) Summary statement
Self-improving algorithms create an iterative, information-seeking process over the space of programs that constructs increasingly compressed, decision-useful representations of their tasks and of their own modification effects. Under stable objectives, evaluability, exploration, and prudent acceptance, this process yields a monotone (often convergent) improvement sequence. Its power and limits are governed by environmental structure, computational complexity, and the fundamental undecidability and incompleteness constraints of self-referential reasoning.

Self-improving algorithms create recursively defined sequences of programs whose expected performance increases by accumulating and reusing algorithmic information about the environment and about themselves, subject to specified resource bounds and undecidability limits.

Expansion

1) Setting and primitives
- Programs and descriptions: Let P be the set of prefix-free binary programs. For p in P, let f_p denote the (partial) function computed by p under resource bound R (time, memory).
- Environment and tasks: Let E be a distribution over tasks T, where each task induces an input-output reward process. Let U(p, E, R) be the expected utility of running p on tasks from E under resource bound R.
- Prior knowledge: Let π be a prior over environments or tasks, encoding the structure that makes improvement possible (No Free Lunch).

2) Improvement relation
- Define p' ≻ p if one of the following holds, given a fixed evaluation protocol:
  a) Utility improvement: U(p', E, R') ≥ U(p, E, R) + ε for some ε > 0, possibly with R' ≤ R, or
  b) Efficiency improvement: For all tasks in a test set representative of E, p' attains at most the previous loss while using strictly fewer resources.
- A metric m(p) may aggregate these criteria (e.g., expected utility minus a penalty for resource use). Then p' ≻ p means m(p') > m(p).

3) Self-improvement operator
- A self-improving algorithm is a pair (p, I) where p is the current program and I is a computable operator such that p_{t+1} = I(p_t, D_t, R_t), with D_t the data and traces observed by p_t.
- The generated sequence p_0, p_1, p_2, ... is the improvement trajectory. The algorithm is self-improving relative to E, π, R if P{m(p_{t+1}) ≥ m(p_t) | history} ≥ 1 − δ_t with ∑ δ_t < ∞.

4) Monotonicity under proof- or test-gated rewrites
- Proof-gated: If I only applies rewrites for which there exists a formal proof that E[U(p', E, R') | π] > E[U(p, E, R) | π] by at least a margin, then E[m(p_{t+1}) | history] ≥ m(p_t). This is the Gödel-machine style guarantee: monotone in expectation relative to the formalized prior and utility.
- Test-gated: If I uses held-out evaluation drawn i.i.d. from E to accept p' only when it beats p_t by a statistically valid margin, then with high probability the empirical improvement implies true improvement, yielding monotonicity in expectation.

5) Information accounting
- Internal state S_t: Let S_t encode the program text p_t plus learned parameters and data structures. The goal of self-improvement is to increase the mutual information I(S_t : Z) where Z are the latent regularities of E relevant to U.
- Data processing constraint: I(S_{t+1} : Z) ≤ I(S_t, D_t : Z). The algorithm cannot create information ex nihilo; it converts observations and compute into stored structure correlated with Z.
- Efficiency as compression: Under MDL or PAC-Bayes lenses, improvement reduces description length of data given the model while controlling model complexity, thus increasing predictive utility. Self-improvement creates more efficient codes for regularities in E and for the algorithm’s own search biases.

6) Recursion and self-reference
- Existence of reflective updates: By Kleene’s recursion theorem, for any computable improvement operator I there exists a program p that embeds and applies I to its own description. Hence self-reference is not an obstacle to definability.
- Fixed points: A rewrite policy may reach a p* such that no admissible p' satisfies p' ≻ p* under the gating criterion. Such p* are local optima with respect to m and the search neighborhood induced by I.

7) Limits from computability and logic
- Rice’s theorem: Nontrivial semantic properties of programs (e.g., “this rewrite improves long-run utility on E”) are undecidable. Therefore, any guaranteed-safe improvement policy must rely on restricted proof systems, statistical tests, or bounded horizons.
- Incompleteness and Löb: Proof-gated schemes can stall if the proof system cannot derive true improvement theorems that exist; lack of provability need not imply lack of actual improvement.
- No Free Lunch: Without a task prior π encoding structure, average improvement over all tasks is impossible. Apparent “creation” of capability is extraction of structure matched to π.
- Blum speedup: There exist problems with unbounded sequences of algorithmic speedups and others with optimal algorithms beyond which no further speedup is possible. Thus, self-improvement may be indefinitely fruitful or finitely exhausted depending on E.
- Exploration-exploitation tradeoff: Improvement requires allocating resources to search for better rewrites; regret bounds depend on the richness of the rewrite class and the variance of measured utility.

8) Order structure over programs
- Define a partial order ≤_m on P by p ≤_m q iff m(p) ≤ m(q). The improvement process induces an ascending chain p_0 ≤_m p_1 ≤_m ...
- Under compactness-like assumptions on the feasible set and continuity of m with respect to program parameters (e.g., in differentiable meta-learners), accumulation points are m-maximal; otherwise, chains can diverge (e.g., unbounded speedup).
- If the rewrite neighborhood is too local, chains can get stuck at suboptimal fixed points; if too global, acceptance tests become weak, risking non-monotone steps.

9) What is “created”
- Performance gradients: By constructing surrogate objectives, proofs, or validation tests, the algorithm creates a usable signal over its own description space that correlates with true utility.
- Algorithmic structure: It creates internal codes, invariants, and search heuristics that compress encountered problems, increasing I(S_t : Z) and reducing expected computational effort per unit reward.
- Self-models: It creates executable models of its own behavior and rewrite effects, enabling higher-order credit assignment and more targeted search.
- Selection pressure: It creates an endogenous prior over program modifications, biasing future search toward regions historically associated with gains.

10) Safety and robustness constraints
- Metric alignment: If m diverges from true U due to misspecification or distribution shift, improving m can reduce U (Goodhart effects). Robust self-improvement requires tests or proofs tied to the true utility and its uncertainty.
- Conservatism: When uncertainty about improvement is large, impose risk-sensitive acceptance criteria or rollback mechanisms to preserve monotonicity in expectation.

11) Practical instantiations (as schemas)
- Proof-gated program search: Maintain a theorem prover that proposes and verifies rewrites implying expected utility gain before self-modification.
- Test-gated meta-learning: Maintain validation protocols and statistical bounds; accept architecture or optimizer changes only with significant out-of-sample gains.
- Resource-reallocation schemes: Reweight internal search portfolios toward generators, solvers, or priors that empirically deliver the most utility per compute, approximating a speed prior.

12) Summary claim
- Under a fixed prior and utility, self-improving algorithms create an ascending, recursively defined trajectory through program space that increases expected performance by transforming observations and compute into compact, self-referential structure aligned with environmental regularities. This creation is fundamentally constrained by undecidability, the need for a task prior, and resource bounds, and its long-run behavior is governed by the existence (or absence) of speedups and fixed points in the induced program order.

Self-improving algorithms create sequences of programs and proofs that implement monotone ascent in a specified objective under explicit resource and uncertainty constraints, until a fixed point is reached, improvement opportunities are exhausted under those constraints, or the process fails due to undecidability or mis-specification.

To make this precise:

1) Model
- Program space P is a set of computable procedures. A resource budget b (time, memory) is fixed. Tasks are drawn from a distribution D. The performance functional is J_b: P → R, e.g., expected utility or negative loss at budget b: J_b(p) = E_{x∼D}[U(p, x, b)].
- An improvement operator T maps programs to programs, potentially using data and randomness: T: P → P.
- A certificate system C is a decidable predicate Cert(p, p′) implying a guaranteed or probably approximately correct improvement, for example J_b(p′) ≥ J_b(p) − ε with probability ≥ 1 − δ under stated assumptions.

2) Self-improvement process
- Starting from p_0, define the sequence p_{t+1} = T(p_t). The process is admissible if, for all t, Cert(p_t, p_{t+1}) holds and J_b(p_{t+1}) ≥ J_b(p_t) − ε_t with high probability.
- A fixed point p* satisfies T(p*) = p*. It is locally optimal with respect to T and J_b under the admissible neighborhood of modifications encoded by T and C.

3) Monotonicity and termination
- If there exists a potential Φ: P → R such that for all admissible steps Φ(p_{t+1}) > Φ(p_t), and Φ is bounded above, then the process terminates in finitely many steps at a T-fixed point.
- In finite P, any strictly J_b-increasing admissible T terminates in at most |P| − 1 steps.
- With stochastic estimates Ĵ of J and a uniform deviation bound sup_{p′∈H} |Ĵ(p′) − J(p′)| ≤ ε holding with probability ≥ 1 − δ over a finite candidate set H, the argmax of Ĵ ensures J does not decrease by more than 2ε with probability ≥ 1 − δ. Hence expected monotonicity can be maintained by controlling estimation error.

4) Limits and impossibility
- Rice’s theorem: Deciding any nontrivial semantic property of arbitrary programs (e.g., “J_b(p′) > J_b(p)”) is undecidable. Therefore general-purpose, sound, complete improvement verification is impossible; practical systems must restrict program classes or accept probabilistic guarantees.
- Blum’s speedup theorem: For some problems, there is no asymptotically optimal algorithm; there exist infinite chains p_t with unbounded runtime improvements. Hence unbounded self-improvement is possible in principle, but is not uniformly identifiable or verifiable.
- No Free Lunch: Averaged over all task distributions D, no improvement operator outperforms another. Effective self-improvement presupposes structured D and matched inductive biases.

5) Information-theoretic characterization
- Let M_t denote the model implicit in p_t. The expected log-loss under D is H(D) + E[KL(D || M_t)]. A strictly improving step reduces expected log-loss iff it reduces the KL divergence; equivalently it increases expected log-likelihood. Thus each improvement step creates measurable information about D, quantified by the reduction in code length under MDL or the gain in predictive mutual information.
- If the algorithm adaptively selects data X_t, expected improvement equals expected information gain I(Θ; X_t | past), where Θ are model parameters or program features. Self-improvement therefore creates its own curriculum that maximizes information acquisition subject to constraints.

6) Resource tradeoffs and dominance
- Define a resource–performance frontier J_b(p) as a function of b. Say p′ dominates p if J_b(p′) ≥ J_b(p) for all b in a budget set B and strictly for some b. A resource-aware T that only accepts dominance-improving p′ yields a monotone ascent on the Pareto frontier rather than at a single b.
- If improvements are composable and J exhibits submodularity over a set of independent improvement modules, greedy selection achieves at least a 1 − 1/e fraction of the optimal total gain under a cardinality or cost constraint.

7) Self-reference and verification
- By the recursion (fixed-point) theorem, programs can access and transform their own code; this enables packaging of modifications and their certificates (proof-carrying code).
- However, strong reflective guarantees are limited: in sufficiently strong systems, Löb’s theorem constrains self-trust. Practical schemes restrict proof systems, use bounded reflection, or rely on probabilistic tests, to avoid paradox while preserving useful guarantees.
- Invariant preservation: Let Inv(p) formalize safety/alignment properties. If for all admissible steps CertInv(p, p′) implies Inv(p′), and Inv(p_0) holds, then by induction Inv holds along the entire improvement sequence.

8) Convergence, cycling, and failure modes
- Without a well-founded potential or with an estimator–objective mismatch, T can cycle or degrade J (Goodhart effects). Calibration or robust optimization bounds on the surrogate objective Ĵ relative to J are necessary for reliable ascent.
- In nonstationary D or changing budgets b, fixed points can lose optimality; continuous improvement then tracks a moving target, with achievable regret bounded by the rate of drift and the adaptation capacity of T.

9) Summary
- Under explicit structure (task distribution, resource bounds, admissible modification classes, and verifiable improvement criteria), self-improving algorithms create directed, mostly monotone trajectories in program space that accumulate actionable information about their environment, compress their effective descriptions, and approach fixed points on a resource–performance frontier.
- Fundamental limits (undecidability, no-free-lunch, reflection constraints) force tradeoffs: one must narrow the domain of admissible changes, accept probabilistic guarantees, or incur residual risk.

Self-improving algorithms create recursively generated sequences of algorithms that monotonically increase expected performance with respect to a specified objective under stated resource constraints, by converting performance feedback into structured internal modifications of code, parameters, and priors.

Precisely:

1) Setup
- Let A be a set of encodable algorithms, P a distribution over tasks/inputs, U a bounded utility, and C a resource budget (time, memory, samples).
- Define performance F: A → R by F(a) = E_{x∼P}[U(a, x) | C].
- An improvement operator I maps current algorithm and state to a new algorithm: a_{t+1} = I(a_t, s_t), where s_t includes code, logs, gradients, proofs, tests, and other artifacts produced when running a_t under C.

2) Improvement property
- A process {a_t} is self-improving (w.r.t. F) if there exists a sequence of confidence levels {δ_t} with Σ_t δ_t < ∞ such that P[F(a_{t+1}) ≥ F(a_t)] ≥ 1 − δ_t for all sufficiently large t. By Borel–Cantelli, almost surely only finitely many regressions occur.
- Stronger forms require F(a_{t+1}) ≥ F(a_t) + ε_t with ε_t ≥ 0 and Σ_t ε_t diverging (unbounded improvement) or converging (approach to a limit).

3) Fixed points and limits
- A fixed point a* satisfies a* = I(a*, s*) for some reachable state s* and is locally F-optimal given I and C; i.e., F(I(a*, s)) ≤ F(a*) for all states s in its reachable neighborhood.
- Sequences may converge to fixed points (lock-in), cycle (if monotonicity is non-strict and I is not contracting), or diverge (if F is unbounded above and improvement remains possible).

4) Information-theoretic view
- Let Y_t be the feedback obtained when evaluating a_t (losses, rewards, tests). The algorithmic change Δa_t is a function of Y_t and prior state s_t.
- The expected improvement is bounded by the information available: roughly, E[F(a_{t+1}) − F(a_t)] ≤ κ · I(Y_t; latent environment regularities | s_t), where κ depends on how effectively I translates feedback into code changes. No channel with zero mutual information can drive systematic improvement.
- Compression interpretation: If L_t is the description length (MDL) needed to encode good behavior for P given a_t, then successful self-improvement reduces L_t; decreases in expected log-loss correspond to coding gains.

5) Feasibility and limits from computability
