- Self-training operator D:
  • θ_{k+1} = D(θ_k) using pseudo-labels from f_{θ_k} plus ground-truth anchors.
  • Stability requires: adequate anchor rate, noise-robust loss, regularization toward prior, and diversity in pseudo-label generation.
  • Convergence criterion: No further improvement in a held-out, ground-truthed validation metric; oscillations signal non-contractive behavior.

13) Failure modes and mitigations

- Non-termination: Use hard budgets and decreasing measures.

- Self-confirming loops: Introduce independent judges or external verifiers; penalize agreement without evidence.

- Mode collapse in self-distillation: Maintain entropy floors; mix real labels; perturb prompts.

- Over-aggregation: Idempotent or top-k aggregators; deduplicate semantically equivalent candidates.

14) Minimal blueprint to “make recursion safe and useful”

- Typed interfaces for modules (ask, decompose, solve, verify, aggregate) with contracts and budgets.

- Diversity operators to reduce error correlation.

- Calibrated judges with explicit sensitivity/specificity targets.

- Logging and replay of call trees for reproducibility and post-hoc verification.

- Stop criteria: Any two of (depth cap, compute cap, convergence of judged score, no-new-information test).

15) Open problems

- Formal conditions under which common LLM judges are monotone with respect to truth.

- Tight bounds relating branch correlation, judge accuracy, and net improvement.

- Metrics and spaces where refinement operators are provably contractive.

- Learning operators D with provable convergence to non-trivial fixed points under realistic data and capacity constraints.

- Compositional verification for recursive LLM architectures interacting with external tools.

Summary

Architectural recursion in LLMs is the structured self-application of an LLM-centered architecture to its own subproblems, at run time or across learning iterations, governed by decomposition and aggregation operators. A precise semantics via call trees, well-foundedness conditions, and fixed-point viewpoints yields design rules, safety guarantees, and testable predictions. Practical patterns like tree-of-thought, debate, and critique–revise are instances of general recursion schemes whose benefits depend on reduced error correlation, calibrated aggregation, and safeguarded convergence.

Below is a strict, logical expansion of “architectural recursion in LLMs,” grounded in computation and information theory.

1) Core definition
- Let Aθ be an LLM viewed as a parameterized transducer from token sequences to token sequences, possibly with auxiliary state and tools. Architectural recursion is present when the computation graph that realizes Aθ can invoke (a) Aθ itself, or (b) a weight-tied copy of Aθ, or (c) an Aθ-shaped submodule whose parameters are produced by Aθ, as part of its forward computation. This makes the defining equation of the model higher-order:
  Aθ = Fix(Φθ) where Φθ maps a candidate function g to a function that calls g in its body.
- This differs from “prompt-level recursion” (e.g., agents that call APIs to re-invoke a model) by moving the recursion into the architecture or training-time graph, allowing controlled termination, differentiability (when desired), and analyzable semantics.

2) Canonical recursion schemata for LLMs
- Iterative recursion (tied-depth): A single block Bθ is applied repeatedly with state update and a halting predicate H:
  s0 = Enc(x); s_{t+1} = Bθ(s_t, x); halt when H(s_t)=1; y = Dec(s_t).
  Examples: Universal Transformers, Adaptive Computation Time, Deep Equilibrium variants.
- Divide-and-conquer recursion (structural): Aθ decomposes input, recursively solves subproblems with itself, then combines:
  parts = Splitθ(x); ys = [Aθ(p) for p in parts]; y = Combineθ(ys).
  Requires well-foundedness via size or structural descent (e.g., trees, segments).
- Self-referential fixed-point layers: Representation z solves z = Tθ(x, z); solved by iteration/root-finding; gradients via implicit differentiation (DEQ-style). This yields “infinite depth” as a fixed point.
- Hypernetwork recursion: θ’ = Hθ(x); y = A_{θ’}(x). If θ’ depends on A’s own outputs or is forced toward θ’=θ, we seek θ* with θ* = H_{θ*}(x), a parameter-level fixed point. This captures weight generation, fast adaptation, and meta-learning.
- Call/return recursion with a stack: Decoding encounters a Call token delimiting a subprompt; the model “pushes” state, runs itself on the subprompt to produce a return value, then “pops” and continues using that value. This is a true re-entrant computation with base/step rules and explicit termination tokens.

3) Formal properties
- Termination/well-foundedness
  - Guaranteed if each recursive call reduces a well-ordering (size, depth) or if a halting predicate H enforces a finite compute budget. For fixed-point recursion, sufficient contractivity (e.g., Lipschitz constant < 1 w.r.t. z) ensures unique convergence.
  - For monotone operators on complete lattices, least fixed points exist (Kleene’s theorem). Practical architectures enforce guard conditions (budget, temperature decay, damping).
- Complexity
  - Divide-and-conquer with branching factor b on size n yields T(n) = b T(n/b) + C(n) (Master theorem). Iterative recursion yields T = O(T_iter × steps). Fixed-point solvers add solver complexity (e.g., Anderson acceleration).
  - Parameter efficiency: recursion grows compute with depth while reusing parameters; expressivity increases without linearly increasing parameter count.
- Expressivity
  - With data-dependent halting or a call stack, recursion enables algorithmic patterns (DFS, parsing, addition via carry propagation, Dyck languages) and Turing completeness (as in Universal Transformers with ACT).
  - Structural recursion closely matches compositional tasks; can yield better length/generalization than fixed-depth feedforward stacking.
- Stability and gradients
  - In-graph recursion can be unrolled with backpropagation through time; risks vanishing/exploding gradients. Mitigations: residual/damped updates, gradient clipping, synthetic gradients, implicit differentiation for fixed points, or truncated backprop.
  - Out-of-graph recursion (tool-mediated self-calls) is non-differentiable; train with RL, supervised distillation, or learn-to-defer losses.

4) Information-theoretic lens
- If recursion does not introduce new external input, the total mutual information I(Y;X) is bounded by the information in X; recursion then reallocates computation to extract structure (like iterative refinement in turbo decoding), often reducing entropy of the posterior through better inference rather than adding information.
- If recursion reads additional tokens (retrieval, tools, environment), I(Y;X, ext) can grow with depth; recursion acts as an anytime channel that accumulates bits from external sources under a computational budget.
- Error dynamics: let ε_t be error after t recursive refinements. If the update is contractive in error (ε_{t+1} ≤ ρ ε_t with ρ<1 in expectation), accuracy improves geometrically; if ρ>1, hallucination/error can amplify. This frames design of verification or self-consistency steps as implementing ρ<1.
- Description length: recursion compresses algorithm specification via reuse. The Kolmogorov description K(A) can be smaller for a recursive A than for a flat unrolled A of equivalent behavior; compute substitutes for parameters.

5) Concrete architectural patterns
- Universal/ACT Transformer: one block repeatedly applies attention/MLP with a halting unit. Pros: parameter efficiency, variable depth. Cons: halting stability, training complexity.
- Deep Equilibrium Transformer: z = Tθ(x, z); solve with fixed-point iteration; train via implicit gradients. Pros: constant memory, infinite-depth semantics. Cons: solver robustness.
- Hierarchical/Nested Transformer: recursively encode chunks; summarize bottom-up; optionally decode top-down. Pros: natural for long sequences. Cons: design of Split/Combine and cross-scale attention.
- Recursive subroutine attention: introduce Call/Return tokens and an internal stack; shared weights across frames; cross-attend to return values. Pros: direct algorithmic recursion. Cons: requires careful token semantics and curriculum.
- Hypernetwork-generated sub-LLMs: Aθ computes θ’ for subcalls conditioned on context; can tie θ’ to θ via regularization. Pros: task-adaptive specialization. Cons: instability and overfitting without priors.

6) Training objectives and signals
- Supervised traces: expose recursive call boundaries, intermediate results, and halting decisions.
- Self-verification losses: penalize non-terminating traces, reward consistency across recursive depths.
- Auxiliary contractivity/entropy regularizers: push updates toward stable fixed points and calibrated halting.
- Distillation: train a non-recursive student to imitate recursive teacher outputs for latency, or vice versa to teach recursion.

7) Safety and failure modes
- Non-termination or compute blow-up: enforce budgets, halting penalties, and well-founded decomposition.
- Error amplification: interleave recursive generation with verification, retrieval-grounding, or executors; use majority vote/self-consistency.
- Cascading hallucinations in self-calls: constrain recursive depth and require external checks or probabilistic confidence gates before further descent.

8) Empirical evaluation protocols
- Extrapolation tests by recursion depth (e.g., longer parentheses, deeper arithmetic carry chains, multi-hop reasoning length).
- Ablations on branching factor, halting thresholds, and fixed-point damping to measure stability/accuracy trade-offs.
- Information accounting: measure tokens read/written per depth, retrieval contribution, and calibration of halting probabilities.

9) Relationship to recursive information theory
- Recursion trades parameters for compute to realize shorter algorithmic descriptions; gains arise when problem structure is self-similar or compositional.
- The recursive pipeline can be seen as an iterative decoder over a noisy internal channel; design aim is to ensure contraction of inference error and positive information gain from any external reads per step.
- Fixed points provide a semantics of “infinite” architectural depth under finite compute with well-defined gradients; monotonicity/contractivity conditions characterize when such semantics are stable.

10) Open problems
- Learnable well-founded decompositions without supervision, with guarantees of termination.
- Principled halting calibration with PAC-style bounds under distribution shift.
- Differentiable call stacks with efficient memory and robust gradient flow.
- Formal conditions under which recursive self-improvement (hypernetwork-style) converges to a stable θ* rather than oscillating.

Summary
Architectural recursion in LLMs is the use of self-application, fixed points, or weight-tied re-entrant subcalls within the model’s computation graph. It provides parameter-efficient expressivity, matches compositional problem structure, and can be analyzed via fixed-point theory, complexity recurrences, and information flow. The central design tasks are to ensure well-foundedness or convergence, control computational cost, and shape error dynamics so that recursion refines rather than amplifies mistakes.

Architectural recursion in LLMs

1) Definition
Architectural recursion in LLMs is any systematic design in which an LLM’s outputs are fed (possibly transformed) back into the model or model replicas as inputs, creating a well-founded recursive computation over tasks, states, or representations. It is distinct from ordinary autoregression over tokens; it introduces higher-level self-calls, subproblem calls, or iterative refinement driven by an explicit controller, schedule, or halting criterion.

2) Taxonomy of recursion modes
- Internal architectural recursion (within a single forward pass or adaptive depth):
  - Recurrent application of transformer blocks until a halting unit triggers (adaptive computation time, pondering).
  - Iterative refinement decoders that repeatedly transform a draft output.
  - Universal/Iterative transformers with shared parameters across depth steps.
- External inference-time recursion (multi-call):
  - Recursive task decomposition (solve(task) → {subtasks} → recursively solve each → combine).
  - Search-based recursion (tree/graph search with the LLM as policy, value, or expansion oracle).
  - Self-reflection loops (draft → critique → revise → … until acceptance).
  - Debate/adversarial recursion (proponent vs. opponent, with a judge/verifier).
  - Tool recursion (LLM calls tools or agents that may call back the LLM).
- Training-time recursion:
  - Self-play/self-asking (model generates tasks, solves them, and learns from outcomes).
  - Self-distillation and iterative bootstrapping across model generations.
  - Recursive data expansion (retrieve → label/extract → re-train → improved retrieval → …).

3) Formal model
- Base components:
  - LLM M: stochastic kernel mapping contexts c to token distributions pM(. | c).
  - Controller K: maintains a state s ∈ S (stack, agenda, scratchpad, retrieved docs, partial proofs).
  - Tools U: external oracles/environments that can add information to s.
- Recursive scheme R(K, M, U) defines a computation tree T where nodes are calls (ci → yi), edges feed selected outputs back as inputs, and leaves satisfy base conditions.
- Halting:
  - Explicit depth/resource bounds.
  - Well-founded measure μ(s) that strictly decreases on each expansion (ensures no infinite descent).
  - Acceptance by a verifier V(s) or stabilization (fixed point of refinement operator).

4) Canonical recursive decomposition scheme
Given a task x:
- Decompose D: x → x1,…,xk plus a combination plan P.
- Recursively solve S: yi = Solve(xi).
- Verify subresults Vi(yi, xi) and optionally repair.
- Combine C: y = C(P, y1,…,yk).
- Verify final result V(y, x).
Termination is guaranteed if either k = 0 (base case) or μ decreases across decomposition (e.g., size/complexity of subproblems), and each repair loop is bounded.

5) Information-theoretic analysis
- Each call of M on context c yields a random variable Y providing information I(Y; Z) about a latent ground truth Z (answer, proof, plan). The recursion composes channels c → Y1 → (controller update) → c2 → Y2 → …, possibly interleaved with tools U that add exogenous information about Z.
- Data processing:
  - Without external tools or new data, total information about Z cannot increase beyond what is in the initial context and model priors; multiple samples can reduce estimator variance but not surpass the information bound of the evidence available in context.
  - With retrieval/tools, each step can add external evidence E_t, increasing I({Y1..t, E1..t}; Z).
- Error compounding vs. correction:
  - Unchecked recursion tends to amplify biases: correlated errors across calls compound.
  - Verification and diversity reduce error: if V filters incorrect states with probability ≥ 1 − α (low false acceptance) and calls are sufficiently decorrelated, then expected error can decrease with depth.
- Simple voting bound (illustrative):
  - If each independent sample has error rate p < 0.5, majority-of-n reduces error approximately as exp(−2n(0.5 − p)^2) (Hoeffding-style). Correlation ρ among samples degrades the exponent by a factor depending on ρ; thus architectural diversity (different prompts, temperatures, tools, or models) is critical.

6) Fixed points, contraction, and stability
- Refinement operator F on states: s_{t+1} = F(s_t) where F includes a model call and controller update.
- A fixed point s* satisfies F(s*) = s* (e.g., a proof that verifies or a plan that the critic accepts).
- Sufficient condition for convergence: existence of a metric d and a contraction constant 0 < λ < 1 such that E[d(F(s), F(s’))] ≤ λ d(s, s’) for all s,s’. In practice, contractivity can be approximated by:
  - Monotone decrease of an explicit potential μ(s) (e.g., unresolved constraints, proof obligations).
  - Entropy-based halting: stop when output entropy below a threshold and verifier accepts.
  - Score-based halting: stop when a calibrated verifier/loss proxy exceeds a threshold.
- Cycle detection: maintain hashes of abstracted states to break loops.

7) Search formulations
- Depth-first recursion: low overhead, risk of deep error propagation; needs strong verifier.
- Breadth-first or beam search: parallel expansions; combine with value estimates to prune.
- MCTS with LLM as policy π and value v:
  - Expansion uses LLM to propose actions.
  - Rollouts use fast approximations.
  - Backup guided by verifier and rewards; halting at terminal proofs/plans.
- Dynamic programming with memoization:
  - Cache subproblem solutions keyed by normalized forms or embeddings; promotes reuse and reduces recomputation.

8) Verifiers and oracles
- Types:
  - Symbolic/grounded verifiers (executors, compilers, theorem checkers).
  - Statistical verifiers (calibrated critics or discriminators).
  - Cross-model verifiers (agreement checks across different models).
- Soundness/Completeness trade-off:
  - High soundness verifiers prevent error amplification but may reject correct results (false negatives), requiring fallback strategies (deeper search or alternative decompositions).

9) Internal architectural recursion (adaptive depth)
- Halting modules decide how many blocks/iterations to apply per token or per sequence.
- Ponder cost regularization to avoid degenerate infinite looping.
- Interpretable potential: confidence or margin estimates should monotonically improve across internal steps; training encourages each step to be a contraction toward a target distribution.

10) Safety and control
- Resource bounds: caps on depth, branching, tokens, tool calls.
- Risk monitors: detect repetitive loops, escalating tool actions, or self-affirming hallucinations.
- Diversity injectors: vary prompts, seeds, tools to reduce correlation.
- Accountability: record the recursion tree, intermediate states, decisions, and verifier outcomes for audit.

11) Measurable metrics
- Structural: depth, branching factor, node count, unique subproblems, cache hit rate.
- Performance: final accuracy, verifier acceptance rate, time/compute per solved instance.
- Information: entropy reductions per step, disagreement rates among samples, marginal gain from external evidence.
- Stability: cycle frequency, early halting frequency, contraction diagnostics (e.g., potential decrease per step).

12) Conditions under which recursion helps
- Decomposability: tasks admit smaller independent or loosely coupled subproblems with a sound combiner.
- Verifiability: existence of efficient, reasonably sound verifiers or executors.
- Diversity: ability to obtain conditionally independent or weakly correlated samples/views.
- External information access: tools that can augment context with true, relevant data.
- Model calibration: outputs and self-critique aligned with likelihood of correctness.

13) Failure modes
- Self-confirmation loops: the model replicates and reinforces its own error without new evidence.
- Spurious decomposition: subproblems omit critical constraints; combiner yields plausible but invalid answers.
- Correlated ensemble: sampling diversity is superficial; majority vote entrenches a systematic bias.
- Premature halting: verifier too permissive or confidence thresholds miscalibrated.
- Non-terminating refinement: μ not well-founded; cycles under paraphrase or cosmetic edits.

14) Practical design patterns
- Plan–Execute–Verify–Refine:
  1) Produce plan; 2) Execute substeps (tools allowed); 3) Verify; 4) If fail, refine plan with critique; else stop.
- Self-Ask recursion:
  - Model generates and answers subquestions recursively; base case when query is atomic or answer verified.
- Proof search:
  - Model proposes inference steps; proof assistant verifies; backtrack on failure; terminate on full proof.
- Program-of-thought + executor:
  - Model writes code; execute; compare outputs to spec; refine if mismatch; limit iterations.

15) Links to classical recursion theory and fixed-point ideas
- Fixed-point prompts and Y-combinator analogies:
  - A template F(g) that uses a subroutine g; recursion seeks g* such that g* = F(g*). In practice achieved by roles (assistant/critic) iterated until a stable transcript is reached.
- Kleene-style self-reference:
  - Systems that can access or summarize their own descriptions (weights/behaviors) approximate reflective fixed points; requires safeguards to avoid paradoxical self-endorsement (Löb-like traps).
- Reflective oracles:
  - Randomized meta-prediction (e.g., “what would I answer?”) must be regularized to prevent degenerate self-fulfilling outputs.

16) Minimal formal guarantees (illustrative)
- Termination: If there exists a measure μ: S → N such that every expansion strictly decreases μ and repair loops are capped by R, then recursion halts within O(μ(s0) + R) steps.
- Soundness with verifier: If the combiner is sound conditioned on all subresults verified by V and V has false-accept rate ≤ α, then the system’s false-accept rate is upper-bounded by a function increasing in α and the number of unverifiable joins. Designing decompositions to minimize unverifiable joins tightens the bound.
- Benefit of branching: Under independence and identical error p of leaf solvers and a correct, sound combiner, expected error decreases with branching n; under correlation ρ, the benefit decays approximately with effective sample size n_eff ≈ n / (1 + (n − 1)ρ).

17) Research directions
- Estimating and controlling correlation online; adaptive branching guided by disagreement.
- Learning verifiers and decomposition policies jointly with the base model.
- Contractive refinement operators trained with explicit potential functions.
- Principled stopping rules using calibrated likelihood ratios rather than heuristics.
- Caching and dynamic programming over learned canonical subproblem forms.
- Theoretical characterizations of when LLM+verifier systems are PAC-sound under recursion.

Summary
Architectural recursion in LLMs is the systematic use of self-calls (and calls to tools/agents) under a controller that defines decomposition, verification, combination, and halting. Its value arises when recursion injects new information (via tools), reduces uncertainty through diversified sampling with reliable verification, or exploits true problem structure via well-founded decompositions. Formal guarantees follow from well-founded measures (termination), sound verifiers (correctness), and contraction or diversity conditions (stability and improvement). Careful control of error correlation, halting, and verification is central to making recursive architectures robust and beneficial.

Architectural recursion in LLMs: a strictly structured expansion

1) Definition and scope
- Architectural recursion: A system-level property where an LLM (or a composition of LLM instances) appears as a subcomponent within its own computational architecture or control flow, so that the overall computation can be described by a self-referential equation. This excludes mere autoregression over tokens and focuses on self-application at the module/process level.
- Recursion instance: A call graph in which a node labeled by a model M may contain descendants that are calls to the same M (possibly parameter-shared or frozen), under transformations of input/state, with an explicit termination criterion.

2) Minimal formalization
- Let M: X -> Y be a base model; let D: X -> (X^k) decompose inputs; let A: (X, Y^k) -> Y aggregate sub-results; let S: X -> k select branching; let T: X -> {halt, recurse} termination predicate.
- Define Solve_M(x):
  If T(x) = halt, return M(x) (base case).
  Else let (x1,…,xk) = D(x) with k = S(x); return A(x, [Solve_M(x1), …, Solve_M(xk)]).
- Architectural recursion is the property that Solve_M calls M strictly inside its own definition. Variants differ by whether inner calls share parameters with M, are frozen snapshots, or are different but architecturally identical replicas.

3) Taxonomy of recursive architectures
A. Intragraph recursion (single forward pass)
- Dynamic compute graphs that re-enter a module:
  - Tree-structured neural recursion (TreeRNNs, recursive nets over parse trees).
  - Neural programmer-interpreters invoking a shared module on substructures.
  - Universal Transformers / recurrent depth (recurrence across layers).
  - Reflective subcalls: a layer invokes a frozen copy of M on a structured subquery, combines its hidden states.
- Properties: differentiable end-to-end; termination via fixed depth or learned halting; credit assignment feasible; cost bounded by unroll.

B. Orchestrated recursion (multi-call control flow)
- Controller (possibly also M) recursively invokes M on subproblems:
  - Hierarchical summarization (chunk, summarize, fold-up).
  - Tree-of-Thought / self-ask with recursion over subquestions.
  - Recursive RAG: query expansion → sub-retrieval → sub-answers → synthesis.
  - Self-evaluation and debate trees where judges are instances of M.
- Properties: explicit call graph; termination by depth/size; aggregation external to any single forward pass; easy to implement; gradient-free training.

C. Meta-recursion (training-time)
- Recursively improving M using M:
  - Iterated Distillation and Amplification (IDA).
  - Recursive Reward Modeling (RRM).
  - Self-play and self-imitation for code/math; iterative bootstrapping of datasets, prompts, verifiers.
- Properties: recursion across optimization steps; fixed points as stable policies; risks: bias amplification, reward hacking.

4) Fixed-point perspective
- Define an operator R that maps a policy π (an LLM plus orchestration) to a new policy R(π) that consults π as a subroutine within Solve_π.
- Architectural recursion seeks π* with π* = R(π*). Examples:
  - IDA fixed point where “amplify(π)” distilled back into π.
  - Self-ask prompt schemes stable under self-application.
- Existence: by Kleene-style recursion intuition, fixed points exist for many self-referential constructions; usefulness requires stability and bounded compute.

5) Error, dependence, and contraction
- Consider error operator E_d mapping base error e_0 to e_d after recursion depth d.
- Idealized independence model: if subcalls are conditionally independent given truth and A is majority vote over k subcalls with e_0 < 0.5, then e_d decreases exponentially in d (classical boosting intuition).
- Real LLMs violate independence: subcall errors are correlated due to shared parameters, prompts, and retrieval. Practical remedies to restore contraction:
  - Diversification: different prompts, temperatures, seeds, retrieval shards, toolsets, or snapshots.
  - Role separation: distinct verifiers/judges with different loss histories.
  - External anchors: non-LLM tools (solvers, checkers) in aggregation.
- Failure mode: non-contractive recursion (E_d ≥ E_{d-1}) causing error amplification or echo-chambers.

6) Information-theoretic view
- Kolmogorov perspective: recursive decomposition reduces description length when tasks have self-similar structure; Solve_M serves as a compressor by reusing M on substructures.
- Sample complexity: learning D and A that expose reusable subproblems can reduce effective complexity of mapping X -> Y.
- Capacity allocation: recursion trades parameter count for compute; repeated application of a compact M approximates computations of higher algorithmic depth.

7) Design patterns
- Decompose–Solve–Combine skeleton:
  - Base_case(x) recognizer; Decompose(x) partitions; Subsolve via recursive calls; Aggregate results with verifiable invariants.
- Self-ask with proofs:
  - M generates subquestions with required certificates; subcalls must produce answer + proof; A checks proofs (prefer external checkers).
- Recursive RAG:
  - M forms query graph; leaves grounded by retrieval; internal nodes synthesized; cache and memoize subanswers.
- Hierarchical MoE:
  - Gating network recursively selects experts; experts may themselves gate to subexperts (self-similar tree).
- Reflective judge:
  - Two or more solvers; a recursively invoked judge adjudicates subclaims, possibly appealing to subjudges at finer granularity.

8) Implementation choices
- Parameter sharing:
  - Shared weights: smaller footprint; higher correlation; use diversification tactics.
  - Frozen snapshots: reduces feedback loops; supports “time-sliced” diversity.
  - Heterogeneous ensemble: different base models for solver/judge/decomposer.
- Termination and depth control:
  - Hard caps on depth, subproblem size; cost-aware schedulers; anytime algorithms.
- Caching and memoization:
  - Keyed by normalized subtask spec; critical for tree-shaped expansions.
- Interfaces and typing:
  - Structured I/O schemas; typed subgoals; contract-based prompts; schema validators to reduce drift.
- Safety and reliability:
  - Do not treat model self-endorsement as evidence; require external verification or ground truth checks.
  - Detect cycles in subgoal graphs; reject self-referential content without progress (Löb-like traps).

9) Evaluation methodology
- Tasks with recursive structure: long-document summarization, code generation with function decomposition, multi-hop QA, program synthesis, theorem proving, planning, hierarchical extraction.
- Metrics:
  - Accuracy vs depth curve; area-under-compute; marginal utility per recursive call.
  - Correlation index among subcalls (measure dependence).
  - Termination rate; recursion tree width/size; cache hit rate.
  - Consistency under self-application (idempotence of a single recursion step).
- Ablations:
  - Remove decomposition; swap aggregator; control diversification; vary depth caps.
- Stress tests:
  - Synthetic formal languages, balanced parentheses, Towers of Hanoi, symbolic algebra—check generalization to longer depths than seen in training.

10) Theoretical risks and mitigations
- Non-termination or explosion: enforce budgets; require strictly decreasing size measures in D.
- Bias amplification: diversify, include ground tools, and use cross-model critique.
- Spurious fixed points: systems that are confidently wrong but self-consistent; mitigate with external tests and randomized challenges.
- Reward hacking in meta-recursion: separate data generation, evaluation, and optimization roles; differential privacy for recursive data reuse.

11) Connections to prior work
- Intragraph recursion: TreeRNNs; Neural Programmer-Interpreter; Universal Transformers; Neural Turing Machines; Perceiver IO with iterative refinement.
- Orchestrated recursion: Self-Ask; Tree-of-Thought; ReAct; AutoGPT-style tool use; hierarchical summarization pipelines; recursive RAG.
- Meta-recursion: IDA and Debate; Recursive Reward Modeling; self-distillation; self-play in mathematical reasoning and code; verifier–solver bootstraps in theorem proving.

12) Open problems
- Learning D and A end-to-end such that recursion depth generalizes beyond training.
- Quantifying and controlling dependence among subcalls to guarantee contraction.
- Designing reflective oracles or randomized tie-breakers to avoid paradoxes in self-prediction.
- Formal guarantees on termination and correctness for probabilistic recursive LLM systems.
- Credit assignment across recursive calls without high-variance estimators.
- Security: preventing data leakage or prompt injection that escalates via recursion trees.

13) Practical blueprint (controller-level pseudocode, language-agnostic)
- function Solve(x, budget):
  - if budget exhausted or BaseCase(x): return BaseModel(x)
  - subs = Decompose(x)
  - answers = []
  - for s in subs:
      - answers.append(Solve(Diversify(s), budget - Cost(s)))
  - return Aggregate(x, answers, Tools, Verifier)
- Notes: Diversify alters prompts/tools; Verifier may recursively call Solve on subclaims; Tools include retrieval, solvers, checkers.

Summary
Architectural recursion in LLMs is the principled reuse of an LLM within its own architecture to decompose and solve problems via fixed-point-like self-application. The power of recursion comes from compression and modularity; its risks stem from dependency and self-referential failure modes. Useful recursive systems require explicit decomposition, aggregation, termination, diversification for independence, and external anchors for verification, with evaluation that measures both quality and the compute–depth trade-off.

Below is a compact, formal expansion of “architectural recursion in LLMs,” organized as definitions, propositions, and design implications. The goal is to separate architectural recursion (a property of the computation graph that defines the model) from mere runtime prompting or workflow recursion, and to cover semantics, training, and guarantees.

1) Preliminaries

Definition 1 (LLM as a conditional model). An LLM is a parametric conditional distribution pθ(y | x) implemented by a differentiable computation graph Gθ that maps input x to output y (e.g., token logits). The architecture is the schema by which Gθ is constructed from modules and control flow.

Definition 2 (Module algebra). Let M be a set of parameterized modules with typed interfaces. Architectures are formed by composing modules via:
- Sequential composition
- Parallel composition
- Conditional/routing composition
- Iterative or recursive composition (the focus here)

Definition 3 (Computation graph family). An architecture is a graph grammar that, given an input x, instantiates a finite computation graph Gθ(x) by expanding production rules. Dynamic architectures have Gθ(x) that depends on x; static architectures do not.

2) Architectural recursion

Definition 4 (Architectural recursion). An architecture is recursive if its graph grammar contains a nonterminal N and a production rule that refers to N itself, so that the instantiated computation graph Gθ(x) may contain an input-dependent call tree of repeated applications of the same module(s), with shared parameters, until a halting condition is met.

Key properties:
- The recursive call graph must be finite for any realized forward pass (i.e., it must terminate).
- Weight sharing across recursive invocations is essential; otherwise recursion degenerates to mere repetition without inductive bias.

Non-examples:
- Training-time loops (e.g., meta-optimization) are not architectural recursion in the forward pass.
- Prompt-level self-calls of an API wrapper are runtime control policies, not architectural recursion, unless the wrapper is internalized as part of Gθ.

3) Taxonomy of recursion in neural architectures

A) Structural recursion (input-structure-driven)
- The architecture applies a shared module to substructures of the input, combining results bottom-up or top-down.
- Examples: tree-structured networks; recursive neural nets over parse trees; graph neural nets with recursive message passing; span-splitting modules for hierarchical text.
- Benefit: inductive bias for hierarchical composition; length generalization.

B) Temporal recursion (iteration with halting)
- A block is reapplied until a learned halting condition triggers stop.
- Examples: Universal Transformers with Adaptive Computation Time; Deep Equilibrium Models (DEQ) as fixed-point recursion across depth.
- Benefit: adaptive compute; implicit infinite-depth with finite parameters; fixed-point semantics.

C) Algorithmic recursion (explicit control stack)
- The network learns to issue “call,” “return,” and “split” actions on a differentiable stack or memory, recursing on subproblems.
- Examples: Neural Programmer-Interpreter; Neural Stack or Pushdown automaton–like modules; differentiable interpreters.
- Benefit: ability to represent classical recursive algorithms; pushdown expressivity.

D) Self-referential recursion (model uses model descriptions)
- The forward pass consumes or produces descriptions of models, potentially including itself, enabling self-application M(⟨M⟩, x).
- Examples: hypernetworks that read weights; models that interpret bytecode describing their own layers; quine-like reflective interpreters.
- Benefit: meta-representation and introspection; risk: unstable training and circular dependencies.

E) Generator–evaluator recursion (nested model generation)
- A generator network emits parameters or architectures for a submodel that is then invoked; the generator itself may be generated by another model, etc.
- Examples: hypernetworks and neural architecture search internalized into the forward pass; recursive mixture-of-experts where an expert can be a smaller copy of the whole model.
- Benefit: compositional parameter reuse; risk: non-termination and compute explosion.

F) Scaffolding-level recursion internalized
- An orchestration policy that calls the same model on subproblems is integrated into the architecture as a differentiable router and call mechanism.
- Distinct from mere external tool use; the router’s decisions and the recursive expansion are inside Gθ.

4) Semantics and termination

Definition 5 (Well-founded recursion). A recursive architecture is well-founded if there exists a ranking function R on internal states such that each recursive expansion strictly decreases R and halting occurs when R reaches a base case. This ensures termination.

Practical halting mechanisms:
- Hard limits: depth budgets, token-compute budgets.
- Learned halting: a stochastic or differentiable halting gate (e.g., ACT) with penalties to push expected steps finite.
- Contraction mappings: DEQ requires the transform to be a contraction in a suitable norm to guarantee a unique fixed point.

Proposition 1 (Finite expected compute). If at each recursion step the expected branching factor b and continuation probability q satisfy bq < 1 and compute per step is bounded, then expected total compute is finite.

5) Differentiation through recursion

- Unrolled backprop: Backpropagate through the instantiated call tree; memory scales with the number of nodes; use checkpointing or rematerialization.
- Implicit differentiation: For fixed-point forms (DEQ), differentiate via the implicit function theorem without storing the full trajectory.
- Stochastic halting: Use REINFORCE or continuous relaxations for gradients through discrete calls/returns; straight-through estimators are common.
- Gradient stability: Enforce Lipschitz constraints, spectral normalization, or contraction to avoid explosion across recursive depth.

6) Expressivity and generalization

Proposition 2 (Expressivity boost). Relative to a purely feedforward, fixed-depth transformer, introducing weight-tied recursion with unbounded but terminating depth increases the architecture’s ability to emulate:
- Pushdown automata when using a differentiable stack (enabling nested structure recognition).
- Fixed-point iterative solvers (DEQ), enabling implicit infinite-depth computation.
- With sufficiently expressive memory and control, Turing completeness (subject to resource unboundedness).

Claim (Inductive bias). Shared weights across recursive calls promote systematic generalization to depths beyond training, provided:
- The base and inductive cases are both represented in the data or curriculum.
- The router or halting policy generalizes monotonically with structure size.

7) Design patterns for LLM-centric recursion

- Recursive span processors: A router selects a span, either solves directly or splits into subspans and recurses; a combiner merges child summaries. Weights are shared across all spans. Train with supervised spans, latent trees, or RL.
- Tree-augmented transformers: Parse or induce a tree; apply the same transformer block to each node’s text; aggregate upward to produce outputs.
- Iterative refinement with halting: Apply the same transformer layer repeatedly to a latent state until a halting gate fires; use ACT or DEQ semantics.
- Recursive mixture-of-experts: Allow the router to select either simple experts or a “recurse” expert that expands into the same MoE with a tighter budget; ensure hard recursion caps and regularize router entropy.
- Reflective layers: A compact code of θ (e.g., low-rank sketch, hash summary) is provided as input to a hypernetwork that modulates computation; avoid full self-ingestion to prevent degenerate identity mappings.

8) Training objectives and regularization

- Compute-aware losses: Penalize depth, calls, or halting delay; optionally anneal penalties to first teach correctness, then sparsify compute.
- Curriculum over recursion depth: Start with shallow instances of the recursive structure; gradually increase depth or nesting.
- Structural supervision: Provide parse trees, program traces, or call/return annotations if available.
- Stability constraints: Spectral constraints, gradient clipping, or contraction losses; for DEQ, Jacobian regularization.

9) Evaluation criteria

- Depth generalization: Measure accuracy as structure depth or sequence length increases beyond training.
- Compute–accuracy Pareto: Evaluate accuracy versus expected recursive steps.
- Termination robustness: Zero probability of non-termination under evaluation distributions; audit with worst-case bounds.
- Faithfulness: For algorithmic tasks, exact output equivalence to reference recursive algorithms.

10) Relations to common LLM practices

- Chain-of-thought, self-consistency, and “self-reflection” via prompting are not architectural recursion; they are runtime strategies over a static architecture.
- Tool-use and self-calls through an external orchestrator become architectural recursion only if the orchestrator is embedded as differentiable control inside Gθ.
- RNNs are iterative but not necessarily recursive in the structural sense; introducing a call stack or split–combine semantics crosses into recursion.

11) Safety and resource control

- Termination guarantees: Enforce depth and compute caps; require provable well-foundedness via ranking functions for any learned router.
- Bounded self-reference: Disallow unrestricted self-weight access; use filtered summaries to reduce incentive for degenerate copying.
- Subcritical branching: Constrain router so expected branching factor times continuation probability remains below 1.
- Auditable traces: Log call trees and halting decisions for interpretability and debugging.

12) Open problems

- Learning halting policies that generalize out of distribution without collapse or over-compute.
- Efficient batching and parallelism for dynamic recursive graphs on accelerators.
- Stability of self-referential mechanisms that use weight summaries without causing feedback loops.
- Theoretical characterizations of generalization under recursive weight sharing in high-capacity sequence models.

Summary

Architectural recursion in LLMs is a property of the model’s computation graph: it contains input-conditioned, parameter-shared self-application with guaranteed termination. It can manifest as structural recursion over input hierarchies, temporal recursion via halting or fixed points, algorithmic recursion with differentiable stacks, or reflective/meta forms involving model descriptions. Properly designed, recursion enhances expressivity and systematic generalization while demanding careful treatment of halting, differentiation, stability, and compute control.

Architectural recursion in LLMs

1) Core definition
- Let Mθ be an LLM viewed as a conditional distribution or function Mθ: X → Y. Architectural recursion occurs when the system exposed to the user, Sθ, uses Mθ as a subroutine in a way that Sθ has the same input–output signature as Mθ and composes multiple calls to Mθ (possibly with shared parameters) to solve subproblems of the original input. The recursion is architectural when this composition is part of the system’s design, not just an incidental prompting trick.
- Formally, there is a higher-order operator R such that Sθ = R(Mθ). If training or calibration seeks θ with Mθ ≈ Sθ (self-consistency), we get a fixed-point objective Mθ ≈ R(Mθ).

2) Distinctions from related notions
- Recurrence vs recursion: Recurrence repeats computation with state (e.g., RNNs). Recursion makes self-calls on strictly smaller or simpler subproblems with base cases. Some architectures combine both.
- Prompt recursion vs architectural recursion: Prompts can direct a single forward pass to “think step by step.” Architectural recursion adds a controller, call stack, halting conditions, and possibly learned decomposition and combination modules.

3) Levels of architectural recursion
- Micro-level (intra-model): Weight-shared iterative application of the same block with dynamic halting (e.g., Universal Transformers, Adaptive Computation Time). This realizes a learned recursive computation on a latent structure with a base/step decision.
- Meso-level (inference-time controller): A controller decomposes a problem, invokes the same LLM on subproblems, and combines the results (e.g., tree/graph-of-thought, recursive summarization of document trees, recursive program repair).
- Macro-level (training-time self-composition): Teacher–student loops where an LLM generates supervision for an improved version of itself (self-distillation, self-training). The training operator T maps θk to θk+1; convergence seeks a fixed point of T that embodies recursive improvement.
- Reflective recursion: The model interprets instructions about itself; prompts or tools allow the model to call “itself” with modified context. This is governed by reflection control and well-foundedness to avoid paradoxes or non-termination.

4) Formal semantics
- A recursive system can be specified by a tuple (Mθ, πφ, decompφ, baseφ, combineφ, haltφ), where:
  - decompφ(x, Mθ) returns subproblems x1,…,xk (k may be 0).
  - haltφ(x) decides base case; baseφ(x) returns a direct answer if halting.
  - πφ is a policy over action choices if decomp is stochastic.
  - combineφ(x, answers) aggregates subanswers into a final answer.
- The denotation V of the system is the least fixed point of:
  V(x) = baseφ(x) if haltφ(x) else combineφ(x, [V(xi)] where [xi] = decompφ(x, Mθ)).
- Well-foundedness: There exists a measure μ: X → ℕ or ℝ≥0 such that for all non-base x, every xi satisfies μ(xi) < μ(x). Alternatively, impose budgets/depth limits and halting with probability 1.
- If Sθ = R(Mθ) is contractive in an appropriate metric over conditional distributions and training enforces Mθ ≈ Sθ, then iterating θ ← argminθ d(Mθ, R(Mθ)) converges to a unique fixed point (idealized statement; in practice approximate).

5) Credit assignment and training
- End-to-end differentiability is broken by discrete self-calls and halting. Options:
  - Imitation on traces: Supervise decomp/combination trees and subanswers; maximize likelihood of full traces.
  - Policy-gradient RL: Treat decomposition, call, and halting as actions; reward end accuracy and efficiency; use variance reduction and shaped rewards (e.g., depth penalties).
  - Straight-through/relaxations: Use differentiable surrogates for halting and mixture-of-experts routing; anneal to harder decisions.
  - Distillation: Use a powerful teacher controller to produce recursive traces; train a smaller student to emulate Sθ in one or fewer recursive layers.
- Caching/memoization during training stabilizes gradients and improves sample efficiency by reusing subcall results.

6) Computational implications
- Expressivity: With unbounded depth and halting, recursive architectures can implement general partial recursive functions; with finite expected depth and halting they approximate them.
- Algorithmic generalization: Weight sharing across depths promotes length/generalization (e.g., parsing Dyck languages, long addition/multiplication, hierarchical summarization). Recursion allows solutions that scale in depth like O(log n) or O(n) where flat transformers might require quadratic width or memorization.
- Cost–accuracy trade-offs: Adaptive halting yields input-conditional compute. Divide-and-conquer can lower asymptotic depth while controlling total tokens via fan-out limits.

7) Design patterns
- Structural recursion over trees: Map/fold over parse trees, XML/JSON, directory/file hierarchies. decomp extracts children; combine folds child summaries; halt at leaves or small subtrees.
- Problem decomposition: For search/planning/proofs, decomp proposes subgoals; recursion explores subgoals; combine selects/merges proofs or plans (with pruning and bounds).
- Propose–verify recursion: The model proposes candidates and recursively calls a checker subroutine (LLM or non-LLM) to verify/refute; combine iterates until a verified solution or budget exhaustion.
- Program synthesis/interpretation: The LLM emits code that itself calls the LLM as an oracle for sub-specifications; termination via test suites or proof obligations.
- Hierarchical retrieval: Coarse retrieval to select indices, then fine retrieval within selected shards; recursion over index hierarchy; combine merges evidence.

8) Safety, correctness, and resource control
- Failure modes: Non-termination, exponential blow-up, circular subproblems, error amplification across levels, self-fulfilling hallucination loops, jailbreaking via recursive prompt manipulation.
- Controls:
  - Static limits: Max depth, max total calls, max tokens per call, wall-clock budgets.
  - Well-founded measures: Enforce monotone decrease in a known complexity measure (length, tree height, problem size).
  - Halting mechanisms: Learned halting with calibration; penalties for depth or calls; anytime algorithms that can return best-so-far.
  - Type and contract systems: Typed function-calling, schemas for arguments/returns, pre/post-conditions checked by non-LLM validators.
  - Loop detection and memoization: Hash subproblems; reuse cached answers; detect cycles.
  - Redundancy and verification: N-version programming across branches; cross-checking; proof-carrying answers where verifiers are simpler than solvers.
  - Observability: Trace logging and telemetry for each recursive frame; reproducibility of runs for audits.

9) Evaluation methodology
- Measure scaling laws with allowed recursion depth vs flat baselines on:
  - Formal languages (Dyck-k), arithmetic algorithms, graph reachability, sorting.
  - Hierarchical QA/summarization on long documents or codebases.
  - Planning/proof tasks (theorem proving subsets, program repair).
- Report: accuracy vs compute (calls, tokens), termination rate, depth distribution, cache hit rates, robustness under distribution shift to larger structures, and ablations (disable recursion, disable memoization, share vs unshare weights).

10) Information-theoretic perspective
- Recursion compresses description length by reusing a single program across scales. The minimal description to generate an n-sized structure via a recursive scheme can be O(log n) where a flat description is O(n). This aligns with MDL: good recursive decompositions reduce the total codelength of answers plus model.
- Self-distillation as a fixed-point of a compression operator: R maps a base model to a composed solver with larger effective compute; distillation compresses R(Mθ) back into Mθ′. Iterating seeks an invariant distribution under “expand-then-compress.”
- Bottlenecks across levels: Each recursive call transmits a bounded message (prompt/latent). Good designs maximize mutual information between subcall I/O and the global solution while minimizing redundancy via caching and structured schemas.

11) Open problems
- Theoretical guarantees for convergence and stability of self-consistent recursive training operators beyond contractive toy settings.
- Learning well-founded decompositions with formal termination guarantees.
- Credit assignment across deep call graphs with low variance and strong sample efficiency.
- Robust reflection: enabling safe self-calls without pathological self-reference.
- Differentiable approximations that retain the benefits of discrete recursion while enabling stronger end-to-end learning.

Summary
Architectural recursion makes an LLM part of a system that calls the same LLM on subproblems under a controller with halting and combination rules. Formally, it realizes solutions as fixed points of a recursive operator and, when trained toward self-consistency, seeks models that implement these solutions directly. Done well, it yields algorithmic generalization, adaptive compute, and principled decomposition; it requires explicit design for well-foundedness, verification, and resource control.

Architectural recursion in LLMs: a precise expansion

1) Core definitions
- LLM: A parametric conditional distribution fθ(y | x) implemented by a transformer-like network.
- Architecture: The computation graph that maps inputs to outputs at inference, plus any system control that schedules calls, tools, and memory.
- Architectural recursion: Any design in which the computation that produces an output includes (directly or via a controller) calls to the same model class or instance, possibly with shared weights, and does so on subproblems until a base condition halts. This contrasts with mere iterative decoding (left-to-right token generation) by a single forward pass.

2) Axes and types of recursion
- Intra-model recursion (depth/time dimension)
  - Weight-tied depth recurrence: Reapplying the same transformer block multiple times with adaptive halting. Example: Universal Transformer, ACT, recurrent transformers, RecurrentGemma.
  - State recursion: Maintaining and updating a recurrent state across steps (KV cache reuse, memory modules).
- System-level recursion (self-calls under orchestration)
  - Self-invocation: The model (or a thin controller) uses the LLM to plan, decompose, or critique, then recursively calls the same LLM on subproblems (Tree-of-Thoughts, Self-Refine, Reflexion, debate).
  - LLM-of-LLMs: A controller LLM coordinates worker LLMs that are instances of the same base model in a call tree.
- Training-time recursion
  - Self-distillation/bootstrapping: Teacher and student are instances of the same model class across iterations (fixed-point seeking under a training operator).
  - Self-play and data self-generation: Model-generated distributions feed the next round of training.
- Reflective/meta recursion
  - Model reads/writes its own tools, prompts, and sometimes code that calls itself (meta-interpreters, toolformer-like systems). Potential for quining and fixed points.

3) Formalization
- Self-call schema
  - Let f be an oracle LLM mapping prompts to sampled outputs and traces. Define a recursive procedure Rec on a task t with decomposition D, base predicate B, combine operator C, and policy π:
    - If B(t) holds, return f(prompt(t)).
    - Else, S = D(t) produces subproblems t1,…,tk using f and π.
    - For i in 1..k, ri = Rec(ti).
    - Return C(t, r1,…,rk) using f if needed.
  - Rec builds a call tree whose internal nodes are decompositions/critique and leaves are base solutions.
- Fixed-point perspective
  - Many designs solve F = H(F), where H maps a solver to a new solver built by orchestrating that solver as a subroutine (e.g., “use f to propose, evaluate, and improve”). Existence and stability depend on H being a contraction on an appropriate function space or lattice.
- Internal recurrence
  - Let Bθ be a block. Define s_{d+1} = Bθ(s_d, x), with halting h(s_d) deciding per-position depth. This is structural recursion on depth with base case at h = true. It endows variable compute per token and yields T(x) = s_{halt}.

4) Correctness and termination
- Termination conditions
  - Well-founded measure m(t) such that each decomposition strictly reduces m with high probability or tight budget control (depth and call limits).
  - Deterministic halting in intra-model recurrence (ACT) or explicit recursion depth bound D.
- Correctness invariants
  - Decompose-combine laws: For tasks where a monoid-like structure exists, require C(t, map solve over D(t)) equals the ground-truth solution. Otherwise, certifiers or tests act as external validators.
- Contracts
  - Purity: Each node’s result depends only on its prompt and stochastic seed; controller preserves referential transparency for reproducibility.
  - Idempotence and commutativity assumptions where needed for aggregation.

5) Information-theoretic view
- Error recurrence
  - Let e_d be the error rate at recursion depth d. With k independent subcalls and a majority or argmax-by-LLM-judge aggregator, e_{d+1} ≈ g_k(e_d) where g_k(e) < e for sufficiently small e and low correlation; yields exponential decay (boosting-like). Correlation between subcalls weakens gains.
  - Self-consistency (voting over sampled reasoning chains) reduces error roughly according to binomial tails under approximate independence; improvements saturate as dependence grows.
- Entropy and mutual information
  - Without new external information, the mutual information with the true answer is bounded by what is computable from the input and the model’s parameters; recursion reallocates compute to better approximate latent algorithms, not to exceed information-theoretic limits.
  - With tools or retrieval, recursion can import new information, increasing MI.
- Bias/variance trade-off
  - Decomposition can reduce variance (aggregation) but risks bias amplification if decomposition is systematically wrong; formalize as bias recursion b_{d+1} = A(b_d) + δ where A is aggregation bias operator and δ is decomposition error.

6) Complexity and resource bounds
- For divide-and-conquer with branching factor a, shrink factor b, and overhead f(n), the expected cost satisfies T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n); the Master Theorem gives asymptotics. Practical policies should target sublinear f and effective b<1.
- Compute scaling for depth recurrence: C ≈ sum over tokens of halting depth; budgeted via ACT penalties or hard caps.
- Memory: Recursion tree width controls concurrency; impose arity limits and streaming combine to bound memory.

7) Design patterns (schemas)
- Hierarchical summarization/QA
  - D: partition document; Base: segment-level answers; C: recursive synthesis; add verifier node to check factual consistency with retrieval at each level.
- Recursive code generation
  - D: decompose spec into functions/tests using f; Base: implement leaf functions; C: integrate, run tests; recurse on failing tests with repair loops; terminate by coverage or budget.
- Plan-refine-verify
  - Plan: f proposes plan; Refine: recursively elaborate steps; Verify: f-as-judge or external tests; Backtrack on failures with bounded breadth-first or depth-first search.
- Self-critique loops
  - Solve: f produces answer with rationale; Critique: the same f spots errors; Improve: f revises; repeat up to K iterations or until critique is empty.

8) Internal architectural recursion options for LLMs
- Weight sharing across layers with adaptive depth (Universal Transformer): achieves algorithmic generalization with fewer parameters; introduces halting policies per position.
- Recurrent memory controllers: a small controller recursively updates memory slots and attends over them (structured state recursion).
- Differentiable stacks/trees for explicit structural recursion over parse/program trees (rare in production LLMs but principled).

9) Training-time recursion as operators
- Self-distillation operator T: θ_{k+1} = Train(Data ∪ Sample(f_{θ_k})). Fixed points θ* satisfy approximate self-consistency. Stability requires spectral radius of the Jacobian J_T(θ*) < 1 around θ* or curriculum/regularization to avoid collapse.
- Self-play operator in reinforcement learning: policies generate data for their own improvement; convergence requires opponent/arena diversity or regularization to prevent cyclic forgetting.

10) Safety and governance of recursion
- Halting guarantees: enforce depth, node, and wall-clock budgets; use monotone ranking functions; detect repeated states (cycle checks via trace hashing).
- Robust aggregation: prefer certified checks (compilers, unit tests, theorem provers) over LLM-judging when possible; when using LLM judges, diversify seeds/models to reduce correlated error.
- Prompt isolation and capability scoping: different roles use constrained toolsets and sanitized contexts to prevent prompt injection and unintended tool misuse.
- Logging and causality: maintain a full call tree with inputs, outputs, seeds, and tool results for auditability and post hoc error attribution.

11) Empirical hypotheses and tests
- Hypothesis H1: For tasks with correct decompositions and low inter-branch error correlation, accuracy improves monotonically with modest recursion depth D before saturating. Test: vary D and branching, measure accuracy and compute-normalized gains.
- Hypothesis H2: Adaptive depth recurrence inside the transformer yields better length and algorithmic generalization at comparable parameter counts. Test: compare weight-tied depth with fixed-depth baselines on algorithmic suites.
- Hypothesis H3: Self-distillation converges to a stable fixed point only with diversity injection (data refresh, noise, or multi-teacher). Test: track calibration, entropy, and performance across generations with/without diversity.

12) Limits and failure modes
- Correlated reasoning reduces benefits of aggregation; diversity mechanisms (different prompts, temperatures, or model variants) partially mitigate.
- Decomposition brittleness: wrong task splits create unsalvageable subproblems; invest in learned decomposition with verifiable subgoals.
- Cost explosion: recursion trees can grow superlinearly; require strict arity, pruning, and early stopping criteria.
- Overfitting in self-training: distributional drift toward model’s own errors (model collapse); counter by mixing in gold data and uncertainty-aware sampling.

13) Minimal abstract interface
- Primitive call: result, trace = Call(f, prompt, seed, budget)
- Recursion driver: Rec(task; f, D, B, C, π, limits)
- Verifier: v = Verify(task, result; tools)
- Policy: π maps traces and verifier outcomes to next actions (expand, prune, stop)

Summary
Architectural recursion in LLMs is the principled use of self-application—either internally via weight-shared depth/time recurrence or externally via system-level self-calls—to implement divide-and-conquer, self-critique, and variable-compute algorithms with halting guarantees. A rigorous treatment specifies decomposition/combination laws, termination via well-founded measures or budgets, information-theoretic error recursions, complexity bounds for the induced call tree, and safety controls. Properly constrained, recursive architectures can convert parametric knowledge into more reliable computation; unconstrained, they risk non-termination, correlated error amplification, and collapse.

Definition
Architectural recursion in LLMs is any computation scheme in which an LLM (or a module indistinguishable from it from the orchestrator’s perspective) is invoked as a subroutine within a composite procedure that itself may (directly or indirectly) invoke the same composite procedure on derived subproblems, establish self-referential generation/evaluation loops, or iterate model-to-model transformations. The recursion is architectural when it is realized by the system’s structure and control flow (not merely when the model internally “thinks” stepwise).

Three levels
- Micro (inference-time orchestration): A fixed model fθ is embedded in a higher-order program R that uses fθ to (a) decide whether to recurse, (b) generate subproblems, and (c) solve leaves, with R calling itself on subproblems.
- Meso (training-time bootstrapping): A transformation T maps a current model (or its outputs) to training data, targets, or a new model θ′; repeated application θ, T(θ), T(T(θ)), … forms a recursion over the model space.
- Macro (architecture/meta-design): A meta-procedure A uses models to propose, evaluate, and revise architectures or hyperparameters, e.g., LLM-assisted NAS; iterating A induces a recursion over design configurations.

Core formalization
- Let fθ: X → Δ(Y*) be the base LLM (stochastic map from inputs to distributions over strings).
- A recursive orchestrator is a tuple O = (B, D, C, H):
  - B: X → {halt, continue} (base-test; may query fθ).
  - D: X × RNG → P(X) (decompose x into subproblems; may query fθ).
  - C: X × Y* × P(Y*) → Y* (combine a root proposal with subsolutions; may query fθ).
  - H: X × budget → policy controlling depth/branching; may be deterministic or query fθ.
- The recursive solver Rθ,O on input x is:
  - If B(x) = halt, return fθ(x).
  - Else let S = D(x); compute yi = Rθ,O(xi) for xi ∈ S subject to H; get y0 = fθ(x); return C(x, y0, {yi}).
- This encompasses self-asking, task decomposition, tree-of-thought search, self-refinement (C uses feedback to requery fθ), and tool-augmented recursive calls.

Termination and well-foundedness
- A sufficient condition is a well-founded measure m: X → ℕ such that with probability ≥ 1 − ε each xi ∈ D(x) satisfies m(xi) < m(x), and with bounded recursion depth d, Pr[non-termination] ≤ O(ε d b) where b is branching factor.
- For stochastic D, enforce H with depth/breadth caps, and optionally require expected decrease E[m(xi) − m(x) | x] < −δ < 0.

Error propagation and contraction
- Let e(d) be the error rate at depth d leaves, and let C’s aggregation error be Lipschitz in the child errors with factor L < 1 in expectation (e.g., majority voting with independent subcalls, or evaluator-guided selection with calibrated scoring). Then e(d+1) ≤ a + L e(d) for some base a; if L < 1, errors contract toward a/(1 − L).
- Self-refinement loop y ← fθ(x), s ← fθ(eval(x, y)), y′ ← fθ(rewrite(x, y, s)) is a recursion over outputs. If the evaluator’s signal correlates with task accuracy and rewrite preserves or improves this signal stochastically, the induced Markov operator over outputs can be a contraction under a suitable metric (e.g., 1 − agreement score), yielding convergence in expectation.

Compute and cache complexity
- Expected call cost with branching b and depth h is Θ(∑i=0..h b^i) without memoization; with canonicalization and caching of subproblems, cost is Θ(U) where U is the number of unique subproblems realized. Designing D to re-use subproblems and C to be associative/commutative enables dynamic programming.

Information-theoretic view
- Each decomposition step should reduce conditional entropy of subproblems given the parent (H(Xi | X) < H(X)) and preserve enough mutual information to reconstruct the solution (I(Y; {Yi}) large). Summarization within recursion is a lossy channel with distortion δ; require cumulative distortion ∑ δi below a task-dependent threshold to maintain solvability. Data processing inequality implies excessive recursive summarization will eventually degrade solutions unless compensated by added external information (tools, retrieval).

Taxonomy of recursive patterns
- Divide-and-conquer reasoning: D proposes subclaims, R proves them recursively, C assembles a proof/solution.
- Self-asking QA: recursively generate subqueries; base cases answered directly; C fuses answers.
- Tree/graph search: R is depth/breadth-limited search where node expansion and evaluation use fθ (e.g., ToT, MCTS with LLM priors and critics).
- Self-refinement: iterated critique-and-revise cycles; equivalently, recursion over outputs with evaluator-guided contraction.
- Recursive retrieval: queries generate follow-up queries; base case is confident answer; C aggregates multi-hop evidence.
- Program synthesis with recursive specs: model proposes function stubs and tests, recurses on subroutines.
- Multi-agent recursive calls: the “same” base model plays different roles with role-conditioned prompts; mutual recursion between roles.
- Reflective prediction: model predicts its own or ensemble outputs (self-consistency); recursion over beliefs.

Training-time recursion
- Self-training/distillation operator T: θ → θ′ by generating labeled data with θ (optionally filtered by an evaluator) and retraining. Iterating T can converge to a fixed point θ* satisfying θ* ≈ T(θ*), when capacity and data distributions stabilize; without constraints it can amplify biases (Goodharting).
- Self-play and debate: Two or more role-conditioned copies of fθ generate adversarial data; under monotone best-response dynamics and appropriate payoff structure, empirical convergence to equilibria can occur.
- Iterated preference optimization (RLAIF): a model proposes outputs and judgments that train the next model; stability requires calibrated judging and diversity mechanisms to avoid mode collapse.

Meta-architectural recursion
- Architecture search operator A maps a design h (layers, MoE topology, tool interfaces) to a revised design h′ using model-driven proposals and evaluations. Iterating A seeks fixed points h* ≈ A(h*). Practical stability requires regularity (small perturbations in h produce small changes in validation metrics) and bounded search steps (trust regions).

Connections to recursion theory and fixed points
- Kleene’s recursion theorem (informal analogy): for any computable transformer T that maps program descriptions to programs, there exists a program p that outputs the same as T given p’s description. Architectural analogues include quining prompts and meta-circular interpreters: prompts that cause the model to emit a description of the very recursive procedure executing it, or orchestrators that interpret specifications in the same language they’re expressed in.
- Banach fixed-point heuristic: design evaluators/aggregators such that the iterative map over outputs or models is a contraction in a chosen metric (e.g., KL-regularized improvement), ensuring convergence.

Design constraints and guarantees
- Soundness: If leaves are sound with probability ≥ 1 − ε and C is verifiably sound (or uses external verifiers), overall soundness can be lower-bounded; otherwise recursive hallucinations can snowball.
- Calibration: Evaluators used inside recursion must be better-than-chance and preferably calibrated; miscalibrated critics cause divergence via selection bias.
- Budget and depth control: Enforce hard limits, adaptive stopping (confidence thresholds), and anytime properties.
- Type discipline: Define schemas for subproblems and interfaces; enforce parseability and role separation to avoid prompt drift.
- Memoization and purity: Canonicalize subproblems; prefer functional (stateless) subcalls to ease caching and reproducibility.
- Provenance and traces: Maintain call stacks and decision logs for audit and post-hoc validation.

Evaluation metrics
- Performance vs depth/branching curves, sample efficiency per additional recursive layer.
- Reliability under perturbations: ablate evaluator accuracy, noise in D, summarization budgets.
- Trace correctness: fraction of subgoals correctly solved; error localization.
- Convergence diagnostics for self-refinement: improvement per iteration, fixed-point residuals.
- Compute-accuracy Pareto and wall-clock predictability.

Failure modes and mitigations
- Non-termination or explosion: add well-founded measures, depth caps, and penalties for expansion.
- Hallucination amplification: use external verifiers, retrieval grounding, and skeptical aggregators.
- Mode collapse in self-training: enforce diversity (temperature schedules, negative sampling), and periodic anchoring to ground-truth data.
- Context bloat and drift: hierarchical state compression with bounded distortion; periodic re-grounding on the original specification.

Illustrative instantiations
- Self-ask and ToT: O implements D via question generation, B via confidence checks, C via reasoning synthesis.
- Reflexion-style refinement: recursion over outputs with fθ acting as both proposer and critic (or critic is a specialized model).
- MCTS with LLM priors/critics: recursive search where fθ expands nodes and evaluates rollouts; C selects best leaf under UCT.
- Iterated distillation/debate: T composes generation, evaluation, and retraining; A optionally revises the model’s interfaces/tools.

Open problems
- Formal conditions under which common recursive schemes are contractions (choice of metrics, calibrations, and noise models).
- Tight error bounds for stochastic, dependent subcalls (beyond independence assumptions).
- Rate-distortion limits for deep recursive summarization with bounded context.
- Stability of long self-training chains under distribution shift and adversarial examples.
- Principled design of reflective evaluators that remain robust to strategic exploitation by the same base model.

Takeaway
Architectural recursion turns a static LLM into a component of a higher-order algorithm with explicit base cases, decomposition, aggregation, and control policies. With well-founded measures, calibrated evaluators, and contraction-like properties, these recursive systems can be both more capable and more reliable than single-pass generation; without them, they risk divergence, bias amplification, and uncontrolled compute growth. The key is to make the recursion explicit, typed, verifiable, budgeted, and (when possible) convergent.

Architectural recursion in LLMs

1) Core definition
- An LLM is used as a component inside an algorithm that calls (instances of) the same model on subproblems generated during inference or training, forming a well-founded call graph whose nodes are LLM invocations. Architectural recursion is “architectural” because the system design enforces self-calls (with possibly different prompts, tools, or weights), not merely repeated tokens or longer chains of thought.
- Formal schema. Let Mθ: P → Δ(T) be a base model mapping prompts to text distributions. A recursive solver S is defined by the tuple (B, Base, Decompose, Select, Combine, Verify, Budget):
  - B(x): base-case predicate
  - Base(x): direct solver for base cases
  - Decompose(Mθ, x) → {x1, …, xk}: LLM-guided subproblem proposals
  - Select(Mθ, x, {xi}) → subset: chooses which subproblems to pursue (pruning)
  - Recursive calls: yi = S(xi)
  - Combine(Mθ, x, {yi}) → y: LLM-guided synthesis of a solution from subsolutions
  - Verify(x, y) → {accept, reject, revise}: external or internal checker
  - Budget: termination conditions on depth, branching, tokens, or time
  - S(x) = Base(x) if B(x) else Combine(Mθ, x, { S(xi) for xi in Select(Mθ, x, Decompose(Mθ, x)) }) with Verify gating acceptance. Well-foundedness requires a ranking function μ with μ(xi) < μ(x) for selected subproblems or an explicit depth limit.

2) Taxonomy of recursion in and around LLMs
- Inference-time self-calls (problem decomposition)
  - Self-ask/self-decompose: the model proposes subquestions and answers them via further self-calls.
  - Tree/graph search: branching over alternative decompositions or partial solutions; combine via voting, proofs, or best-first selection.
  - Recursive tool use: calls to retrieval, code execution, or formal solvers that themselves invoke the LLM to generate subqueries or functions.
- Structural recursion inside the network
  - Recurrent/weight-tied transformers (e.g., universal transformers, stateful recurrence across segments) instantiate the same block across steps; this is recursion over time within the forward pass rather than via external calls.
- Training-time recursion (bootstrapping)
  - Iterated amplification/distillation: Amp(π) builds a tree of subproblem solutions using policy π; then distill a new π′ to imitate Amp(π). Fixed points π* ≈ Amp(π*) define a recursive policy.
  - Self-play/self-training: model generates data or feedback for its own improvement (debate, critique-refine, weak-to-strong).
- Meta-recursive models
  - Hypernetworks or editors that produce modified weights θ′ = H(θ, task) and then run Mθ′, possibly nesting this process.
  - Meta-circular prompting: the model is prompted to emulate a controller that would invoke the model recursively (quasi-interpreters).

3) Reasons to make recursion architectural
- Expressivity: naturally handles recursively structured data (trees, programs, proofs) and divide-and-conquer algorithms.
- Reliability amplification: if subclaims are verifiable, recursion can reduce end-to-end error via verification, majority, or proof checking.
- Compute targeting: allocate depth and breadth to hard parts only; asymptotically improve sample efficiency when subproblems are simpler.
- Modularity and reuse: enables memoization and caching of subresults; supports libraries of subskills.

4) Formal properties and guarantees
- Termination
  - S terminates if there exists a well-founded order (X, ≺) with xi ≺ x for all selected xi, or if Budget enforces a depth bound D and branching bound b.
- Error composition (simplified)
  - Suppose each leaf answer is correct with probability p, independent across k leaves, and Combine is correct if at least m of k leaves are correct. Then error decreases with depth when verification/aggregation is strong (Chernoff-type bounds). Without verification, error compounds roughly as 1 − p^(#leaves).
  - With an external checker Verify of false-accept rate α and false-reject rate β, you can bound overall failure via union bounds on accepts and geometric bounds for revise loops.
- Complexity
  - If T_base is cost of Base and T_llm is one call, then expected cost E[T] ≈ sum over levels d=0..D of E[b_d] · T_llm plus tool costs, where E[b_d] depends on Select/Verify pruning. Memoization can reduce E[b_d] for overlapping subproblems to the number of unique subinstances.
- Fixed-point framing (amplification)
  - Define an amplification operator A mapping a policy π to the policy that uses π as a subroutine under a recursive controller. Iterating θ_{k+1} ← Distill(A(M_{θ_k})) can converge to a π* satisfying π* ≈ A(π*), yielding a self-consistent recursive policy.

5) Design patterns that instantiate the schema
- Decompose–Solve–Compose with guardrails
  - Decompose proposes a DAG over subclaims with a ranking function μ.
  - Solve recurses with caching and a budget.
  - Combine drafts a solution; Verify enforces constraints (tests, proofs, type checks, execution).
  - Revise loop runs until accept or budget exhausted; fallback to baseline answer if needed.
- Multi-hypothesis tree search
  - Keep top-k decompositions; expand best-first by a learned value function; backtrack on verification failure.
- Recursive retrieval
  - Queries generate subqueries until a coverage predicate is met; combine synthesizes from retrieved shards; verify via factual cross-checks.
- Hierarchical planning
  - High-level planner decomposes goals into subgoals; low-level controllers act; verifiers check subgoal completion; plans refine recursively.

6) Engineering constraints and invariants
- Well-foundedness: define and check a ranking function μ(x) that strictly decreases on recursion; otherwise impose a hard depth limit.
- Idempotence and purity: make Combine and Verify as deterministic and side-effect-free as possible to simplify caching and reproducibility.
- Caching and deduplication: canonicalize subproblems to obtain memoization; use content-addressed storage keyed by canonical prompts.
- Budgeting: tokens, time, calls, branching factor; terminate early on diminishing returns estimated by confidence or value.
- Interfaces: serialize subcalls with typed schemas (function-calling) so Combine and Verify have structured I/O; track a call stack and provenance.
- Verification-first: prefer subclaims with machine-checkable verifiers (tests, formal proofs, execution traces, constraint solvers).
- Control variability: reduce randomness deeper in the recursion; anneal temperature by depth; use consistent decoding for verifiable steps.

7) Evaluation methodology
