Definitions and setup
- Fix a universal Turing machine U. Write ⟨p⟩ for the binary encoding of program p.
- A performance measure P : Programs × Environments → R is a (total) function that quantifies how well a program performs in an environment. Examples: expected reward, worst-case running time (negated so “larger is better”), success probability, etc.
- Environment E is any (possibly probabilistic) source of inputs and feedback; E may be compactly described or have high entropy.
- A self-improving algorithm S is a computable program that, when run, may (possibly using randomness and interaction with E) output a new program S′ intended to satisfy P(S′, E) > P(S, E) (or increase P in expectation). More generally, S may output a sequence S0 = S, S1, S2, … where Si+1 = S produces Si+1.

We are interested in what S “creates” when it outputs S′ (or a sequence of Si): new program descriptions, algorithmic information, performance improvements, empirical knowledge, etc.

Proposition 1 — creation of program descriptions (trivial)
A self‑improving algorithm can produce new binary descriptions ⟨S′⟩.  
Proof sketch: S is itself a computing entity; outputting a string ⟨S′⟩ is a standard computable operation.

Remark: This is the weakest sense of “create”: emitting syntax. The interesting questions are about information content, provability of improvement, and limits.

Proposition 2 — bound on algorithmic information produced without external input
If S is a computable program that, without reading any external input other than its own code and its internal randomness r, outputs ⟨S′⟩, then
K(⟨S′⟩) ≤ K(⟨S⟩) + K(r) + O(1),
and in particular, for deterministic S (no external randomness), K(⟨S′⟩) ≤ K(⟨S⟩) + O(1).
Here K(·) is prefix Kolmogorov complexity (relative to U).  
Proof sketch: Given ⟨S⟩ and r we can simulate S to produce ⟨S′⟩; by definition of K, the complexity of the output is at most the complexity of the inputs plus a constant for the simulator. If S is deterministic, r is empty, giving the stated bound.

Corollary 2.1 — no unbounded creation of algorithmic information from nothing
A self-improver that has access only to its own finite code cannot generate outputs whose Kolmogorov complexity exceeds that code by more than a constant. Thus a completely closed self-improver cannot create arbitrarily large new algorithmic information.

Interpretation: “Creation” of algorithmic (Kolmogorov) information requires either (a) external inputs of high complexity (data, oracles, randomness) or (b) already having high complexity in the initial program.

Proposition 3 — external data / randomness as information sources
If S uses external data I (a string) or true random bits r as input when producing ⟨S′⟩, then
K(⟨S′⟩) ≤ K(⟨S⟩) + K(I) + K(r) + O(1).
Thus any increase in K(⟨S′⟩) above K(⟨S⟩) is accounted for by the complexity of the external inputs consumed.  
Proof sketch: same simulation argument with S plus inputs I,r.

Proposition 4 — empirical/semantic information can increase even when algorithmic information cannot
Although Kolmogorov complexity is bounded as above, a self‑improver can increase its empirical knowledge and improve expected performance in environment E by absorbing observations from E and incorporating them into its code or parameters. This increases mutual information between the program’s behavior and E and can increase P(S′, E).  
Explanation: Empirical data need not be algorithmically incompressible relative to the observer; storing relevant statistics or models increases the program’s effective competence in that environment even if the description complexity (K) doesn’t increase dramatically.

Proposition 5 — existence of arbitrarily large speedups (Blum speedup phenomenon)
There exist computable problems (total functions or decision predicates) for which there is no single "optimal" program: for any program p computing the function, there is another program q that computes the same function but is strictly better according to some complexity measure (e.g., time) on infinitely many inputs, and one can construct infinite sequences of asymptotically improving programs.  
Consequence: In principle, there are tasks for which self‑improvement can keep producing strictly better programs indefinitely (in the chosen measure).

Caveat: The sequence of successively better programs may be pathological and hard or impossible to effectively find/prove optimality of each step — see Proposition 6.

Proposition 6 — undecidability and limits of provable improvement
For nontrivial semantic properties about program behavior (e.g., “program q computes the same function as p and is strictly faster on all inputs” or “P(q,E) > P(p,E) for all inputs”), Rice’s theorem and related undecidability results imply such statements are undecidable in general. Therefore:
- A general-purpose self-improver cannot always effectively verify that a candidate output is a true improvement over all inputs.
- Any scheme that claims to produce provably optimal self‑improvement must rely on restricted domains, or on heuristics, or on external oracles (or be incomplete).  
Proof sketch: Rice’s theorem: any nontrivial semantic property of computable functions is undecidable; comparing global performance is such a property.

Proposition 7 — self-reference and fixed points (Kleene recursion theorem)
For any computable operator F that maps program descriptions to program descriptions, there exists a program p such that U(⟨p⟩) = U(F(⟨p⟩)) (i.e., p can obtain the effect of applying F to its own code). As a corollary, a program can construct a transformed version of itself in a way that depends on its own description. This enables consistent self-referential self‑improvement procedures.  
Consequence: Self‑improvement can be made self-consistent; there exist programs that “know their own code” up to the extent used in the transformation.

Proposition 8 — resource accounting: improvements shift resource usage but don’t violate conservation
A self‑improver that achieves faster running time may do so at the cost of other resources (more precomputation, larger memory, larger code size). Formal tradeoffs follow from time-space complexity theorems. In particular, any asymptotic improvement often redistributes resource consumption; nothing thermodynamically free appears. If external randomness or oracle answers are used to obtain an improved program, those resources must be accounted for.

Synthesis — what self-improving algorithms create (strictly and logically)
From the above propositions we conclude, with minimal assumptions, the following logically precise characterization:

1. Syntax: Self‑improvers create new program descriptions (syntactic artifacts) trivially. (Prop. 1)
2. Algorithmic information: They cannot generate unbounded new algorithmic information from nothing; any increase in Kolmogorov complexity of outputs is bounded by the complexity of the program plus the complexity of external inputs (data, randomness, or oracles). (Props. 2–3)
3. Empirical/semantic competence: They can create empirically useful information and behavior (better performance in a specific environment) by absorbing and encoding environment-specific data; this is not in conflict with (2) because the relevant information originates in the environment. (Prop. 4)
4. Sequences of improvements: For some tasks there exist infinite sequences of strictly improving programs (speedups). So self‑improvement in principle can be unbounded with respect to some performance measures. (Prop. 5)
5. Limits of verification: Whether a candidate is globally an improvement is, in general, undecidable; thus guaranteed, provable self‑improvement is limited to restricted domains, heuristics, or reliance on external oracles/proofs. (Prop. 6)
6. Self-reference: Self‑improvers can be made self‑referential and can output transformations of their own code (fixed points exist). (Prop. 7)
7. Resource tradeoffs: Improvements typically redistribute resource usage and consume external resources (data, randomness, compute) rather than create free computational power. (Prop. 8)

Short formal corollary (compact)
Let S be a computable self‑improver that, without external inputs, produces a sequence ⟨S0⟩, ⟨S1⟩, … . Then sup_i K(⟨Si⟩) ≤ K(⟨S0⟩) + O(1). If the sequence exhibits strictly increasing performance P(Si,E) → ∞ (or approaches an unattainable optimum), then the required information for those improvements must, at some steps, come from either:
- external input/data drawn from E, or
- noncomputable processes/oracles, or
- hidden complexity already present in S0 (i.e., S0 must encode an index into the improvements).

Practical implications for designing self‑improvers
- To create genuinely new algorithmic sophistication, supply high‑quality external data, randomness, or oracles; do not expect a small bootstrap program to magically invent unbounded novel algorithmic content.
- Expect undecidability and provability limits; design verification and improvement criteria to be empirical or domain‑restricted.
- Use self‑referential constructions (recursion theorem) to make self‑improvement pipelines internally coherent.
- Track resource tradeoffs: improvements rarely come for free — they substitute or require other resources.

- or explore how these statements change when we replace Kolmogorov complexity with resource‑bounded complexity (time‑bounded K, circuit complexity, etc.). Which would you prefer?

I will treat “self-improving algorithms” as a formal object in the intersection of computability/recursion theory and algorithmic information theory (Kolmogorov complexity). Below I expand the concept strictly and logically: I give a formal model, state concrete propositions (with sketches of why they hold), and list the main logical consequences and limits. I state assumptions explicitly.

Setup and definitions (formal model)
- Fix a finite alphabet Σ and identify programs with finite strings in Σ*.
- Let K(x) denote plain Kolmogorov complexity of string x (relative to some fixed universal Turing machine), up to O(1) additive constants.
- A self-improvement operator S is a partial computable function S: Σ* × Σ* → Σ*. Intuitively, given a current program p ∈ Σ* and a datum d ∈ Σ* (which may encode observations, tests, proofs, random bits, etc.), S(p,d) outputs a new program p' = S(p,d). S is the mechanism by which a program generates its successors.
- A self-improvement run is a finite or infinite sequence p0, p1, p2, … with pi+1 = S(pi, di) for some data items di (possibly produced by interacting with an environment). The tuple of data items up to step n is Dn = (d0,…,d_{n-1}).
- We call pi an improvement over pj (for some performance measure Perf) when Perf(pi) > Perf(pj) according to a specified metric (correctness, runtime on a task class T, expected reward, etc.).

Proposition 1 (Information budget: algorithmic information cannot be created ex nihilo)
Let S be a fixed computable self-improvement operator and p0 an initial program. For any finite run p0 → p1 → … → pn with data Dn, the Kolmogorov complexity of pn satisfies
K(pn) ≤ K(S) + K(p0) + K(Dn) + O(log n).
(Equivalently, K(pn) ≤ K(S) + K(p0) + Σ_{i< n} K(di) + O(log n).)

Sketch of proof.
- The pair (S, p0, Dn) determines pn via the computable function that simulates the run. Therefore, pn can be described by a program of size K(S)+K(p0)+K(Dn)+O(log n) (the O(log n) encodes n or a self-delimiting encoding); by definition of K(·) the inequality follows.

Corollary (No free algorithmic information without external input).
If the data sequence Dn is empty or has bounded complexity independent of n (for example di are constant or low-complexity), then K(pn) is bounded by K(S)+K(p0)+O(log n). Thus a self-improver that receives no new algorithmically-complex inputs cannot produce arbitrarily high algorithmic complexity in its outputs.

Interpretation:
- A self-improving process can only "create" algorithmic information to the extent that information was present in its initial state, in S itself, or in the incoming data. It can transform/redistribute information (for instance compressing repeated structure into concise code), but it cannot produce arbitrarily more Kolmogorov complexity than its inputs provide.

Proposition 2 (Compression and reuse vs. genuine novelty)
A self-improver can transform large amounts of observational data into compact programs (structure extraction). This can make pn appear much more "powerful" than p0 while K(pn) remains small because the useful information was present in Dn in describable (possibly redundant) form.

Example/Remark:
- Learning from many labeled examples can yield a compact model (small K) even though performance improves dramatically; the apparent "creation" of structure is in fact extraction and compression of environmental information.

Proposition 3 (Fixed points and self-reference: Kleene recursion theorem)
For any computable transformation T that maps program texts to program texts, there exists a program q such that q and T(q) compute the same function; more concretely, there exists q with q ≡ T(q) (where ≡ denotes extensional equality of the computed partial function).

Implication:
- There exist self-referential programs that can output “improved” versions that know their own code or maintain invariants; this underlies reliable self-replication and certain forms of provable self-modification.

Proposition 4 (Limits from undecidability: no general computable operator guaranteeing (semantic) improvement)
There is no computable operator S that, given an arbitrary program p and arbitrary specification of a nontrivial semantic property (e.g., “has strictly smaller worst-case runtime on problem class T” or “computes the same function but faster”), always produces p' such that the desired nontrivial semantic property holds, uniformly for all inputs. More precisely, deciding whether a candidate p' has the semantic property is in general undecidable (Rice’s theorem), and hence no computable S can reliably and uniformly produce guaranteed correct semantic improvements for all p.

Sketch of reasoning.
- Rice’s theorem: any nontrivial extensional property of program behavior is undecidable. To guarantee semantic improvement one would need to decide such properties across arbitrary programs, which is impossible computably. Thus general guaranteed self-improvement that verifies arbitrary semantic gains cannot be accomplished by a computable operator.

Corollary (Verification bottleneck)
- A computable self-improver cannot, in general, verify that a proposed change yields a genuine semantic improvement except in restricted classes where the property is decidable or provable within some formal system and the search is effective.

Proposition 5 (Blum speedup phenomenon: no single optimal algorithm for some problems)
There exist computable problems f such that for every program p that computes f, there is another program q computing f whose resource usage (e.g., time) is asymptotically strictly better on infinitely many inputs. That is, for some problems no optimal program exists—there is an infinite strictly improving chain of programs.

Implications for self-improvers:
- Theoretically, a self-improver could produce an infinite sequence of asymptotically improving programs for such problems. But constructing each successive improvement may require runs whose resource costs or search complexity are prohibitive or even nonconstructive. Some speedups are themselves not effectively enumerable.

Proposition 6 (Limits from provability: Gödel/Löb consequences)
If a self-improver only accepts modifications that it can prove within a fixed formal system F to be improvements, then there are true improvements that it will never accept because the corresponding correctness or improvement statements may be unprovable in F. Moreover, an agent that reasons about its own future behavior faces Gödel-Löb style constraints in proving soundness of self-modifications; careful formalizations show that requiring strong self-trust forces trade-offs or the use of stronger axioms.

Interpretation:
- Proof-based self-improvement strategies (search for provably-better code) are sound in the sense of avoiding many mistakes, but are inherently incomplete: provability limitations block some genuine improvements.

Proposition 7 (Oracles and relativization)
If S is allowed oracle access to a set O (e.g., the halting oracle), the bounds and possibilities above relativize: K^O(pn) ≤ K^O(S) + K^O(p0) + K^O(Dn) + O(log n), and some previously impossible searches become possible relative to O. In particular, with powerful oracles one can solve some verification/search problems that are otherwise undecidable. But even with oracles, practical resource constraints and new relativized limits may remain.

Synthesis: what self-improving algorithms “create”
- They create new program texts (syntactic outputs) and associated behaviors (algorithms) by transforming their own code and/or using external data.
- In the algorithmic-information sense they do not conjure arbitrary new Kolmogorov information: the complexity of their outputs is bounded by the complexity of the self-improver mechanism plus the information in the inputs/environment.
- In the computational-power and performance sense, they can produce genuine and unbounded (in principle) improvements for some tasks (e.g., Blum-type speedups), but these improvements are constrained by undecidability, provability, and resource limitations. Some improvements are non-uniform or nonconstructive and may not be reachable by any effective S.
- In the epistemic/verification sense, there is a tension: methods that rely on empirical testing can be fooled or fail to generalize; methods that rely on formal proof are incomplete because of Gödel-style barriers; methods that search exhaustively for better code are limited by computability and resource costs.

Concrete logical corollaries (quick list)
1. Any compact description of a powerful self-improver (small K(S)) implies that the sequence of outputs cannot contain arbitrarily high Kolmogorov complexity unless Dn supplies that complexity.
2. No computable self-improvement operator can universally and provably transform arbitrary programs into semantically strictly better programs for arbitrary nontrivial semantic criteria (Rice).
3. There exist problem instances for which provably better algorithms always exist (Blum speedup), so in principle a self-improver might continue improving indefinitely—yet constructing those improvements may not be algorithmically achievable in general.
4. Augmenting S with stronger oracles removes some impossibility results but replaces them by relativized versions and introduces new practical constraints.

Conclusion (compact)
Formally: self-improving algorithms are computable operators that output new programs using their code plus input data. They create new program text and can extract and repackage information from the environment into more effective algorithms. However, they cannot create unbounded algorithmic information out of nothing (Kolmogorov bounds), cannot in general guarantee or verify arbitrary semantic improvements (Rice/halting), and are limited by provability barriers (Gödel/Löb) unless given oracles or stronger formal systems. The most productive kinds of self-improvement in practice therefore trade off between empirical search (uses environmental data), provable safe transformations (uses formal verification but is incomplete), and resource-bounded algorithmic search (may find improvements but is constrained by time/space).

- Explore specific models (probabilistic self-improvers, resource-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, learning-theoretic views).
- Apply the framework to a concrete design of a provable self-improver and analyze what it can/cannot do.

Below I expand the fragment “Self-improving algorithms create …” into a precise, strictly logical account. I give a formal framework, definitions, a set of propositions (with brief proofs or proof-sketches), and immediate corollaries. The aim is to show exactly what a self‑improver can and cannot “create” in the sense of algorithmic (Kolmogorov) information, computational power, and performance, and which constraints (computability, resources, environment) determine that.

Framework and notation
- Fix a universal Turing machine U. For a binary string x, K(x) denotes plain Kolmogorov complexity (the length of the shortest U-program that outputs x), up to an additive constant depending on U.
- An algorithm/program is a finite binary string p. Its semantics when run on U are U(p).
- Let E denote the environment: a (possibly stochastic) source that can supply data streams or random bits. Let E_{<=t} denote the data observed up to time t.
- Let Perf(p, E_{<=t}) be a (task-dependent) performance measure of program p given environment observations until time t. Perf is a function with values in R (higher is better). We will distinguish when Perf is computable or not.
- An improvement operator I is a (possibly resource-bounded) computable mapping that, given a program p and observations E_{<=t} and possibly resource bounds r, produces a candidate program p' = I(p, E_{<=t}, r). (I itself can be part of the initial system.)
- A self-improving sequence is p_0, p_1, p_2, … with p_{n+1} = I(p_n, E_{<=t_n}, r_n) and Perf(p_{n+1}, E_{<=t_n}) > Perf(p_n, E_{<=t_n}) for the chosen times t_n and resources r_n.

Definition (creates new algorithmic information)
- We say p_{n+1} creates algorithmic information relative to p_n and E_{<=t_n} if K(p_{n+1} | p_n, E_{<=t_n}) is large (greater than some threshold), i.e., p_{n+1} is not compressible given p_n and the observed environment so far.

Proposition 1 (closed deterministic system: no large net creation of algorithmic information)
- Let I be a computable operator that receives no external data (E provides no new bits) and acts deterministically on p. Then for every n,
  K(p_n) ≤ K(p_0) + O(1).
Proof sketch:
- If p_n is produced by running the computable operator I repeatedly on p_0 with no external input, then p_n is computable from p_0 and a fixed-size description of I and n. Hence K(p_n) ≤ K(p_0) + K(I) + K(n) + O(1). For bounded n (or K(n) = O(1) in the model where n is fixed), this gives K(p_n) ≤ K(p_0) + O(1). Even allowing growing n, K(n) only adds log n bits — so no unbounded creation beyond the information in p_0 and the loop counter.
Consequence: purely internal deterministic self-modification cannot create arbitrarily large new algorithmic information.

Proposition 2 (external information bounds creation)
- For any computable I that uses observations E_{<=t}, for each update step
  K(p_{n+1}) ≤ K(p_n) + K(E_{<=t_n} | p_n) + O(1).
Proof sketch:
- p_{n+1} is computable from (p_n, E_{<=t_n}, I, r_n). Thus K(p_{n+1}) ≤ K(p_n) + K(E_{<=t_n} | p_n) + K(I) + O(1). Drop constants to obtain the stated bound.
Interpretation: new algorithmic information in p_{n+1} beyond that already present in p_n cannot exceed the amount of new algorithmic information supplied by the environment observations E_{<=t_n} (plus small overhead). Therefore, to “create” new algorithmic information the algorithm must import it from outside (environment, sensor data, randomness).  

Proposition 3 (Kleene recursion (fixed-point) enables self-referential improvement)
- There exists a program p that, when run, outputs a program p' that contains information about p (for example, p' can be “p modified”). More generally, for any computable transformation T, there exists a program q such that U(q) = U(T(q)).
Proof sketch:
- This is Kleene’s recursion theorem. It guarantees the existence of fixed points under computable program transformations; hence self-inspection and self-modification are possible in principle.
Consequence: self-modifying programs that reference their own code are constructible without oracles.

Proposition 4 (verification/selection is limited by undecidability)
- Let P be a nontrivial semantic predicate on program behavior (e.g., “program halts on all inputs with runtime ≤ t” or “program solves problem X correctly”). There is no computable operator that, given an arbitrary program p, always finds p' such that P(p') is true whenever such a p' exists, unless P is decidable on the relevant class.
Proof sketch:
- Rice’s theorem: nontrivial semantic properties of programs are undecidable. Hence any operator that would require solving such undecidable properties for arbitrary inputs cannot be computable.
Interpretation: an improvement operator that must universally certify “is strictly better” for arbitrary tasks cannot exist as a total computable function. In practice, self-improvement must either restrict to decidable/approximable performance measures, use oracles, or accept probabilistic/heuristic verification.

Proposition 5 (resource-bounded search + Levin universal search gives theoretical improvement but with resource cost)
- If an improvement is judged solely by asymptotic runtime on a decidable task, then Levin universal search can in principle find asymptotically faster programs by enumerating and validating candidates, but the search cost can be exponentially (or arbitrarily) larger than the runtime improvements gained.
Proof sketch:
- Levin’s universal search interleaves all candidate programs proportionally to 2^{-|q|}. If a short program q exists that runs fast, Levin search will eventually find it but may spend resources exponential in |q| to do so. Thus improvements are theoretically discoverable but may be impractical.
Consequence: self-improvement operators that rely on exhaustive search can create programs with better asymptotic properties, but the cost to discover them may negate practical gains.

Proposition 6 (Blum speedup-like phenomena)
- There exist computable problems for which no single best algorithm exists: for every algorithm A there exists A' that is strictly faster on infinitely many inputs. Thus there is an infinite ladder of asymptotic “improvements.”
Interpretation:
- Existence of speedup sequences does not imply a computable self-improvement operator that climbs the ladder effectively; constructing the next improvement may require solving problems as hard as the original.

Synthesis: what a self-improving algorithm can “create”
1. Re-encoding and compression of existing information
   - A self-modifier can reorganize and compress its internal representation so that apparent complexity or runtime improves without creating new algorithmic information beyond the initial contents plus environment. Example: discovery of a learned heuristic that compresses a large lookup table into a small program.

2. Algorithmic information imported from the environment
   - New algorithmic information can be incorporated when the system consumes observations, labeled data, or randomness from E. The amount of new information is bounded by K(E_{<=t} | p) (Proposition 2). Thus learning from a rich environment enables genuine creation of new useful behavior.

3. New algorithms found by search (but limited by resource cost)
   - By searching program space, a self-improver can discover shorter or faster programs (Levin search, enumerative methods). Such discovery does “create” (produce) programs with lower K relative to the task, but the search cost and verification cost are the limiting factors.

4. Self-referential construction (using recursion theorem)
   - Self-improvers can construct programs that include references to their own code and so implement self-revision strategies. This allows elaborate bootstrapping, but does not by itself create new Kolmogorov information beyond what was available in the inputs.

5. Provable but nonconstructive improvements require oracles / noncomputable information
   - Some theorems (e.g., existence of arbitrarily better algorithms for some tasks) are nonconstructive: you may know an improved algorithm exists but cannot computably produce it. Therefore “create” in the effective sense fails without additional (possibly noncomputable) information.

Important corollaries and limitations
- Conservation-like bound: In the absence of external information (or a source of genuine randomness), a deterministic self-improver cannot increase the Kolmogorov complexity of its code by more than an additive constant. Thus there is no magic source of algorithmic novelty hidden solely in self-transformation.
- Practical improvement requires either (a) access to new information (data, randomness, or an oracle), (b) an effectively verifiable and decidable performance metric, and (c) resources to search/verify candidate improvements.
- Undecidability of semantic properties imposes a fundamental barrier to universal improvement: no computable routine can, for every input and every nontrivial improvement goal, find and verify an improved program.
- Even when improvements exist (e.g., via Blum speedup), they can be uncomputable or only discoverable at prohibitive resource cost; hence theoretical “infinity of improvement” does not equate to practical, effectively executable runaway self-improvement.

Toy models (illustrative)
- Closed deterministic toy: p_0 prints “I will improve myself” and includes a fixed routine I that rewrites parts of the code according to a fixed rule. All p_n are computable from p_0 and n, so K(p_n) grows at most by O(log n). No significant new algorithmic information is produced.
- Learning toy: p_0 is a learner that, from input samples E which encode a sophisticated algorithm (e.g., O(n log n) sorting comparator discovered in data), infers and outputs p_1 implementing that algorithm. Then K(p_1 | p_0, E) can be large — new information was created only because it was present in E.
- Search toy: p_0 enumerates short programs and tests correctness; upon finding p*, it replaces itself with p*. If p* is shorter (or faster) than p_0, the system “creates” a better program, but the enumerative cost may dwarf any gained efficiency.

Concluding statement (precise completion of the concept)
- Self-improving algorithms create algorithmic improvements only to the extent that (1) they can import new algorithmic information from outside (data, randomness, or oracles), (2) they can feasibly search and verify candidate improvements under resource bounds, and (3) the performance predicates they optimize are computable or otherwise verifiable. Internally, deterministic self-transformation alone cannot produce unbounded new algorithmic information; it can only reorganize, compress, and reallocate the information already present (including what is provided by the environment).

I will expand the fragment "Self‑improving algorithms create..." within the formal language of algorithmic (recursive) information theory. I give precise definitions, state and prove (sketches of) key formal constraints, then draw the logical consequences and examples. The main takeaway is: a self‑improving algorithm can only “create” algorithmic information to the extent that information is present in its initial description, its update rule, its random/oracle inputs, and the data it harvests from the environment; what it can legitimately be said to create is increased mutual information with the environment (useful structure) and compressed encodings of environmental regularities, subject to strict conservation inequalities and undecidability limits.

1. Framework and definitions

- Use prefix Kolmogorov complexity K(·) (up to an additive constant).
- Mutual algorithmic information:
  I(x : y) := K(x) + K(y) − K(x, y) (again up to O(1)).
- Model a self‑improving system as a discrete-time process. At time t the system has internal program/state p_t (a finite binary string). There is an environment e (a (possibly infinite) binary string or stochastic process). When p_t acts in e it produces data d_t (the observable feedback), and an update rule U (itself a computable program) produces p_{t+1} = U(p_t, d_t, r_t) where r_t are nondeterministic/random/oracle bits used in the update.
- Performance is some utility/performance function V(p, e) (not required to be computable for later conceptual statements; when needed assume computable or semicomputable).

2. Basic conservation facts (known results from algorithmic information theory)

Theorem A (complexity under computable maps).
If F is a computable function, then for every x,
K(F(x)) ≤ K(x) + K(F) + O(1).
(Proof sketch: a description of x and of a program for F suffice to produce F(x).)

Theorem B (mutual information non‑increase under computable maps).
If F is computable, then for all x,y,
I(F(x) : y) ≤ I(x : y) + K(F) + O(1).
(Proof sketch: use K(F(x),y) ≥ K(x, y) − K(F) − O(1) and rearrange.)

These are standard “conservation of algorithmic information” inequalities: a computable transformation cannot inflate Kolmogorov complexity or mutual information by more than the complexity of the transforming program (plus constants).

3. Application to self‑improvement

Apply the above to one update step p_{t+1} = U(p_t, d_t, r_t) where U is fixed (the update algorithm) and d_t was produced by running p_t in environment e.

Proposition 1 (bound on increase of mutual information with environment).
I(p_{t+1} : e) ≤ I(p_t : e) + K(U) + I(d_t, r_t : e) + O(1).

Proof sketch:
- Treat the tuple (p_t, d_t, r_t) as input to computable U, then use Theorem B with F = U and x = (p_t, d_t, r_t), y = e:
  I(U(x): e) ≤ I(x : e) + K(U) + O(1).
- Observe I(x : e) = I(p_t : e) + I(d_t, r_t : e | p_t) + O(1) ≤ I(p_t : e) + I(d_t, r_t : e) + O(1).
- Combine to get the stated bound.

Interpretation: the increase in information that the internal program p has about the environment e in one update step is bounded by (i) the complexity of the update rule K(U) and (ii) the environmental information contained in the feedback and random/oracle bits I(d_t, r_t : e). If d_t and r_t carry no new information about e, then p cannot suddenly acquire more information about e except for up to K(U) bits of description-change coming from U itself.

Corollary (no free algorithmic information).
If U is fixed and there is no external feedback (d_t is empty) and r_t is absent, then for all t:
I(p_t : e) ≤ I(p_0 : e) + K(U) + O(1).
Thus, without obtaining new information from outside, the internal program cannot come to know more about the environment than it already did plus at most the description length of U.

4. What a self‑improving algorithm does (expanded statement)

Putting the formal facts together, complete the fragment:

Self‑improving algorithms create
- (a) updated programs p_{t+1}, p_{t+2}, … (syntactic objects whose Kolmogorov complexity may increase or decrease),
- (b) records/traces of interaction D = (d_0, d_1, …) with the environment (these traces contain the objective source of any new algorithmic information about the environment),
- (c) increased mutual information with the environment (I(p_t : e)) only to the extent permitted by the information content of their interaction traces and their own update procedure,
- (d) compressed encodings (shorter descriptions) of environmental regularities when such regularities are extractable from D — i.e., they can convert repeated patterns in feedback into shorter program fragments, producing more efficient representations for the task distribution,
- (e) apparent new (high) Kolmogorov complexity if they incorporate random/oracle bits, though such complexity may be uninformative about e unless correlated with e.

Put succinctly and formally:
A self‑improving algorithm cannot conjure algorithmic information about an environment ex nihilo; any genuine increase in the program’s information about e is bounded by the information harvested from the environment plus the description complexity of the update mechanism:
I(p_{t+1} : e) − I(p_t : e) ≤ K(U) + I(d_t, r_t : e) + O(1).

5. Further consequences and qualifications

- Useful vs. syntactic information. Kolmogorov complexity and mutual information are syntactic. “Useful” improvement (higher expected utility V) can be achieved even when K(p_t) decreases (the program becomes simpler) by extracting and encoding regularities. That is consistent with conservation laws: compressing data into shorter programs transfers information into a different representation but does not magically create information beyond the data and U.
- Role of randomness. True random bits can raise K(p) but do not increase I(p : e) unless the random bits are correlated with e. So random self‑mutation alone can make programs more complex but not more knowledgeable about the environment.
- Interaction is essential. Continuous improvement requires ongoing supply of informative feedback d_t. If the environment is static and provides no new observable data, improvement halts except for changes encoded in U itself.
- Uncomputability and provable improvement. Certain guarantees of improvement (e.g., provably strictly better performance in all cases) may be impossible to decide because of undecidability of general program equivalence, the halting problem, and related limits (Löb/Gödel‑style obstacles for provability). This constrains what a computable self‑improver can provably accomplish.
- Oracles and unbounded improvement. If the updater U has access to an unbounded oracle supplying genuinely new information about e (or solving undecidable problems), then the constraints above are relaxed by including the oracle's information in I(d_t : e) or K(U) (if the oracle is fixed, its description length is counted in K(U); if it supplies varying information, that increases I(· : e)). Thus unbounded, provable self‑improvement requires external sources of information beyond the original program and the computable updater.

6. Examples

- Learning from data: A learner compresses training data D into a model p′. The increase in I(p′ : e) is bounded by I(D : e) + K(U). Thus improvements come from training data (feedback), not from the learner’s code alone.
- Pure self‑rewrite without feedback: a program that rewrites itself deterministically according to a fixed rule U cannot gain information about an external environment; it only permutes or re‑encodes existing information and the rule’s code.
- Random search for better programs: random mutation may discover better programs, but the algorithmic information about e only grows if the discovered programs encode environment correlations (and then that information came via whatever observations led to selecting them).

7. Final formal completion

Complete the sentence in one logically tight statement:

Self‑improving algorithms create updated program descriptions and interaction records and can increase the program’s mutual information with the environment (i.e., acquire useful information) only to the extent provided by (a) the information present in the feedback they obtain from the environment and (b) the descriptive content of the update mechanism (and any random/oracle inputs); they cannot algorithmically generate provable new information about the environment beyond these sources (formalized by I(p_{t+1}:e) − I(p_t:e) ≤ K(U) + I(d_t,r_t:e) + O(1)).

If you want, I can:
- Formalize a multi‑step bound summing across t to show a global conservation statement.
- Expand the relation to expected utility improvements and semicomputable rewards (Solomonoff / Bayesian learning connections).
- Give concrete toy constructions illustrating each case (no feedback, noisy feedback, oracle access).

Below I expand the concept "Self‑improving algorithms create..." in a strict, logically structured way. I give precise definitions, show what is created, present simple formal claims (with sketch proofs or rationale), and state the main limits that follow from computability and information theory. The goal is to make explicit what it means, what can be proved, and what cannot.

1) Setup and notation

- Let A be the space of programs (algorithms) expressed as finite binary strings; view each a ∈ A as a (deterministic or randomized) partial computable function a : X → Y, where X is an input space and Y an output space.

- Let E be the space of possible environments. Concretely an environment μ is a probability distribution over input–feedback sequences (or simply an input distribution on X together with a loss/feedback function); assume μ is an arbitrary computable or noncomputable distribution depending on context.

- Let L : A × E → R≥0 be a performance measure (loss) of algorithm a in environment μ. Typical choices: expected loss L(a, μ) = E_{x~μ}[ℓ(a(x), x)] or expected runtime or description-length-based loss.

- A self‑improvement operator (update rule) is a (possibly noncomputable) mapping U : A × S → A, where S represents the experience/data available up to that point (S can be generated by running the algorithm in environment μ). A self‑improving process is the sequence (a0, a1, a2, ...) with a_{t+1} = U(a_t, S_t).

2) What self‑improving algorithms create (informal summary, to be made formal below)

- A sequence of algorithms (a0, a1, ...).
- A sequence of performance values (L(a0, μ), L(a1, μ), ...).
- Information about the environment μ encoded into later algorithms — i.e., later a_t typically have greater mutual information with μ.
- Potentially fixed points or limit algorithms a* with U(a*, ·) = a* (stability).
- Under some constructions they can create increasingly compressed/efficient descriptions of μ or of the optimal solution, or unbounded speedups for specific tasks.

3) Formal definition of “improvement” and of a self‑improving sequence

Definition (Improvement). Fix μ and loss L. We say a_{t+1} strictly improves over a_t under μ when L(a_{t+1}, μ) < L(a_t, μ). Monotone improvement means L(a_{t+1}, μ) ≤ L(a_t, μ) for all t.

Definition (Self‑improvement process). Given initial a0 and update U, define a_{t+1} = U(a_t, S_t) where S_t is the history of interactions (inputs, outputs, feedback) generated by running a_0,...,a_t in μ. The process is computable if U is computable and the algorithms a_t are computable.

4) Existence and construction (positive statements)

Proposition 1 (Existence of improving sequences in principle). If one has access to (i) a perfect evaluator of L(·, μ) or to an oracle that returns the true loss of any candidate program, and (ii) unlimited search resources over A, then there exists a computable procedure U that, given a_t, returns some a_{t+1} with strictly lower loss, as long as a strictly better program exists.

Sketch. Given oracle access to L(·, μ), run an exhaustive search over programs and pick a program with strictly smaller loss. If one exists, this finds it. This is a conceptual existence result; it requires an evaluator/oracle and unbounded search.

Proposition 2 (Self‑reference is possible — Kleene style). There exist programs that output descriptions of improved versions of themselves (self‑modifying programs). Constructions using the Kleene recursion theorem produce a program p that, when run, outputs a program q = f(p) for some computable f. Thus self‑referential self‑improvement is logically possible.

Sketch. Kleene's recursion theorem ensures for any computable transformation f of program codes there is a program p whose output depends on p's own code in the required way.

Proposition 3 (Information‑theoretic improvement: reduction in expected code length). Suppose μ is a computable distribution on X and we measure algorithm quality by expected negative log-likelihood loss L(a, μ) = E_{x~μ}[-log P_a(x)] where P_a is the predictive distribution implemented by a. Then an update that moves towards the Bayes mixture over a hypothesis class reduces expected loss and thus reduces expected code length of μ under the predictor. Thus self‑improvement can be seen as creating shorter descriptions of μ (in probabilistic coding sense).

Remark. The ideal Bayesian update is typically noncomputable in general, but the statement identifies what "improvement" means in coding terms.

5) Limits and impossibility results

The strictly logical limits come from computability, undecidability, and complexity theory. The following are important constraints.

Theorem A (Rice‑type impossibility to decide global improvement). Any nontrivial semantic property of programs (for example, “this candidate program has lower loss than that candidate program on all inputs”) is undecidable in general. Consequently, no computable U can, in general, decide for arbitrary programs and arbitrary environments whether replacing a program by a candidate will always improve performance.

Reason. Follows from Rice’s theorem: semantic properties of program behavior over infinite domains are undecidable.

Consequence. Verifying a global (for-all-inputs) improvement is, in general, uncomputable; only statistical or empirical verification is possible without additional structure.

Theorem B (No universal computable monotone self‑improver). There is no single computable operator U that, given any computable environment μ and any start program a0, guarantees a computable, monotonically improving sequence that converges to an optimal program for all μ and all a0.

Intuition. This is a corollary of general undecidability and “no free lunch”-type considerations: if there were a single computable U that universally and provably monotonically improved over any computable μ, it could be used to solve undecidable problems by encoding them as optimization tasks. More concretely, Blum’s speed‑up and related diagonal constructions show there are tasks for which optimizing performance entails solving arbitrarily hard/undecidable subproblems.

Remark on Blum’s speedup theorem. There are decision problems for which no optimal time bound exists; for such problems, one can produce infinite sequences of algorithms with strictly decreasing asymptotic runtime (computable improvement), but verifying optimality or deciding when improvement halts is not possible in general.

Theorem C (No free lunch for average improvement). Averaged uniformly over all possible environments, no algorithm can do better than any other. So one cannot expect universal improvement across all tasks without additional assumptions about the environment distribution.

6) Information‑theoretic description of “what is created”

We can formalize one sense of “creation of information” by self‑improvement as increase in mutual information between the algorithm code and the environment.

Definition (Algorithm–environment mutual information, algorithmic version). For a fixed environment μ described by a finite object e (or by a computable distribution with finite description), let K(·) denote prefix Kolmogorov complexity and K(e|a) the conditional complexity. The algorithm a encodes information about e if K(e) − K(e|a) > 0. Define I(a : e) := K(e) + K(a) − K(e, a) ≈ K(e) − K(e|a).

Claim. If a_{t+1} is an improved algorithm for μ because it has absorbed patterns of μ into its code, then I(a_{t+1} : e) > I(a_t : e). Thus self‑improvement increases (in this algorithmic sense) the mutual information between code and environment.

Caveat. Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable; this gives a formal but not operational test. For bounded‑resource analogues one can use MDL (minimum description length) or compression-based proxies and measurable mutual information under probabilistic models.

7) Types of self‑improvement and their formal properties

Distinguish classes:

- Empirical self‑improvement: U searches for a' with lower empirical loss on collected S_t (statistical guarantees: generalization depends on sample complexity).

- Verified self‑improvement: U only accepts a' if it can provide a formal proof that L(a', μ) ≤ L(a, μ) (requires a formal model of μ and is often infeasible).

- Oracle self‑improvement: U has access to an oracle for L or for solving hard subproblems; with oracles one can get stronger guarantees but they are not implementable.

Each class has different provable properties: empirical can give high‑probability improvement under i.i.d. assumptions and finite hypothesis classes; verified gives absolute guarantees when proofs exist; oracle yields theoretical existence results.

8) Convergence and fixed points

Definition. a* is a fixed point of U under history S if a* = U(a*, S) (S is the history produced when running a*). Fixed points correspond to self‑consistent algorithms that do not change themselves given their own behavior.

Proposition. If U always selects a program minimizing true expected loss over a finite hypothesis class H, then the sequence reaches an equilibrium in finitely many steps (it cannot strictly improve indefinitely if H is finite).

If H is infinite, sequences of strict improvements can be infinite (Blum speedup phenomenon). Convergence properties depend on search power, hypothesis space, and evaluation fidelity.

9) Practical corollaries (operationally useful statements)

- To build practical self‑improvers with reliable behavior you must restrict the hypothesis space, environment model, or allowable transformations (this makes verification feasible).

- Statistical improvement (decreased expected loss) can be achieved under standard PAC‑style conditions with high probability if update is based on sufficient data and appropriate regularization.

- For tasks where the optimal program is noncomputable or where semantic properties are undecidable, we can still get empirical and probabilistic improvement but not universally provable global improvement.

10) Summary (tight logical statement)

Self‑improving algorithms, when run in an environment μ and accompanied by an update operator U, create a computable or uncomputable sequence of program descriptions (a_t) and a corresponding sequence of performance outcomes (L(a_t, μ)). Formally, they create (i) algorithmic artifacts (the new programs), (ii) encoded information about the environment (increased mutual/conditional information between program code and environment description), and (iii) dynamical objects such as fixed points, limit points, or infinitely improving chains. Which of these are achievable computably and verifiably depends on assumptions: with oracles or unbounded search one can in principle produce monotone improvement and arbitrarily good programs; under computability, undecidability results (Rice, halting, Blum speedup) and no‑free‑lunch constraints show there is no universal computable operator that guarantees provable, global self‑improvement for all tasks. Operationally useful self‑improvement therefore requires restricted model classes, empirical evaluation, or explicit formal verification frameworks.

Below I expand the phrase "Self‑improving algorithms create..." into a strict, logically organized account: definitions, existence results, limits, and conditional theorems (with sketches). I treat "algorithm" as a program (e.g., a Turing machine, or a program in a fixed programming language L) and make performance notions explicit.

1. Basic formal setup

- Let P be the set of all programs in a fixed computable programming language L (encodings ⟨p⟩ are natural numbers).  
- Let T be a set of tasks or inputs; let D be a probability distribution (or family of distributions) over T.  
- Let M: P × T → R be a measurable performance function (e.g., runtime, loss, accuracy). Extend to expected performance under D: M̄(p) = E_{t∼D}[M(p,t)]. (If multiple metrics are relevant, treat M as vector-valued and use a preorder on vectors.)  
- Define an improvement relation ≻ on P by p' ≻ p  iff  M̄(p') > M̄(p) (or ≥ with strictness on a positive-measure set). One may require improvements to be significant (≥ margin ε) or Pareto-improvements across multiple metrics.

2. Definition: self‑improving algorithm

- A program s ∈ P is self‑improving (relative to M̄ and a class of allowed transformations F ⊆ P → P) iff, on some (possibly empty) input, s outputs a description ⟨s'⟩ such that s' = F_s(⟨s⟩) for some computable transformation F_s and s' ≻ s. More generally, s is an iterative self‑improver if it effectively produces a computable sequence ⟨s0⟩,⟨s1⟩,⟨s2⟩,… with s_{n+1} ≻ s_n for all n (or for all sufficiently large n).

Remarks:
- "Self‑improving" can be narrow (single step, modifies its own code) or iterative (bootstrap sequence).
- The allowed transformation class F models constraints (resource limits, proof obligations, language restrictions).

3. Existence: self‑referential construction

Proposition 1 (existence of self‑referential programs).
There exist programs s that inspect/encode their own source and produce outputs that depend on that source (Kleene recursion theorem).

Sketch: Kleene’s Recursion Theorem implies that for any computable binary operator G(x,y) there exists e such that φ_e = φ_{G(e,·)}. Concretely, one can construct a program s that obtains its own index and computes any computable function of that index; therefore it can output a candidate program s' = h(⟨s⟩) for any computable h. Hence existence of programs that write modified copies of themselves is not a barrier.

4. Potential for unbounded improvement (speedups)

Proposition 2 (Blum speedup phenomenon).
There exist computable problems for which no single program is optimal: for every program p that computes a certain function f, there is a program p' that computes the same f but is asymptotically faster. Consequently, there are sequences of programs with strictly improving runtime.

Implication: In some formal senses, self‑improvers can produce arbitrarily large (unbounded) improvements in resource efficiency by discovering more efficient algorithms; there is no computable ultimate optimum in such cases.

5. Fundamental barriers (undecidability and unprovability)

Theorem A (Rice’s theorem — limitation).
Any nontrivial semantic property of programs (e.g., "p' improves expected performance over p on distribution D") is undecidable in general. Therefore no algorithm can decide for all pairs (p,p') whether p' ≻ p.

Consequence: A self‑improver cannot, in general, mechanically verify that an arbitrary transformed program is truly an improvement.

Theorem B (Halting/verification limits).
Because program behavior may depend on nondecidable predicates (e.g., halting of subcomputations), verifying arbitrarily expressed correctness or performance claims is undecidable. Thus global safety guarantees for unrestricted self‑modification are impossible.

Remark on logical self‑knowledge: results related to Gödel/Löb show that a sufficiently expressive system cannot, in general, prove certain global properties about its own future outputs without careful design. This constrains schemes that rely on a system proving "this future version is safe/optimal."

6. Tradeoffs and practical constraints

- Resource cost of search: Searching the program space for improvements can be arbitrarily expensive; a candidate improvement may itself require huge resources to validate.  
- Local optima: Under restricted transformation sets and empirical evaluation, self‑improvers can get stuck at local maxima.  
- Overfitting/sampling error: If evaluation is empirical (finite samples from D), apparent improvements may be statistical artifacts. Explicit statistical bounds (sample complexity) are needed to control this.

7. Guarantees under restrictions

If we restrict the environment, then stronger theorems hold.

Proposition 3 (provable-safe self‑improvement under decidability).
Suppose we fix:
  a) F, a computable set of allowed transformations;  
  b) a decidable predicate V(p_old,p_new) that implies M̄(p_new) ≥ M̄(p_old) (sound verification); and  
  c) computational resources sufficient to decide V on any candidate.

Then a program s that enumerates candidates via F, tests V, and adopts any p_new with V(p_old,p_new) true, is a correct self‑improver: every adopted change is a provable improvement.

Sketch: Because V is decidable and sound relative to M̄, s can safely adopt only verified improvements; iterating yields a monotone sequence.

Limitation: Conditions (b) and (c) are strong. V must be decidable and sound — typically achievable only in restricted languages or when M̄ is syntactically characterizable (e.g., derivable correctness proofs). In Turing-complete generality, V cannot be both complete and decidable.

8. Fixed points, convergence, and attractors

- A fixed point p* is a program such that no allowed transformation yields a verified improvement: for all p' in allowed neighborhood, ¬(p' ≻ p*) or the verifier rejects p'. Fixed points can be local optima, global optima, or verification-limited optima.  
- Convergence of iterative self‑improvement depends on search dynamics, verification criteria, and the topology induced by F; convergence is not guaranteed in general (may oscillate or diverge).

9. Consequences and precise restatement

Putting the pieces together:

A. In theory, self‑improving algorithms can create sequences of programs with strictly improving measurable performance; Kleene’s recursion theorem and Blum’s results show self‑reference and unbounded speedups are possible.

B. In general, it is undecidable whether an arbitrary candidate program is an actual improvement (Rice, halting), so unrestricted self‑improvement cannot provide algorithmic, universal guarantees of correctness, safety, or optimality.

C. Therefore, any practical design that requires provable safety or correctness must impose restrictions (restrict the language, restrict allowed transforms, use provable verification conditions, or rely on empirical sampling with statistical controls). Under such restrictions, one can prove monotone improvement and safety properties, but these proofs do not scale to arbitrary program spaces.

10. Minimal formal summary (three crisp statements)

1. Existence: There exist computable self‑modifying programs s that produce improved versions s' (Kleene recursion allows self‑reference; concrete constructions exist).  
2. Potential: There exist tasks for which arbitrarily large computable improvements exist (Blum speedup): no single optimum program need exist.  
3. Limitation: The general problem of deciding whether p' improves on p is undecidable (Rice’s theorem), so no algorithm can universally and soundly certify arbitrary self‑improvements.

11. Practical prescriptions (logical corollaries)

- To get provable safety/useful guarantees, design the self‑improvement process so that verification is decidable and sound (e.g., restrict language, require machine‑checkable proofs, use proof‑carrying code).  
- Combine empirical evaluation (with statistical guarantees) and formal proofs where possible: empirical methods give practical progress; formal methods prevent pathological failure modes.  
- Expect inevitable tradeoffs: search cost vs improvement magnitude, expressivity vs decidability, and local vs global optimality.

I will expand the concept in a formal, logically explicit way within the standard framework of recursion theory / algorithmic information theory. I state definitions, assumptions, propositions and proof sketches, and draw tight conclusions about what is possible and what is forbidden for self‑improving algorithms.

Notation and basic model
- Fix a universal Turing machine U. Programs are finite binary strings, written p, q, r ∈ Σ*.
- The semantic value of a program p is the (partial) function U(p) it computes.
- Let Perf be a performance measure: Perf : Σ* → R ∪ {±∞}. (Perf may be total or partial, computable, semicomputable, etc.; I will state assumptions about Perf where needed.)
- We treat a self‑improving system as a computable procedure that generates or transforms program indices (strings) over time.

1. Definition (Self‑improving sequence and self‑improver)
- A sequence (p0, p1, p2, …) of programs is strictly improving (w.r.t. Perf) if for every i, Perf(pi+1) > Perf(pi).
- A self‑improver is a program s that, on empty input, enumerates a sequence of program indices p0, p1, p2, … (e.g. it outputs them or stores them) intended to be successively better with respect to Perf.
- We call s a computable self‑improver when s is a total computable function (i.e., a program that actually enumerates the sequence).

Remarks: “Improvement” can be defined in other ways (nonstrict ≥, improvement in expected utility, improvement under resource bounds), but I use strict > for simplicity.

2. Elementary necessary condition
If Perf is bounded above by some B ∈ R, then any strictly improving sequence is finite (it can increase only a finite number of times without exceeding B). Thus unbounded infinite improvement requires an unbounded Perf range.

3. Two important kinds of Perf
A. Perf computable: there exists a total computable procedure that, on input p, returns Perf(p) (a real represented to required precision).
B. Perf semidecidable (lower semicomputable): there is a computable sequence of rationals increasing to Perf(p). (Many natural measures, such as negative description length approximations, are of this sort.)

Different results use different assumptions about Perf’s computability.

4. Existence and trivial examples
- If there exists an infinite computable strictly increasing sequence of reals r0<r1<r2<… in the image of Perf and one can effectively produce programs p_i with Perf(p_i)=r_i, then a computable self‑improver exists: output these p_i. This is trivial but depends on there being an effective way to enumerate better and better programs for the chosen Perf.

5. Limits: no universal computable always‑improving operator
Proposition (informal): There is no total computable operator R : Σ* → Σ* such that for every input program p, Perf(R(p)) > Perf(p), provided Perf is a nontrivial semantic property (i.e., Perf attains at least two distinct values on Σ*) and Perf is defined in the usual semantic way (depends on the function computed, not on syntactic form only).

Proof sketch:
- Suppose R is total computable and always produces a strictly better program. Use Kleene’s recursion (fixed‑point) theorem to construct a program p* that, informally, looks at R(p*) and arranges its own semantics so that Perf(R(p*)) ≤ Perf(p*). More concretely: build a program p* that (through self‑reference) simulates R on its own index and then behaves so as to make R(p*) not be strictly better (e.g., switch behavior to equal or dominate R(p*)’s measured behavior). This contradicts the assumption that R produces strictly better programs for every input.
- Variations of this diagonalization argument are standard in recursion theory and show that no computable transformer can certifyably and uniformly increase a nontrivial semantic measure for all inputs.

Remarks: The exact formalization of the diagonalization depends on the precise definition of Perf; if Perf is defined in a way that an adversarial program can arrange its semantics relative to R(p*), the contradiction follows. This is the classical impossibility of a universal “oracle” that transforms any program into a strictly better one on all semantic measures.

6. Rice’s theorem / undecidability of improvement detection
Rice’s theorem: any nontrivial semantic property of programs is undecidable. Consequence: for a nontrivial Perf, the predicate “Perf(q) > Perf(p)” (for arbitrary p and q) will typically be undecidable in general. Thus a self‑improver cannot, in general, decide for arbitrary candidates whether a proposed modification actually improves Perf. That obstructs verification and rule‑based universal improvement.

7. Provable (safe) self‑improvement: Gödel‑style constructions
A constructive way to get provable self‑improvement is to combine an explicit formal proof system with program rewriting:

- Let A be a system with a formal axiomatic theory S in which the semantics of programs and Perf can be expressed.
- A Gödel‑machine style agent (as in Schmidhuber) searches for a proof in S that "replacing current program p by candidate q yields higher expected utility (Perf) under the agent’s model and resources". If such a proof is found, the agent rewrites itself to q.
- This is safe in the sense that the agent only self‑modifies when it can prove the modification increases utility relative to its axioms.

Limitations:
- The agent’s improvements are bounded by what is provable in S. There may exist true improvements that are not provable, so the agent may miss them.
- The approach trades undecidability for provability: it avoids incorrect rewrites but may be conservative and miss unprovable yet true improvements.

8. Blum’s speedup phenomenon and unbounded but nonuniform improvement
Blum’s speedup theorem: there exist computable problems for which, for any given program solving the problem, there is a strictly faster program — and indeed infinitely many progressively faster programs. This shows that in terms of time complexity, arbitrarily large improvements can exist.

Implication for self‑improvers:
- There can exist an infinite sequence of strictly better programs (w.r.t. a resource measure like run time), but the mapping from a program to a provably better one need not be computable or effectively predictable.
- Thus unbounded self‑improvement in a semantic/computational sense is consistent with recursion theory, but there is no general computable strategy guaranteed to find the next provably better program for arbitrary problems.

9. Tradeoffs and resource bounds
- Improvement must be qualified by resources: time to search for improvements, proof search cost, verification cost. A program that “improves” Perf but only after exorbitant search time may be worse in overall utility if Perf includes cost measures.
- Local optima: in the discrete space of program indices, computable search procedures can get trapped in local maxima. Without an oracle or provable criterion, escaping is not decidable in general.

10. Formal summary of possibilities and impossibilities
- Possible:
  - For restricted classes C of programs or problems (e.g., finite or effectively enumerable families), computable self‑improvers exist that find optimal elements in C.
  - Self‑improvement that is empirical (test candidate modifications on data or benchmarks) is practically feasible, but verification remains heuristic.
  - Gödel‑machine style provable self‑improvement is possible: the agent can only apply modifications for which it has formal proof of improvement.
  - Blum speedup shows there exist problems admitting infinite strictly improving sequences in terms of resource performance.

- Impossible (in general):
  - No total computable operator can, for every program p, produce a program q with strictly higher semantic Perf(p) for every nontrivial semantic Perf (diagonalization / recursion theorem).
  - One cannot in general decide whether an arbitrary candidate q improves a given p (Rice’s theorem). There is no algorithmic guarantee that will always find the optimal next step in program space.
  - No computable self‑improver will provably and uniformly reach globally optimal programs for arbitrary Perf unless additional oracular/axiomatic power is supplied.

- Model C (oracle or learning‑theoretic improvement): Allow access to an oracle (e.g., halting oracle or Kolmogorov complexity oracle). Determine which impossibility results collapse when oracles are allowed.

Self‑improvement is a legitimate and rich concept with both constructive and limiting results:
- Constructive: For many restricted classes, empirical settings, or provability‑restricted frameworks, self‑improving algorithms can and do produce successively better programs.
- Fundamental limits: Recursion theory (recursion theorem, Rice’s theorem), incompleteness, and undecidability place absolute barriers on any single computable procedure that claims to reliably and uniformly produce provably better programs for all possible programs and semantic performance measures.

I will expand the concept "Self‑improving algorithms create..." in a strict, logical, and formal way, using notions from computability theory, algorithmic information theory (Kolmogorov complexity), and elementary information theory. I state definitions, propositions, and concise proofs or proof sketches, and then summarize the qualitative implications for recursive information theory.

Definitions and setup
- Fix a universal Turing machine U as the reference machine for Kolmogorov complexity K(·). Treat programs as finite binary strings that U interprets as Turing machines.
- A self‑improving algorithm is a computable operator S that, given a description of a program p and (optionally) interaction history or environment data e, outputs a new program p' = S(p, e). We treat S as an effective procedure described by a finite string s.
- A performance metric M assigns to each program p (and environment e) a value M(p, e) ∈ R measuring "quality" (e.g., expected reward, runtime, correctness rate). M may be partial or total; when needed we assume M is a computable function of a program and observed data.
- Consider iterative self‑improvement: p_0 given; p_{n+1} = S(p_n, e_n) where e_n is data collected up to step n (possibly including randomness r_n). The sequence (p_n) is the trajectory of the self‑improver.

I. What a computable self‑improver necessarily creates (formal claims)

Claim 1 (Sequence of programs).
A computable self‑improver S generates a computable sequence of program descriptions (p_n) when the environment data (e_n) and any randomness used are computable (or fixed). Thus S produces an effectively enumerable list of programs.

Proof sketch.
S is a fixed computable function; if inputs e_n (including any chosen randomness) are determinate or computable, the iteration p_{n+1} = S(p_n, e_n) is a computable function of n and p_0, so (p_n) is computable/enumerable.

Corollary 1.1 (Monotone improvement).
If improvement is defined by a computable, decidable predicate M(p_{n+1}) ≥ M(p_n), then it is decidable—relative to the data available—whether each step improved. But global properties like "there exists n with M(p_n) ≥ c" may be undecidable in general (Rice‑type limitations; see below).

Claim 2 (Information content bounds — algorithmic).
Let s be a fixed description of S. For any n,
K(p_n) ≤ K(p_0) + n·K(s) + O(log n).
More generally, if e_0,...,e_{n-1} are inputs used, then
K(p_n) ≤ K(p_0) + K(s) + K(e_0,...,e_{n-1}) + O(log n).

Proof sketch.
Each p_{i+1} is computably obtained from p_i, s, and e_i; the chain implies an upper bound on complexity of p_n in terms of complexities of the initial data and s plus a small overhead for indexing the iteration count.

Interpretation.
A purely computable self‑improver cannot create arbitrarily large unconditional Kolmogorov complexity out of nothing; the algorithmic information in its outputs is upper bounded by the information initially available (initial program, S, and input/environment data) up to additive terms.

Claim 3 (Randomness can inject high complexity, but not guaranteed).
If S uses truly random coins r_n during improvement, then with positive probability p_n may have high Kolmogorov complexity. However, such randomness injects information from outside the original program; the creation of high algorithmic complexity is not a pure derivation from the original finite description s and p_0.

II. Limits given by computability and undecidability

Proposition 1 (Rice‑style limitations).
Any nontrivial semantic property of programs (e.g., "S will eventually produce a program p with M(p) ≥ c") is, in general, undecidable. Thus one cannot have a general algorithm that, given S and p_0, decides whether the self‑improver will eventually reach a given performance level.

Reason.
Rice’s theorem: any nontrivial semantic property of program behavior is undecidable. The eventual attainment of a performance threshold is a semantic property of the infinite trajectory.

Proposition 2 (Fixed points and self‑reference — Kleene).
Kleene’s Recursion Theorem implies existence of programs that can obtain their own description. Concretely, for any computable S there exists p* such that p* = S(p*, e) for some e (possibly empty) under suitable conditions; i.e., fixed points of S exist.

Implication.
Self‑improvers can construct self‑referential programs that embed proofs or certificates about their own behavior, but the strength of what they can prove is constrained by logical limitations (see Löb and Gödel phenomena below).

III. What is created in an information‑theoretic sense

Definition (Algorithmic mutual information).
For program p and environment e, define I(p : e) = K(p) + K(e) − K(p, e). This measures shared algorithmic structure.

Claim 4 (Self‑improvement as information integration).
Iterated self‑improvement integrates information from environment/history into program descriptions. Under mild assumptions, I(p_{n+1} : e_{≤n}) ≥ I(p_n : e_{≤n−1}) minus small overheads — the program accumulates information about the environment that is relevant to performance improvements.

Informal justification.
Each improvement step can be seen as compressing observed regularities into the new program; the program’s description therefore comes to encode (part of) the environment data useful for future performance.

Distinguish two senses of “create information”:
- Algorithmic information creation (Kolmogorov): A purely computable self‑improver cannot create unbounded new algorithmic information beyond what is available in its initial description plus oracle/randomness. It can, however, reencode or compress environmental information into shorter programs (increase mutual information I(p_n:e)).
- Shannon information (uncertainty reduction): Interaction with a stochastic environment can reduce uncertainty about environment parameters; the self‑improver creates Shannon information (reduces entropy of environment models) by observing data and embedding models into p_n.

IV. Logical and proof‑theoretic issues

- Löb’s theorem and proof of reliability: A system cannot generally produce a proof of a sufficiently strong statement about its own future improved behavior without circularity. Thus a self‑improver that modifies its own code cannot always certify that its modifications preserve safety or increase performance within the same proof system unless the system is extended.
- Consequently, trustworthy self‑improvement (provably safe improvements) often requires meta‑levels or stronger reasoning principles than those available within the agent’s initial proof system.

V. Typical behaviors and asymptotics

- Convergence to a fixed point: If S reaches p* with S(p*) = p*, then no further change occurs.
- Cycles: S may enter cycles p_i = p_{i+k}.
- Unbounded improvement: Possible only if the environment or external randomness supplies unbounded new information, or if the performance measure allows unbounded increases achievable by computable transformations of bounded description length (rare).
- Computability of the trajectory: Determined by computability of S and inputs; undecidable global properties are common.

Summary (concise, logically organized)
1. A computable self‑improver S deterministically (or stochastically, if using randomness) generates a sequence of programs (p_n). So one formal sense in which "self‑improving algorithms create..." is that they create an effectively describable trajectory of program descriptions.
2. They create compressed encodings of experience: each improvement step can embed observed regularities into p_n, thereby increasing the mutual information between program and environment. This is genuine creation of useful information (Shannon sense, and relative algorithmic sense).
3. They do not magically create unbounded algorithmic information ex nihilo: the unconditional Kolmogorov complexity of outputs is bounded by the complexity of initial data, S, and any external inputs or randomness (up to additive terms). To obtain genuinely new algorithmic information beyond that bound requires new external information (random bits, environment data, or an oracle).
4. There are fundamental limits to what can be decided about their long‑term behavior (Rice’s theorem), and limits to what they can prove about their own future correctness/improvement (Gödel/Löb phenomena).
5. Kleene’s recursion theorem and related fixed‑point results guarantee self‑reference constructions; these enable programs that reason about and transform their own code but do not remove the computability and proof‑theoretic limits.

Concluding remark (interpretation for recursive information theory)
In recursive information theory terms, “self‑improving algorithms create” a hierarchy of descriptions (a recursion of descriptions of descriptions) that accumulates environment‑specific information and reencodes it into program form. Formally this is a computable sequence (when inputs are computable) whose algorithmic information content is governed by the usual Kolmogorov upper bounds, while its semantic outcomes are subject to classical undecidability and proof‑theoretic constraints. Thus the phenomenon is rich and productive (creation of useful, higher‑order, and task‑specific information) but not unbounded or logically unconstrained.

1) Computational model and primitives
- Programs, environments, performance:
