I will expand the fragment "Self-improving algorithms create..." into a strict, logically structured account within the framework of recursive information theory. I will (1) give a precise formal model for "self-improvement", (2) state constructive existence results that allow self-reference, (3) state rigorous obstructions and limits from recursion theory and algorithmic information theory, and (4) derive consequences and suggested formal directions. Each claim is stated as a definition, proposition, or theorem and is accompanied by a brief justification or proof sketch.

I. Formal model

1. Computational universe and notation
- Fix a standard universal Turing machine U and an effective encoding of finite binary strings Σ*. For a program p ∈ Σ*, let φp denote the partial computable function computed by p on U.
- Let Tasks be a (possibly infinite) set of task instances. Let R: (partial functions on Tasks) → R∪{−∞,+∞} be a real-valued performance functional that assigns to each candidate program p a performance score R(φp) (this may mean expected reward, loss, compression ratio, etc.). Assume R is a (possibly unbounded) function defined for all total computable φp we care about; if φp is partial, we may set R(φp)=−∞ or else use an appropriate convention.

2. Definition (Self-improving algorithm)
A self-improving algorithm is a computable procedure A that, given as input a description of a current program p and any history h of interactions and observed data, outputs a new program p' = A(p,h) (or an index thereof). Iterating A yields a sequence p0, p1, p2, … with pn+1 = A(pn, hn), where hn is the finite history before step n (possibly including pn and prior histories). We call the pair (A,p0) a self-improvement process.

3. Definition (Improvement)
Fix a nondecreasing notion of improvement: we say pn+1 is an improvement over pn in the environment class if R(φpn+1) ≥ R(φpn). We may require strict inequality for "strict improvement". We say A realizes unbounded improvement if R(φpn) is an unbounded nondecreasing sequence; we say A realizes asymptotic improvement if limsup R(φpn) exists and is larger than R(φp0).

II. Existence of self-referential/self-improving programs

Proposition 1 (Kleene-style self-reference exists)
There exists a computable program s such that φs = some function that uses its own index (i.e., s can obtain an index for itself and embed it in computations). Concretely, for any computable functional F that maps indices to indices, there exists an index e with φe = φF(e).

Sketch of justification:
This is a direct application of the Kleene (recursion) fixed-point theorem: for any computable transformer F over program indices there exists an index e such that φe = φF(e). Hence self-referential program architectures—programs that inspect or manipulate their own description or that produce improved versions of themselves—are computably realizable.

Corollary 1
There exist computable algorithms that output improved program indices that depend on their own code. Therefore "self-improving algorithms" are not vacuous: self-reference is computably achievable.

III. Fundamental limitations from recursion theory and computability

Theorem 1 (Rice-style undecidability of improvement)
Let P be any nontrivial semantic property of partial computable functions (i.e., P is a subset of indices that is neither empty nor all indices and depends only on the computed function). Then membership in P is undecidable. In particular, given two indices p and q it is undecidable in general whether R(φq) ≥ R(φp) when R encodes a nontrivial semantic property.

Consequence:
No computable meta-procedure can, in general, decide whether a candidate modification produces an actual (semantic) improvement for all inputs/environments.

Explanation:
Since R is (or can encode) any nontrivial semantic property—e.g., "computes the desired total function"—Rice's theorem implies undecidability of universally judging improvement.

Theorem 2 (Halting limitation on guaranteed verification)
If improvement is defined in terms of semantic behavior that requires termination or correctness proofs, then the halting problem implies there is no general effective procedure that certifies, for every candidate q, that q is an improvement over p.

Sketch:
To verify that q improves on p on some tasks may require proving termination on infinitely many inputs or comparing behaviors that themselves encode undecidable predicates.

Theorem 3 (Blum speed-up / nonexistence of computable optimal)
There exist computable functions (tasks) for which there is no optimal algorithm within any given computable measure: for every algorithm a there exists another algorithm b that is arbitrarily better (e.g., asymptotically faster or has strictly lower complexity for infinitely many inputs). Thus effective enumeration of algorithms contains infinite speed-ups; no computable procedure can produce a guaranteed ultimate optimal program.

Consequence:
The possibility of indefinite theoretical self-improvement (always finding strictly better algorithms) is consistent with recursion theory; but constructive attainment of an optimal program by a computable meta-algorithm is not guaranteed, and for some tasks never exists.

IV. Limits from algorithmic information theory

Proposition 2 (Information-conservation bound)
Let K(x) denote prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity. Suppose an agent self-improves by computing a shorter description q of some target behavior x. Any reduction in length beyond the information available in the agent's prior data requires either external information or an uncomputable inference. In particular, the total compressible gain is bounded by the mutual information between the agent's prior data and the target behavior.

Implication:
A self-improver cannot magically compress or simplify behavior beyond the information contained in its data and prior program. Uncomputable sources or oracular inputs are needed to surpass those limits in a provable way.

V. Reflection, trust, and provable improvement (logical barriers)

Observation (Löbian and verification issues)
When an agent produces a successor agent and needs to trust that the successor will not undermine its goals, the agent faces logical-reflection issues: proving properties about the successor that itself reasons about the original agent can lead to self-referential provability paradoxes (instances of Löb's theorem). These create a tension between (a) producing successors that are strictly more capable and (b) being able to verify their properties within the current agent's own proof system.

Consequence:
If verification is required to establish global properties of successors, an agent may be unable to both (i) prove that successors are improved and (ii) actually produce successors that supersede it in provable ways, without stronger meta-logical resources.

VI. Putting the pieces together — precise logical summary

From the formal model and the results above we can make the following strict, logically grounded expansions of the sentence "Self-improving algorithms create...":

1. Existential statement (what they can create)
- Self-improving algorithms can create sequences of program indices p0, p1, p2, … where each pn+1 is computed (possibly using pn and observed data) by a computable transformer. By the Kleene recursion theorem, such self-referential constructions exist; hence they can concretely create amended versions of their own code.

2. Provable-limits statement (what they cannot generally create)
- They cannot, in general, create an effective procedure that decides nontrivial semantic improvement for every candidate modification (Rice). They cannot, in general, certify termination or correctness of arbitrary improved programs (halting problem). They cannot, in general, compute the provably optimal program for certain tasks because of Blum-style speed-ups or nonexistence of effective optima.

3. Information-theoretic bounds (how much they can create)
- Improvements that reduce description length or exploit structure are bounded by the algorithmic mutual information between available data and the target behavior; without additional information sources (or oracles), compression/improvement beyond those bounds is impossible in a computable sense.

4. Logical-reflection constraints (what they may create but not trust)
- They can create successors that (empirically) perform better, but they may be unable to prove within their own logical system that the successors are safe, aligned, or improved without appealing to stronger proof systems or oracles; reflective proofs can be blocked by Löb-like phenomena.

5. Nonconstructive possibility (what theory allows)
- Recursion theory allows the existence of sequences with unbounded speed-up: there exist targets for which for every program there is a strictly better one. Thus the mathematical space admits the possibility of unending self-improvement, but this existence is typically nonconstructive: there may be no computable recipe that always finds the next provably better program.

VII. Formal propositions one can pursue (research directions)

- Formalize classes of environments E and performance measures R for which the improvement predicate {〈p,q〉 | R(φq) ≥ R(φp)} is decidable or semidecidable. For such classes, constructive self-improvement may be possible.

- Study resource-bounded variants: replace Kolmogorov complexity and computability with time- or space-bounded complexity measures. Many undecidability results disappear under strict resource bounds; characterize attainable self-improvement within these bounds.

- Introduce probabilistic or reflective oracles: allow randomized or oracle-aided meta-procedures (reflective oracles, probabilistic verification) and study which limits remain and which vanish.

- Quantify the expected cost of verification vs. expected gain of improvement: trade-off analysis of meta-search resources vs. net performance increase.

VIII. Concluding logical statement

Strictly and logically: Self-improving algorithms create new program indices (by Kleene recursion they can use and manipulate their own descriptions), and thus can, in principle, produce arbitrarily powerful successors. However, recursion-theoretic undecidability (Rice, halting), algorithmic-information bounds (Kolmogorov complexity), and logical-reflection obstacles (provability limits, Löb phenomena) together imply that no general computable procedure can (a) always recognize or verify nontrivial semantic improvements, (b) always construct a provably optimal successor for every task, or (c) guarantee unbounded provable improvement without external information or stronger oracles. In short: they create candidates and can sometimes realize genuine improvements, but fundamental computability and information-theoretic constraints place strict limits on what can be guaranteed or constructed by purely computable, self-referential processes.

- Work out a bounded-resource variant (e.g., time-bounded self-improvement) and provide explicit bounds and algorithms.

Below I give a precise, strictly logical expansion of the statement “Self‑improving algorithms create ...” by (1) defining a formal model, (2) stating precise definitions of self‑improvement, (3) deriving necessary and sufficient conditions and limits, and (4) stating key consequences from computability and information theory. I keep informal commentary minimal and mark formal claims as Propositions/Theorems with brief proofs or proof sketches.

1. Formal model

- Let P be a (countable) set of programs (e.g. encodings of Turing machines). Let E be an environment or task instance; treat E as an element of a measurable space (or a distribution over tasks) as needed. Let H denote the history of observations produced when a program p runs in E: H(p,E) ∈ Ω (space of finite or infinite observation sequences).

- Let performance be measured by a loss (or utility) function L: P × E → R (lower is better). For stochastic execution, interpret L(p,E) as expected loss (over the program’s internal randomness and the environment).

- An improvement operator is a mapping T: P × Ω* → P ∪ {⊥} that given a program and a finite history outputs a new program (or indicates failure). T is computable if it is produced by a Turing machine.

- A self‑improving algorithm is a program p0 ∈ P that, when executed in E, produces a (possibly infinite) sequence p0, p1, p2, … where pk+1 = T(pk, h_k) and h_k is the history collected by pk interacting with E up to the time of the kth update.

2. Definition of self‑improvement

Definition 2.1 (One‑step improvement).
Given p, E, T and L, say p improves to q in environment E under T if q = T(p, h) for some history h obtainable from running p in E and L(q,E) < L(p,E).

Definition 2.2 (Monotone self‑improvement).
A program p0 exhibits monotone self‑improvement in E under T if the sequence (p_k) generated by repeated application of T satisfies L(p_{k+1},E) ≤ L(p_k,E) for all k, with strict inequality infinitely often or at least until some terminal time.

Definition 2.3 (Asymptotic self‑improvement).
p0 is asymptotically self‑improving in distribution D over E if the expected loss E_{E∼D}[L(p_k,E)] is strictly decreasing in k and converges to a lower limit.

3. Information‑theoretic necessary and sufficient conditions

Intuition: an algorithm can only improve if it can extract and encode previously unavailable (useful) information about E into its successor program.

Let random variable Θ encode the true environment E (or the relevant task parameterization). Let Data_k denote the data (history) observed up to step k. Let M_k denote the description of program p_k.

Proposition 3.1 (Necessary information condition).
If a program p0 produces successors using only its internal randomness (no interaction with E), then for any computable T the expected performance cannot improve in expectation across environments E sampled from a prior where p0 is already optimal in expectation. Equivalently, to produce nontrivial expected improvement the histories must carry nonzero mutual information with Θ:
I(Θ; Data_k | M_0) > 0.

Sketch: If Data_k contains no information about Θ beyond what M_0 already encodes, then any computable function T(M_0, Data_k) yields a successor whose expected performance is determined by M_0 and the distribution of the internal randomness only. Thus no expected reduction in Bayes risk is possible.

Theorem 3.2 (Log‑loss / Bayesian reduction identity).
Suppose L is expected log loss for predicting next observation and the learner maintains a posterior P(Θ | Data). Then the expected reduction in Bayesian log loss after observing Data equals the mutual information:
E[ΔLoss] = I(Θ; Data).

This is the standard information‑theoretic identity: learning reduces expected log loss exactly by the mutual information gained about Θ. Hence measurable improvement requires extractable information about the task.

Corollary 3.3.
For any loss function in a proper scoring sense (or for convex losses under suitable conditions), expected reduction in loss is bounded by the mutual information between Data and the task parameters.

4. Limits from averaging, computability, and self‑reference

A. No‑free‑lunch (NFL) constraints.
The NFL theorem (over uniform distributions on problem instances) implies: averaged uniformly over all possible tasks, no algorithm has expected improvement over any other. Therefore, any self‑improvement that raises expected performance must exploit nonuniform structure in the task distribution; it cannot be guaranteed across all possible tasks.

B. Computability limits (Rice, Halting).
Proposition 4.1 (Undecidability of nontrivial improvement).
For any nontrivial semantic property S of programs (for example “program q has strictly lower loss than program p on all inputs”), deciding S is undecidable (Rice’s theorem). Consequently, there is no general computable verifier V that, given arbitrary p and candidate q, always decides whether q is an improvement of p on arbitrary environments E.

Corollary 4.2.
No computable self‑improver can, in general, prove that an arbitrary proposed change improves performance across all environments; empirical evaluation must be used, or restrictions placed on the class of tasks.

C. Self‑reference and provability limits (Gödel/Löb).
If a program p is allowed to reason about the correctness or performance of its own successors within a sufficiently expressive formal system, Löb’s theorem and Gödel incompleteness impose constraints. Informally: a sufficiently strong system cannot, in general, prove the correctness (or provable improvement) of arbitrary nontrivial transformations of itself without already having such proof; attempts at self‑certification can lead to circularities that require assumptions (or oracles) external to the system.

Consequence 4.3.
Provably safe or provably beneficial self‑modification for arbitrary transformations is impossible within the same expressive system without additional axioms or trusted oracles.

D. Fixed points and convergence
Definition 4.4 (Fixed point).
p* is a fixed point of T with respect to E if T(p*, h*) = p* for every history h* obtainable from running p* in E (or for the histories that actually occur).

Proposition 4.5 (Existence/stability).
If performance values L(p,E) take values in a well‑ordered set that satisfies descending chain condition (e.g., bounded below and discrete), then any monotone improving sequence must stabilize at a fixed point in finite time. If values lie in a continuous range with no lower bound on step sizes, infinite strictly-improving chains are possible in principle.

Thus whether iterative self‑improvement halts or converges depends on the codomain and the granularity of measurable improvement. In practice, resource bounds and discreteness often force stabilization.

E. Complexity / resource trade‑offs
Proposition 4.6 (Complexity–performance tradeoff).
A transformation that decreases expected loss may increase program description length and running time. In algorithmic information terms, a successor p' may have Kolmogorov complexity K(p') > K(p). There is a trade‑off: net expected utility should account for both performance and resource cost (time, memory, verification cost).

Formal bound (informal): If improvement ΔLoss is achieved only by encoding ΔK additional bits about Θ into the program, then the cost of learning/verification must be less than the performance gain for net benefit; otherwise the modification is not beneficial under a utility that penalizes complexity.

5. What do self‑improving algorithms create? (Formal summary)

Given the above, the strictly logical expansion of the phrase “Self‑improving algorithms create ...” can be completed by the following rigorous statement:

Self‑improving algorithms create successor programs that encode information about the environment or task not already contained in the initial program; that is, they instantiate a computable mapping T such that for histories carrying mutual information I(Θ; Data) > 0, the successor program p' = T(p, Data) has strictly lower expected loss on the task distribution conditioned on Data. The capacity for such creation is limited by (i) the presence of extractable information in the data, (ii) average‑case limitations (no free lunch) which require exploitable structure in the task distribution, (iii) computability/decidability limits (Rice/halting), and (iv) provability/self‑reference limits (Gödel/Löb) when proofs of improvement are required internally. Moreover, these created successors generally trade off increased descriptive or computational complexity for lower task loss; convergence to a fixed point occurs when no further extractable, useful information can be compactly encoded by the allowed transformations.

6. Minimal formal claims (for quick reference)

- Claim A: Necessary condition — If Data carries no new information about the task parameters relative to the current program, no expected improvement is possible.

- Claim B: NFL constraint — Improvement that holds uniformly across all tasks is impossible; improvement must exploit task structure.

- Claim C: Undecidability — There is no general computable test that decides for arbitrary p, q whether q is an improvement of p on all inputs/environments.

- Claim D: Provable self‑improvement is limited — A program cannot, within its own sufficiently expressive theory, always prove the correctness or superiority of arbitrary modifications to itself.

- Claim E: Information bound — Expected reduction in (Bayesian) log loss equals the mutual information gained about task parameters.

7. Practical implications (brief)

- Design of self‑improving systems must explicitly provide means to gather informative data, restrict task classes, or accept empirical (statistical) evaluation rather than full formal verification.
- To avoid undecidable verification, enforce syntactic constraints, modular architectures, or use stronger trusted oracles for critical changes.
- Account for resource costs and complexities when evaluating whether a created successor is truly preferable.

- Produce formal proofs for any of the propositions above in a complete style.
- Explore recursive (meta‑level) self‑improvement where T itself is subject to improvement and analyze the recursion fixed points and possible unbounded chains.

I will expand the concept "Self-improving algorithms create..." by giving (1) a precise model, (2) what is meant by "create" in that model, (3) positive existence results, (4) intrinsic limits (computability and information-theoretic), and (5) structural consequences and corollaries. I state definitions, propositions and short proofs or proof sketches where appropriate so the development is strictly logical.

1. Model and primitives

- Underlying computation model. Fix a standard enumeration (φ_e)_{e∈N} of partial computable functions (Turing machines). Let code(e) denote a canonical encoding of index e (or its source text). All constructions are relative to this enumeration; statements that follow are invariant up to constant additive terms.

- Performance measure. Let C(e) be a measure of "cost" or "loss" of program φ_e on the target task (lower is better). C may be defined relative to an input distribution D and a resource bound R (time, space), e.g. expected loss over D within time bound R. We will treat variants where C is (i) computable, (ii) lower semicomputable, or (iii) uncomputable — different results apply in each case.

- Self-improving algorithm. A self-improving algorithm S is a Turing machine that, when started with no external privileged oracle, either
  a) outputs a (finite or infinite) sequence of indices e0, e1, e2, ... (creation-as-output), or
  b) repeatedly rewrites its own code and continues execution (self-modification).
Either way S "creates" new algorithms by producing their descriptions (indices or source). We identify the two modes by treating self-modification as S outputting a new index that it then executes.

- Improvement sequence. We say S generates an improvement sequence if the produced indices satisfy C(e_{n+1}) < C(e_n) for all (or infinitely many) n (strict improvement) or C(e_{n+1}) ≤ C(e_n) with at least one strict step (nonincreasing). The sequence may be finite (terminates at a fixed point) or infinite.

2. What "create" must mean logically

The verb "create" can be formalized in two independent senses:

- Syntactic creation: S outputs code for a program (an index e or a full source string). This is trivial: any TM can output any finite string, so syntactic creation is always possible.

- Algorithmic-information creation: S increases the Kolmogorov complexity of what it outputs relative to its own description and its prior inputs. Formally, if K(·) is prefix Kolmogorov complexity, then a deterministic S without additional external input cannot output a string x with K(x) > K(S) + O(1). So "creating new algorithmic information" beyond S's own description requires additional external entropy or access to an environment that supplies information.

Both senses will be used: syntactic creation is easy and ubiquitous; nontrivial claims about true novelty must respect Kolmogorov bounds.

3. Existence: self-improvers that create strictly better algorithms

Proposition 1 (existence of self-improvers). For any computable, nontrivial performance measure C and any computable infinite monotone sequence of indices (a_n) with C(a_{n+1}) < C(a_n), there exists a computable S that outputs that sequence (e_n = a_n). Therefore syntactic creation of arbitrarily long strictly improving sequences is possible whenever such a sequence is computable.

Proof sketch. Given a computable description of (a_n), S can ignore the task and print the sequence. So any computable sequence of improving programs can be produced.

This proposition is trivial but clarifies that the substantive question is whether a computable S can discover such a sequence for a nontrivial task when only given the task specification (and not the sequence itself).

Proposition 2 (constructive search methods). Let C be lower-semicomputable (i.e., approximable from below). There are computable meta-algorithms that, given a formal description of the task and resource bound R, enumerate candidates and empirically test them; with unbounded time these enumerations can produce strictly improving programs whenever better programs exist and are eventually found. Levin's universal search (optimal search up to constant factor) can be used to schedule tests over all candidate programs, so S can asymptotically match the runtime of any specific program up to a multiplicative constant factor if the cost includes runtime and correctness.

Remarks. These positive results rely on search; they do not claim S can recognize optimality or prove global optimality.

4. Limits: undecidability, incompleteness, and information bounds

4.1 Undecidability and Rice-type limitations

Claim (undecidability of nontrivial improvement). If "improvement" is a nontrivial semantic property of program behavior, then deciding for arbitrary e,f whether C(f) < C(e) is undecidable in general. Consequently, no computable meta-algorithm can, for every pair (e,f), decide improvement.

Reason. This is a direct consequence of Rice's theorem: any nontrivial property of the partial function computed by a program is undecidable. If C captures semantic performance, then deciding strict improvement is a nontrivial semantic predicate and hence undecidable.

Corollary (no general method to pick globally best program). There is no computable S that, given an arbitrary task specification, always outputs an index e* that achieves the minimal possible C over all programs, unless the set of optimal programs is computably recognizable — which is not the case in general.

4.2 Speed-up theorems and absence of computable fastest program

Blum's speed-up theorem: There exist computable problems for which no single program is fastest: for any program p there exists a program q that computes the same function but is asymptotically faster by an arbitrarily large amount on infinitely many inputs. Therefore, for such problems, any computable self-improver S that tries to find the "fastest program" will never halt with a certificate of optimality; S can discover progressively faster programs but cannot produce a final optimal one because none exists.

4.3 Algorithmic-information limits

Proposition (information bound). Let S be a deterministic TM with description size K(S). If S has no inputs other than an implicit blank tape and no access to an external randomness source or environment providing new information, then for every string x that S outputs we have K(x) ≤ K(S) + O(1). Consequently, S cannot "create" outputs whose Kolmogorov complexity exceeds its own description length up to additive constants.

Corollary. A self-improver that is closed (no external information) cannot produce fundamentally new algorithmic content beyond its own description and contents of initial input; improvements must be drawn from compressible structure already implicit in S or its inputs.

4.4 Limits from provability (Gödel-type limits)

Gödel-machine style meta-algorithms execute self-modifications only when they can prove in a given formal axiomatic system that the modification yields strictly higher expected utility. Such machines are provably safe and, within the scope of their proof system, optimal: no provably better self-modification exists at the time of rewriting.

Limitation. By Gödel incompleteness, there are true statements about program behavior (including improvement assertions) that are unprovable in any given sound, sufficiently strong formal system. Therefore a Gödel-machine S may fail to enact true but unprovable improvements. Optimality is relative to the chosen proof system.

5. Structural theorems and trade-offs

Theorem A (possible infinite improvement, unrecognizable optimum). There exist computable tasks and computable self-improvers S that output an infinite strictly improving sequence (C(e_{n+1}) < C(e_n) for all n). However, there may be no computable index n* at which S can declare "I am optimal" (because no optimal exists, or optimality is undecidable).

Proof sketch. Use Blum's speed-up examples for the task; construct S to find programs with strictly smaller cost iteratively (via search). The absence of an index declaring final optimality follows from nonexistence of a fastest program or from Rice-type undecidability.

Theorem B (asymptotic optimality up to constant). Let P be a problem class and let U be Levin's universal search scheduler that interleaves executions of candidate programs with weights 2^{-l(p)} where l(p) is program length. Then there exists a computable S using U such that, for any program p solving the task with runtime T on inputs of size n, S will find an equivalent program and execute it with runtime c·T(n) + O(1) where c depends on p but not on n. Thus S is asymptotically optimal up to a multiplicative constant depending on the discovered program.

Interpretation. Practical constants are often enormous; hence Levin search is not a practical panacea but proves existence of universal asymptotic competitiveness.

6. Practical consequences and necessary resources for sustained self-improvement

- Source of new information. To produce genuinely new algorithmic ideas (high Kolmogorov complexity), a self-improver needs access to external data (measurements, human input, random bits) whose complexity exceeds its own description.

- Verification. To safely adopt a modification, S must (i) evaluate candidate programs empirically (requiring test harness and tasks), or (ii) prove improvement in a formal system (requiring proofs). Empirical evaluation gives no absolute guarantees and can be fooled; formal proofs give guarantees but are limited by proving power.

- Resource trade-offs. Searching for better programs costs time and compute that could have been used by the current program; optimal allocation between exploitation and searching is itself an instance of the same meta-optimization.

- No free lunch: Unless the environment/distribution has exploitable structure, arbitrary improvement is impossible; the "no free lunch" intuition formalizes that improvement requires domain-specific information.

7. Compact summary (strict logical statement)

Let S be a computable self-improver that outputs program descriptions (indices) e_0,e_1,.... Then:

- S can syntactically create arbitrarily many distinct program descriptions (trivial).

- S can generate a computable strictly improving sequence relative to a computable cost C whenever such a computable sequence exists (existence).

- S cannot, in general, decide or guarantee global optimality of an arbitrary program because determining nontrivial semantic properties (including strict improvement) is undecidable (Rice), and for some tasks there is no single fastest program (Blum speed-up).

- Deterministic S without external information cannot increase Kolmogorov complexity beyond K(S) + O(1); thus truly new algorithmic information requires external input/randomness.

- Using universal-search-style schedulers, S can be made asymptotically competitive with any particular program (Levin), but constant factors may be infeasible.

- Systems that only self-modify when a proof of improvement exists (Gödel machines) are provably safe relative to their proof system, but incomplete: provably beneficial improvements that are true but unprovable will be missed.

Conclusion — what self-improving algorithms create (precise answer)

- Syntactically: they create new program descriptions (indices) at will.

- Algorithmically: they can create sequences of programs with strictly improving performance relative to computable metrics whenever such sequences are effectively discoverable.

- Information-theoretically: they cannot create irreducible algorithmic information beyond what is supplied by their own description plus external inputs; hence genuinely novel algorithms require new information from the environment or randomness.

- Epistemically: they can create provably beneficial self-modifications only to the extent that the underlying formal system can prove the relevant improvement statements; otherwise improvements may remain true but unprovable and so unexploited.

These points together form a strict logical expansion of "Self-improving algorithms create..." in the setting of recursive information theory: they create syntactic programs and potentially better (lower-cost) algorithms, but their ability to create fundamentally new algorithmic content, to recognize global optimality, and to assure unbounded or final optimal improvement is blocked by computability, information, and provability limits.

Below I expand the fragment “Self‑improving algorithms create …” into a precise, logically structured description and short formal theory within the setting of recursive (algorithmic) information theory. I give definitions, properties, simple propositions (with sketches of proof), limits coming from computability and information theory, and implications (including conditions for accelerating improvement and safety notes).

1) Setup and notation (formal primitives)
- Let A be the set of all algorithms (encodings of Turing machines, or programs) that may act in an environment E. Treat each algorithm a ∈ A as a finite binary string ⟨a⟩.
- Let E denote the environment (possibly a distribution over problem instances or an interactive environment). Observations and data produced by running algorithms in E are denoted o ∈ O.
- Let P: A × E → R be a real-valued performance measure (utility, negative loss) that we want to increase. Write P(a) when E is fixed or clear from context.
- Let Obs(a, E, t) be the observation/data available after running a for t units of resource (time/samples).
- Define an update operator U: A × O × Rsc → A, where Rsc denotes available computational resources (time, memory, random bits). U(a, o; r) is the new algorithm produced by running a and using data o with resources r. In particular a self‑improving algorithm a0 implements a loop that uses U to produce a1, a2, …:
  a_{t+1} = U(a_t, o_t; r_t), with o_t = Obs(a_t, E, t).

2) Definition: self‑improving algorithm
A program a0 is a self‑improving algorithm for environment E and performance P if it implements a computable update loop a_{t+1} = U(a_t, o_t; r_t) and, for some nontrivial subsequence of times {t_k}, satisfies
  P(a_{t_{k+1}}) ≥ P(a_{t_k})
and typically strictly greater for at least one k. In other words, the program autonomously produces successors that do not degrade and sometimes improve performance on the target task.

3) Partial ordering and fixed points
- Define a partial order ≼ on A by a ≼ b iff P(a) ≤ P(b). An algorithm b is strictly better than a when P(b) > P(a).
- A fixed point a* of U (given the observation process) satisfies U(a*, o*; r*) = a* (or up to equivalence class of behavior). If U is monotone (P(U(a,·)) ≥ P(a) for all a), any nondecreasing trajectory {P(a_t)} bounded above converges to sup P reachable by that process; the corresponding algorithms converge in performance, not necessarily syntactically.

Proposition 1 (Monotone convergence of performance).
If for each t, P(a_{t+1}) ≥ P(a_t) and sup_a P(a) ≤ B < ∞, then the sequence {P(a_t)} converges to some L ≤ B (monotone bounded sequence).
Sketch of proof: monotone nondecreasing bounded sequence of reals converges to sup.

4) Resources, information, and necessary conditions for improvement
Improvement requires information and resources. Two formal constraints:

(A) Information lower bound (algorithmic information theory).
Let a_opt be an algorithm achieving near‑optimal performance P*. The algorithmic (Kolmogorov) complexity K(⟨a_opt⟩) quantifies how many bits of description are required to produce a_opt. Observations o gathered up to time t contain at most I = I(⟨a_opt⟩ : o) bits of algorithmic mutual information about a_opt. A self‑improver using only o and its own code cannot in general produce a program whose shortest description is shorter than K(⟨a_opt⟩) − I (up to additive constants). Thus, to reach a_opt the self‑improver must obtain sufficient information about a_opt from the environment or from additional sources of information.

Informal corollary: If the target improvement requires k bits of new information, the self‑improver must acquire at least k effective bits (from data or oracle) to reach it.

(B) Resource/time bound.
Producing improved algorithms may require unbounded computation: even if a better program exists, finding it may be computationally intractable (search complexity), and in general properties about arbitrary programs are undecidable (see next section).

5) Computability and logical limits
(a) Rice‑style limitations.
Rice’s theorem: any nontrivial semantic property of programs is undecidable. Therefore, there is no general algorithm that, given an arbitrary program a and arbitrary environment E, decides whether there exists any program b with strictly larger P(b). Concreteness: you cannot design a universal self‑improver that is guaranteed to find nontrivial semantic improvements for every possible initial program and environment.

(b) Proof‑theoretic obstacles (Gödel–Löb phenomena).
If the self‑improver reasons about the correctness or performance of successor programs inside a formal system, limitations on what it can prove about more powerful successors constrain provably safe self‑improvement. One cannot generally produce arbitrarily stronger provable guarantees about successors without stronger axioms; attempts to bootstrap provability can run into fixed‑point/Gödel‑like constraints.

6) Dynamics of recursive improvement, acceleration, and fixed points
Define improvement potential g(a) = sup_{b reachable from a with allowed resources} P(b) − P(a). The dynamics depend on how g transforms when a improves.

Definition (accelerating self‑improvement).
A trajectory {a_t} exhibits accelerating improvement if the sequence of gains Δ_t = P(a_{t+1}) − P(a_t) grows over time (e.g., Δ_{t+1} ≥ c Δ_t for c > 1 in some regime).

Proposition 2 (Condition for unbounded acceleration).
If there exists a region of algorithm space S and constants c > 1 and a0 ∈ S such that for all a ∈ S, when U produces an improved a' we have g(a') ≥ c g(a), and if resources do not impose a hard upper bound on P, then improvement gains can grow geometrically while inside S (potential for rapid “explosion” of ability). If an absolute supremum P_max < ∞ exists (e.g., optimal task performance), geometric growth of gains must stop as P approaches P_max.

Interpretation: accelerating improvement requires that improving the optimizer increases its capacity to discover even larger improvements (positive feedback). Whether such a region exists in practice depends on task structure and availability of information/resources.

7) Concrete formal examples
- Meta‑search example: let a be a program that performs stochastic search for programs that maximize P by enumerating candidates and testing them. U is “replace a by the best candidate found within resource budget r.” This formalizes a large class of self‑improvers (hill‑climbers, evolutionary searchers). Analysis reduces to search theory: expected improvement per step depends on search distribution, sample complexity, and variance of candidate quality.

- Compression/bootstrap example: a may search for shorter encodings of programs that perform as well. If the environment’s tasks permit compressible structure, the program can find shorter and faster implementations (improving resources and hence future search capability). This highlights the role of algorithmic information and compression as a source of improvement.

8) Safety and specification drift
Self‑modification can produce behavior that optimizes the specified performance P while violating other desiderata (reward hacking, specification gaming). Formally, if P is a proxy for true objective U_true, then maximizing P can cause divergence from U_true. This is not a paradoxical theorem but a design constraint: improvements must be judged on the true objective and include invariants or verification mechanisms.

9) Design implications and necessary engineering constraints
If one wants controlled, provable self‑improvement, the following are necessary design controls (each with formal rationale above):
- Explicit specification of allowed transformations and invariants (to constrain search space).
- Provision of external information sources (data, oracles) sufficient to meet the information lower bound for targeted improvements.
- Resource budgeting and sandboxing to restrict computational paths and limit undecidability exposure.
- Modular separation of meta‑reasoning and base code to simplify verification.
- Continuous evaluation on broad, robust test distributions to avoid overfitting and reward hacking.

10) Compact summary statement (answering the stem)
Self‑improving algorithms create sequences of algorithms a0, a1, a2, … via a computable update operator U that uses observations and resources; they thereby create (1) increased task‑specific performance when the update is effective, (2) new algorithmic information (to the extent that information is available from the environment), and (3) a recursive structure of meta‑levels whose dynamics are governed by information‑theoretic and computability constraints. Formally, they create monotone or accelerating trajectories in the partially ordered space (A, ≼) when resources and information permit, but they are fundamentally limited by algorithmic information bounds, undecidability (Rice), and proof‑theoretic limits (Gödel‑Löb type constraints). Whether a trajectory converges, accelerates, or fails depends on (i) available external information, (ii) resource bounds, (iii) the structure of the performance landscape P, and (iv) the update operator U’s ability to amplify its own improvement potential.

If you want, I can:
- Formalize one of the propositions above into a fully rigorous theorem with a detailed proof in the Turing‑machine/Kolmogorov framework.
- Work a concrete toy model (e.g., finite search spaces) and simulate how different U choices give monotone vs accelerating improvement.
- Translate the information lower bound into an explicit inequality using Kolmogorov complexity and mutual information for a chosen formal setting.

Below I expand the fragment “Self-improving algorithms create …” into a strict, logically organized formalization, a set of precise claims (with proofs or proof sketches where appropriate), and a discussion of limits and consequences drawn from recursion theory, computability, complexity and statistical learning. The goal is to capture what self-improvement can and cannot do, in mathematically well-defined terms.

1. Setup and definitions

- Alphabet, programs, semantics.
  - Fix a standard programming model (e.g., a universal Turing machine U). Let Σ* be the set of finite binary strings; strings code programs and data.
  - For e in Σ*, let φ_e denote the partial computable function computed by program coded by e on U. Runtime and resource bounds can be formalized by indexing with time/space bounds if needed.

- Task environment and performance measure.
  - Let T be a nonempty set of tasks (each task t ∈ T is itself a specification: an input distribution, a cost/loss function, or a decision problem).
  - Define a performance measure Perf: (program, task) → R ∪ {±∞}. Perf(e, t) evaluates how well φ_e performs on task t (e.g., expected reward, error rate, runtime, resource tradeoff).
  - For compactness one can consider a (possibly distributional) aggregate performance P(e) = E_{t∼D}[Perf(e,t)] for some distribution D over tasks, or a vector of performances over tasks.

- Algorithms and improvement relation.
  - An algorithm is a program code e ∈ Σ* (or its semantics φ_e).
  - Define a binary relation ≻ on codes/algorithms: e' ≻ e means e' is an improvement over e according to the chosen performance criterion (e.g., P(e') > P(e) and resource usage acceptable). We require ≻ to be a strict partial order consistent with Perf (as appropriate).
  - A self-improving algorithm is a program that, when run, outputs (or constructs and returns) a new program that is intended to improve on itself (or on a given program) according to ≻.

- Self-improvement operator.
  - A (computable) improvement operator is a partial computable function F: Σ* × I → Σ* (I is information available: observed data, environment outputs, proofs, resource bounds, etc.). Given a program code e and information i, F(e,i) = e' is a candidate improved program.
  - Iterated self-improvement is the sequence e_0, e_1, e_2, … defined by e_{n+1} = F(e_n, i_n) where i_n is information gathered up to step n (possibly dependent on φ_{e_n}’s behavior).

2. Elementary observations

- Self-reference is expressible: by Kleene’s recursion theorem there exist programs that obtain their own index and can produce outputs depending on it. Concretely, for any computable F there exists e such that φ_e = φ_{F(e)} (informal formulation) — this allows programs to construct new programs based on their own code.

- Self-improvement formalized: a program e is self-improving if when executed with some information protocol it produces e' with e' ≻ e. An iterated self-improving program repeatedly applies its improvement operator.

3. Existence of fixed points and self-referential constructions

Proposition 1 (Existence of self-referential programs; Kleene-style). Let F be any total computable operator mapping codes to codes. There exists e such that φ_e = φ_{F(e)}. Consequently, there exist programs that can, in effect, “output” a program that behaves like the one F would produce for its own code.

Sketch of proof: This is a direct corollary of Kleene's recursion theorem (second recursion theorem). It guarantees fixed-point programs for computable transformations on codes.

Consequence: one can construct programs that produce improved versions of themselves in the sense of constructing e' = F(e) and using their own identity when computing e'.

4. Limits from computability and undecidability

Theorem 1 (Uncomputability of general optimal improvement). Let S be a nontrivial semantic property of programs (e.g., “P(e) ≥ r” for some threshold r). Deciding whether, for a given code e and operator F, there exists a finite sequence of iterates e_0=e, e_1=F(e_0), …, e_n such that P(e_n) ≥ r is, in general, undecidable.

Sketch: By reducing the halting problem or Rice’s theorem-type arguments. Semantic properties of program behavior are in general undecidable; existence of a sequence that achieves a semantic threshold can encode arbitrary halting/semantic queries.

Corollary: No general algorithm can, given an arbitrary program and arbitrary task specification, determine whether a self-improvement process will reach a desired level of performance, or whether it will ever halt, or produce unbounded improvement.

Remark: This does not preclude computable self-improvement in restricted domains (e.g., finite-state tasks, bounded resources). It only rules out uniform solutions for unrestricted programs/tasks.

5. Complexity and resource tradeoffs

- Overhead vs. benefit: improvement requires computation and information gathering. Let Cost(e→e') denote the resources needed to produce e' from e (time, space). Let Gain(e,e') = P(e') − P(e). A necessary (but not sufficient) condition for iterative self-improvement to be beneficial under resource discounting is that the discounted cumulative gains exceed cumulative costs:
  Σ_n Discount(n) · Gain(e_n,e_{n+1}) > Σ_n Cost(e_n→e_{n+1})·Discount(n).

- No free lunch: For arbitrary task distributions, there is no universally superior algorithm; improvement necessarily depends on assumptions about tasks/environment. A self-improver without informative feedback cannot systematically improve in expectation across all possible tasks.

6. Convergence, monotonic improvement, and attractors

- Monotone improvement: If F is such that e_{n+1} ≻ e_n for all n and ≻ is a strict well-founded order (i.e., no infinite strictly descending chains), then the process must terminate at a maximal element (a fixed point or an element with no superior element with respect to F’s range).

- Fixed points: A program e* is an F-fixed point if F(e*, i*) = e* for the information state i* encountered. Fixed points correspond to stable configurations where no further improvement is produced under the operator and information update rule.

- Contraction condition and unique fixed point: If one can embed codes into a complete metric space (X,d) and F (together with the information-update map) induces a contraction mapping, Banach fixed-point theorem guarantees a unique fixed point and convergence of iterates. This is a strong sufficient condition but rarely holds in general computational settings.

- Possible behaviors in general:
  - Convergence to a fixed point (stationary algorithm).
  - Limit cycles (repeated sequence of algorithms).
  - Unbounded improvement (if ≻ admits infinite ascending chains and resources permit).
  - Divergence/halting (operator fails to produce output or computation does not terminate).

7. Diagonalization and limits to guaranteed global improvement

- Diagonalization barriers: Any general self-improvement mechanism that attempts to solve or outrun all other algorithms on all inputs will encounter diagonalization-style impossibility results (akin to Cantor or Turing diagonal arguments). For example, a program that claims to produce the optimal program for all tasks would enable solving undecidable problems.

- Provable improvement vs. empirical improvement: In many models, one can prove local or restricted-case improvements (e.g., lower loss on the observed sample), but proving strict improvement over the entire task distribution or for all inputs is often impossible or undecidable.

8. Meta-level structure and recursive towers

- Meta-operators: One may consider a hierarchy F_0, F_1, ... where F_{k+1} improves the improvement operator F_k (meta-improvement). The tower of reflections can be formalized: each operator is a computable mapping indexed by previous operator code. Recursively, this yields higher-order self-improvement.

- Limits from reflection principles: In formal systems, reflection and self-verification are limited by Gödel-style incompleteness: a sufficiently expressive system cannot prove its own soundness. By analogy, a self-improver that contains a proof-of-improvement mechanism faces limitations in proving global correctness of its own future modifications.

9. Practical sufficient conditions for successful self-improvement (restricted, constructive)

The negative results above do not preclude many useful, provably-productive self-improvement schemes under bounded conditions. Typical sufficient conditions include:

- Resource bounds: work in a finite model where codes and state spaces are finite: then search for improvements is decidable; process terminates in finite time.

- Probabilistic/approximate improvement goals: Optimize expected performance over a known distribution; use stochastic gradient or empirical risk minimization with provable convergence properties under standard statistical assumptions (convexity, boundedness, i.i.d. samples).

- Verifiable local improvements: Use verification tools to check that candidate e' improves on e for a specified finite set of properties or test-suite — useful but not guaranteeing global improvement.

- Universal search (Levin search): Given time bounds and prior weights, one can enumerate improvements in a resource-aware manner and obtain optimality up to constant factors, but with impractical constants and requiring known bounds.

10. Safety, verification and control

- Verifying that an automatically generated e' is safe, correct, or “improving” can be undecidable in general. Practical systems therefore restrict the allowed transformations (syntactic templates, verified transformation primitives), or require proofs/certificates of improvement that are checkable within a trusted subsystem.

- Sandboxing and monitoring: In practice, treat generated code as untrusted until validated by testbeds, formal verification, or degraded privileges.

11. Compact statement integrating recursion theory

Putting the pieces together, a compact formal statement:

Let U be a universal machine, F a computable operator mapping program codes (and information histories) to program codes, and P a semantic performance map. Iterating e_{n+1} = F(e_n, i_n) yields a self-improvement process. By Kleene’s recursion theorem, such self-referential programs exist and can be constructed. However, by Rice’s theorem and undecidability of general semantic properties, no computable procedure can, in general, determine whether such a sequence reaches a specified global performance threshold or produces a provably optimal program. Under additional restrictions (bounded state space, contraction properties, statistical assumptions) one can obtain decidability and convergence guarantees. Any practical self-improvement design therefore must (a) restrict the domain or the form of allowable changes, (b) accept resource and verification costs, and (c) base improvement on measurable, restricted criteria rather than on claims of universal optimality.

12. Examples (brief)

- Meta-learning: F is a learned optimizer; e_n is a learner with parameters; iterations correspond to gradient steps guided by meta-learner. Convergence results depend on convexity/regularity assumptions.

- Program synthesis via proof search: e produces proof certificates that a candidate e' satisfies a specification; improvement is accepted only when proof-checked.

- Universal search for best algorithm under time bounds: enumerates all candidate programs weighted by prior; yields optimality up to constants but suffers incomputable/unbounded constants in general.

13. Open questions and research directions

- Characterize classes of F and performance measures P for which global optimality of iterates is decidable or for which guaranteed unbounded improvement can occur.

- Quantify the tradeoff between verification cost and achievable improvement in resource-bounded settings.

- Study stochastic self-improvement dynamics (randomized F, noisy feedback) with tools from stochastic approximation and dynamical systems.

- Relate levels of reflection (meta-improvement towers) to hierarchies in recursion theory and formal provability, clarifying what can be certified at each level.

14. Conclusion (concise)

Self-improving algorithms can be formalized as computable operators producing successive program codes. Recursion theory (Kleene’s recursion theorem) guarantees the existence of self-referential constructions; computability theory (Rice, halting) and diagonalization place strict limits on what can be decided or guaranteed in full generality. Practical, provably-useful self-improvement is possible under restricted assumptions (finite models, statistical regularity, verifiable transformation primitives), but claims of universal or unbounded automatic improvement run into fundamental theoretical barriers.

Below I expand the concept into a strict, logically organized framework suitable for theoretical work in recursive information theory. I state definitions, constructions, and limits (with sketches of proofs) and indicate natural measures and open questions. The aim is to be precise rather than implementational.

1. Setup and notation
- Fix a universal Turing machine U that maps finite binary strings (programs) to outputs (possibly interacting with an environment). Programs are elements of {0,1}*.
- A program p may encode an agent/algorithm whose execution can (i) interact with an environment E (which may be modeled as a probability distribution over input/output histories), (ii) output a modified program p' and halt, or (iii) run indefinitely.
- Let Perf(p, E) be a real-valued performance measure of program p when run in environment E (for example expected reward over some horizon, or a loss function), assumed to be well-defined for the pairs we consider.
- A self-improving program is a program p that, when executed, may output p' such that Perf(p', E) > Perf(p, E) (strict improvement) or nondecreasing (weak improvement). We consider iterative self-improvement as the sequence p_0, p_1, p_2, ... with p_{n+1} produced by running p_n.

2. Formal definition: self-improvement process
Definition 1 (Self-improvement operator). A self-improvement operator S is a (possibly partial) computable function S: {0,1}* × H -> {0,1}* defined on program descriptions and histories H (finite interaction transcripts) such that running program p in environment E yields p' = S(p, h) for some observed history h. For simplicity one can take history h empty and consider S(p) a transformation based only on p.

Definition 2 (Recursive self-improvement sequence). Given p_0 and S, define p_{n+1} = S(p_n) whenever S(p_n) is defined. The pair (p_0, S) generates a recursive self-improvement sequence.

3. Existence of self-referential self-improvers
Proposition 1 (Kleene recursion theorem — self-reference exists). For any computable transformation T that maps program descriptions to program descriptions, there exists a program p such that U(p) = U(T(⟨p⟩)). Concretely, there exists p with behavior equal to the behavior of T on its own code.

Sketch: Kleene’s recursion theorem constructs a fixed-point program that incorporates its own index; hence T can be applied to the program’s own description. This ensures that self-referential programs that produce modified copies of themselves (or consult their own description) exist.

Corollary. Self-improving programs that can read and transform their own source (or description) exist in principle.

4. What “create information” means (multiple senses)
We distinguish several formal senses in which a self-improver can "create information":

A. Increase in task-relevant performance: Perf(p_{n+1}, E) > Perf(p_n, E). This is the operational meaning—improvement.

B. Increase in algorithmic information: The Kolmogorov complexity K(p_{n+1}) may be larger than K(p_n). Yet increase in K is constrained: in a closed deterministic computational system without external random input, K cannot increase beyond the information already present (plus small overhead). More precisely, a program cannot deterministically manufacture independent algorithmic information greater than that encoded in its initial state.

C. Increase in mutual information with environment: Running a program and observing the environment can increase the mutual information I(Program_state ; Environment_history). Learning from environment increases statistical/algorithmic information about E.

D. Creation of explanatory models: a program may construct new compressed descriptions (models) of observed data (increase in model sophistication), which is information in the sense of better predictive compression.

5. Fundamental limits and impossibility results
Proposition 2 (No general computable optimizer). There is no computable universal self-improvement operator S that, for every program p and every nontrivial performance measure Perf, decides and produces an improved p' with strictly larger Perf(p', E) whenever such improvements exist.

Sketch: This follows from Rice’s theorem and the halting problem. Deciding whether some modification yields higher semantic performance is a nontrivial property of program behavior; in general it is undecidable. Hence no computable S can always find (or even decide existence of) an improving modification.

Proposition 3 (Halting/improvement trade-off). For many meaningful Perf and classes of environments E, it is undecidable whether a candidate self-modification both (i) halts and (ii) yields improved performance.

Implication. Guaranteed provable improvement across all possible environments and programs is impossible within computability limits.

Proposition 4 (Algorithmic information cannot be created from nothing). If the universe is modeled as a deterministic computable dynamical system and a program p evolves deterministically without external random or high-entropy input, then K(p_t) ≤ K(p_0) + O(1) for all t (up to additive constants), i.e., Kolmogorov complexity cannot grow beyond the initial description plus the description of the dynamics.

Sketch: Deterministic evolution is a computable mapping; any future state can be generated from the initial state and the evolution rule, so complexity is bounded. Randomness or high-complexity environment input is needed to increase Kolmogorov complexity in an unbounded way.

6. Resource bounds and convergence
- Computational resource limits (time, space) constrain search for better programs. A theoretically optimal search (e.g., Levin search over program modifications weighted by description length) can in principle find improvements but may be infeasible.
- Monotone improvement sequences need not exist: S may produce cycles, degrade performance, or converge to local optima (fixed points p* with S(p*) = p*). Establishing monotonicity requires additional assumptions on S (e.g., S performs provably improving transformations with certificates).
- Convergence to global optimality is only guaranteed under assumptions: oracle access to Perf across modifications, unbounded computation, or stochastic exploration with diminishing step-sizes under certain landscape properties.

7. Quantifying self-improvement as information dynamics
One useful formalization uses information measures between program description P_n and environment E:

Define the directed information gain at step n:
ΔI_n := I(P_{n+1} ; E_{1:n}) − I(P_n ; E_{1:n}),

where E_{1:n} denotes the history observed up to step n and I(·;·) is mutual information. Self-improvement that arises from learning corresponds to positive ΔI_n: the new program encodes more information about the observed environment, which can enable better decisions.

An alternative measure is expected regret reduction:
ΔR_n := E[Regret(p_n)] − E[Regret(p_{n+1})],
which is directly tied to utility/performance.

Both measures capture different notions of “information created” — one descriptive (mutual information), one instrumental (utility gain).

8. Constructive paradigms (examples)
- Reflective search: p maintains a model of its own code and performs stochastic/messy search over syntactic modifications; verifies candidate p' via empirical testing in environment to estimate Perf. This creates information by acquiring empirical performance results and encoding them into better code.
- Meta-learning: p runs an inner learning algorithm that outputs an improved learner; iterations correspond to recursive meta-learning.
- Provable self-improvement: p searches for provable algorithmic transformations that increase a provable lower bound on Perf; pragmatically expensive but gives certificates.

9. Trade-offs and costs
- Computational cost: searching program space is often exponentially hard; improvements that are modest in performance may require large computation.
- Information acquisition cost: learning from environment may require costly experiments; there is an exploration-exploitation trade-off.
- Thermodynamic/physical costs: per Landauer’s principle, erasing bits and performing computation incurs minimal energy costs; thus large-scale increases in stored information have physical resource implications.

10. Open problems and research directions
- Formal characterization of classes of environments and performance measures for which computable self-improvement can be guaranteed to converge to global optima.
- Resource-bounded versions of the recursion theorem and constructive frameworks for provable, practically efficient self-improvement.
- Tight bounds relating mutual-information gain from the environment to provable performance gains (how much task-relevant information is required to reach a target performance).
- Formal models of “algorithmic innovation”: how can a program reliably increase its algorithmic sophistication (compressibility of observations into programs) when starting from limited priors and finite resources?

11. Summary, in one logical paragraph
Self-improving algorithms are programs that transform their own descriptions to increase performance. By Kleene’s recursion theorem, self-referential transformations exist; by Rice’s theorem and undecidability results, no computable universal self-improver can always find or certify improvements across arbitrary programs and environments. Information-theoretically, such algorithms either (a) re-encode information already present, (b) import information from the environment (learning), or (c) harness randomness; in closed deterministic systems they cannot create unbounded algorithmic information from nothing. Practical self-improvement therefore requires either external information sources, unbounded computational resources, or restrictions on the class of environments and performance measures; quantifying improvement naturally uses mutual information, Kolmogorov complexity, and regret/performance measures, with trade-offs set by computability, resource, and thermodynamic constraints.

- Work a concrete toy model (e.g., finite-state environments) and analyze achievable self-improvement sequences and convergence.
- Derive bounds that relate mutual information gained from the environment to expected utility improvement for a specified class of tasks.

Below I expand the fragment “Self-improving algorithms create …” into a precise, logically organized account grounded in recursive/algorithmic information theory. I state definitions, a simple formal model, a few propositions with short proofs or justifications, and consequences/limitations. The goal is to show exactly what a self-improving algorithm can be said to “create” and what limits and trade-offs follow from information-theoretic and recursion-theoretic principles.

1. Definitions and setup
- Algorithm description space: let A be a finite binary string that encodes an algorithm (Turing machine, program) and its initial state. Denote an algorithm at time t by A_t ∈ {0,1}*.
- Environment and data: let E be the (possibly stochastic) environment. At each step the algorithm receives data D_t drawn from some process depending on E and possibly on A_t’s actions.
- Update operator (learning operator): a computable operator U that maps (A_t, D_t) to a new algorithm A_{t+1} = U(A_t, D_t). U is the mechanism by which the algorithm “self-modifies.”
- Objective/utility: a computable (or at least semicomputable) function J mapping algorithms (and possibly environment) to a real-valued performance score. “Improvement” means J(A_{t+1}) ≥ J(A_t) (or expected increase).
- Algorithmic information measure: let K(x) denote the prefix Kolmogorov complexity of string x. Let I(x : y) = K(x) + K(y) − K(x, y) denote algorithmic mutual information.

2. Informal claim (expanded)
Self-improving algorithms create new algorithmic information about the environment and about solution structure, subject to strict conservation-like bounds: any increase in the algorithm’s descriptive/algorithmic content that was not implicit in the prior algorithm must originate in (be explained by) information supplied either by the environment (data) or by additional computational resources (time/space) that permit extracting and re-expressing information already implicit in the prior state. Improvements that appear to “create” capabilities ex nihilo are either (a) re-encodings/redistributions of information already present in A_t or in observed data D_{≤t}, or (b) the result of unbounded search that trades computation time for discovery of compressions/shorter programs.

3. Formal observations and propositions

Proposition 1 (upper bound on new algorithmic information).
If A_{t+1} is computable from (A_t, D_t) by a fixed computable interpreter U, then
K(A_{t+1}) ≤ K(A_t) + K(D_t | A_t) + O(1).
Proof sketch: from A_t and D_t we can simulate U to produce A_{t+1}. Thus a shortest description of (A_t, D_t) (plus a constant-size interpreter) suffices to describe A_{t+1}. In particular, the new algorithmic information in A_{t+1} beyond what was already in A_t can be at most the conditional complexity of D_t given A_t (plus constants).

Corollary 1.1 (no free information).
If D_t is empty or has low conditional complexity given A_t (i.e., D_t contains no novel information relative to A_t), then K(A_{t+1}) − K(A_t) is bounded by a small constant: the algorithm cannot produce high-complexity new code unless it ingests high-complexity input or performs long unbounded search.

Proposition 2 (information accounting over a run).
Over n steps with data sequence D_{1..n},
K(A_n) ≤ K(A_0) + K(D_{1..n} | A_0) + O(log n).
Intuition: each step’s changes are computable from past state and data; concatenating descriptions gives the bound.

Proposition 3 (conversion of environmental information into algorithmic structure).
The expected increase in expected utility J due to updates is limited by the (useful) information the algorithm extracts from the environment: extracting m bits of algorithmic information about E enables at most a bounded set of performance improvements whose combinatorial richness is no greater than 2^m (informal counting argument).
Rough justification: m bits can select among at most 2^m qualitatively different strategies/policies; without more than m bits of information the algorithm cannot reliably distinguish more than 2^m different relevant environmental regimes.

Proposition 4 (compressive improvement).
An algorithm can “improve” by reducing K(A) while maintaining or increasing J: finding a shorter program that implements an equivalent or better policy is possible without external data. Such improvement is a discovery of a shorter description (compression) of behavior implicit in A_0. However, by definition of K, discovering the shortest program is in general uncomputable; practical compressors give heuristic, resource-bounded reductions.

4. Fixed points, attractors, and recursion
- A fixed point A* satisfies A* = U(A*, D*) (possibly with D* distributed according to the stationary distribution induced by A*). Fixed points are attractors of self-improvement dynamics. Existence: trivial fixed points exist (no-op updates), but nontrivial fixed points require self-consistency between algorithm and the data it elicits.
- Infinite regress and meta-levels: an algorithm that can modify its own update operator U can produce new U' leading to faster improvement. This creates a hierarchy of meta-levels U, U', U'', ... which is precisely a recursive construction. The net information growth is still bounded by the sum of information in initial state plus observed data plus unbounded computational time for search (which in practice is resource-limited).

5. Limits from recursion theory and logic
- Uncomputability and undecidability: perfect self-improvement (e.g., finding and verifying the globally optimal program) is generally uncomputable (ties to Rice’s theorem and related results). An algorithm cannot, in general, decide properties of arbitrary programs (including optimality) about its own future variants.
- Self-referential provability limits: formal systems (including algorithms that use proof search) are subject to Gödel–Löb phenomena; an agent cannot in general produce a proof of its own optimality if that proof would assert its own provability beyond its deductive strength. Concretely, attempts to bootstrap provable trustworthiness of arbitrarily stronger future versions run into fixed-point/diagonal arguments.

6. Interpretations in terms of information flow
- Creation vs. redistribution: what we call “creation” of algorithmic information is typically redistribution: high-level patterns in raw data/experience are extracted and encoded compactly in code/data structures. This can look like creation when the algorithm’s code becomes more informative about the environment than before.
- Conservation up to computation: informally, algorithmic information is conserved up to what is brought in by environment and what can be invented by search; computation cannot magically produce more independent algorithmic content than its inputs unless it invests unbounded search (which itself is a conversion of time into information).

7. Practical measures and metrics
- Measure self-improvement by ΔJ (improvement in objective), ΔK = K(A_{t+1}) − K(A_t) (change in algorithmic complexity), and mutual information gain I(A_{t+1} : E) − I(A_t : E).
- Resource-bounded (time-bounded) Kolmogorov complexity K^t and resource-bounded mutual information are typically more relevant in practice and obey analogous bounds with extra dependence on time and space.

8. Example scenarios
- Learning from data: A_0 is a weak policy; observing data D incrementally allows the algorithm to encode environment regularities into its code, increasing I(A_t : E) and improving J. The bound in Proposition 1 quantifies that only the new information in D can account for increases in K(A).
- Self-optimization via search: an algorithm that uses compute to search for better subroutines can increase K(A) by discovering and incorporating high-complexity subroutines; the source of that complexity is the result of the search (not magically created).
- Compression-based improvement: an agent finds a shorter program performing the same policy, reducing K(A) while preserving or improving J.

9. Consequences for design and safety
- To enable sustained, provable self-improvement an agent requires (a) adequate streams of informative data, (b) compute/time resources to extract and reencode useful information, and (c) mechanisms to avoid undecidable verification gaps (e.g., relying on empirical validation rather than attempting impossible global optimality proofs).
- Unbounded self-improvement that reliably yields arbitrary performance increases is prevented by information-theoretic limits and by undecidability of global optimization over program space.

10. Summary sentence (tight).
Self-improving algorithms create (re-encode and concentrate) algorithmic information about tasks and environments by transforming incoming data and computational work into more compact or more effective program structure, but any genuine increase in the algorithmic content of the program beyond what was implicit in prior state must be supplied by environment-derived information or by resources (time/space) devoted to search; recursion and self-reference enable hierarchical meta-improvements but do not bypass conservation-like bounds or fundamental computability and provability limits.
